UK inflation is set to have eased last month in a temporary boost for the new Prime Minister ahead of a jump in the household energy price cap.

Official figures for June’s Consumer Prices Index (CPI) will be published on Wednesday, two days after Andy Burnham took the reins and formed a new Cabinet.

Most economists think a sharp drop in petrol and diesel prices will have helped pull the overall inflation rate down to 2.7% in June, from 2.8% in May.

The RAC said the average price of a litre of diesel at UK forecourts dropped by more than 16p from the start to the end of June – the largest fall since records began in 2000.

open image in gallery Ofgem’s energy price cap increased by 13% in July (Andrew Matthews/PA) ( PA Archive )

This was driven by news of an interim ceasefire deal between the US and Iran, prompting oil prices to fall below pre-crisis levels.

Economists are also expecting inflation across the UK’s services industry to have slowed in June, although live music events like Harry Styles and Take That concerts may have pushed prices up in certain places.

Household energy inflation is expected to have taken a step down last month, but economists are viewing this as temporary relief before Ofgem’s new energy price cap took effect at the beginning of July.

The latest cap was up by 13% compared with the previous rates, meaning the typical household’s gas and electricity bill will increase by £221 to £1,862 a year.

Tensions in the Middle East have also flared again and Brent crude oil prices have been rising during July.

Mr Burnham announced on Tuesday that electricity bills will be VAT-free from October 1, saving households about £45 a year as part of the new Prime Minister’s promise to ease cost-of-living pressures.

open image in gallery

Cutting VAT from 5% to 0% is estimated to reduce CPI inflation by around 0.1 percentage points when it comes into effect, according to the Government.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said falling oil prices after the interim ceasefire agreement will be the “main drag on inflation in June”.

“However, oil prices have rebounded in July as tensions escalate which means inflation is still likely to peak at around 3.4% in November,” he said.

He cautioned that food prices could “rebound later this year, as higher energy and fertiliser prices due to the conflict in the Middle East make their way through supply chains”.

Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist for Deutsche Bank, said to expect a “bumpy path” ahead.

“While we’re nowhere close to the peaks seen during the height of the Iran conflict, the energy disinflation path remains uncertain,” he said.

He also warned that food price rises could be on the horizon.

A fifth person has died in a Legionnaires' disease outbreak in New York City, health officials said Tuesday night.

The New York City Health Department said it has confirmed the presence of the bacteria in 34 cooling towers in 33 buildings, all of which are being cleaned. Officials still haven't identified the source of the bacteria that has sickened more than six dozen people in the last month.

No new patients have come forward with symptoms in the last 10 days, the department said in a news release.

Legionnaires’ disease, a form of pneumonia, is treatable but kills about 10% of patients, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It’s caused by Legionella bacteria, which grow in warm water and can spread in such places as hot tubs and building cooling equipment. People may contract the disease by inhaling contaminated water droplets, but it doesn’t spread person-to-person.

Eight people are still hospitalized and 56 others have spent time in but been discharged from hospitals in the Upper East Side outbreak, officials said.

The city is cleaning and disinfecting a total of 82 cooling towers in 80 buildings, they said.

Inspections have shown that some of the tony neighborhood's fancy apartment buildings, private schools and renowned museums had traces of Legionella bacteria in their air-cooling equipment — despite new regulations that upped testing requirements just this spring, and despite a budget boost to hire more inspectors.

Some owners of buildings that tested positive have said they have worked to stay on top of any Legionella threat. The Guggenheim Museum, for instance, said in a statement that an outside company tests and treats the institution’s cooling tower every month.

The situation is avoidable and frustrating, said Jory Lange, a Texas attorney who represents over 50 people who were affected by an outbreak last year that killed seven people and sickened over 100 in New York’s Harlem neighborhood. He’s representing at least three patients who are recovering in the Upper East Side outbreak.

"There’s no excuse for this to keep happening," Lange said. “New York already has the best and strongest regulations … and yet this still keeps happening.”

New York City Health Commissioner Dr. Alister F. Martin said in a statement that the department's quick action after the first two confirmed cases “saved lives.” Martin said the department will learn what happened from the ongoing investigation and update policies and procedures with the goal of preventing future outbreaks.

After the Harlem outbreak, city leaders authorized the Health Department in November to hire 23 more Legionella-focused water ecologists and supervisors, bringing the intended total to 56. The staff currently stands at 35, the department said in a statement Tuesday, noting that another 14 people are in a monthslong process of orientation, training and shadowing veteran inspectors. The department said it's working to fill the final seven positions.

Nevertheless, the agency said it did nearly 1,600 cooling tower inspections in the first six months of the year, 35% more than during the same period in 2025.

A Trump administration push to keep aging Midwest coal plants alive could cost Americans billions of dollars in the coming years, including $117 million in the state of Wisconsin alone, according to the state’s governor.

“Not only are you making energy bills go up for Wisconsinites with no demonstrated need or benefit, but this practice flies in the face of state, local, and utility planning efforts,” Gov. Tony Evers wrote on Monday in a letter to Energy Secretary Chris Wright.

“Rather than needlessly increasing energy bills for American families, U.S. DOE should follow Wisconsin’s lead by refocusing its efforts on accelerating our nation’s transition to a clean energy economy and lowering costs for working families,” he added.

The Independent has contacted the DOE for comment.

The Trump administration has used emergency authorities to prolong the life of the Campbell Power Plant in Michigan and the R.M Schahfer and F.B. Culley plants in Indiana, which are connected to the Wisconsin energy system via a regional grid.

open image in gallery The Trump administration has pushed to extend the life of aging coal-fired power facilities across the country, costing American ratepayers hundreds of millions of dollars ( Peter Burzynski via Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 Unported license )

“This means Wisconsinites will continue to foot the bill to keep these regional plants online despite their age, inefficacy, and, in some cases, their own operating utilities’ plea to allow these expired assets to be shut down,” Evers wrote of the extensions, which the energy department claims are needed to bolster reliability.

The Campbell plant, whose closing has been delayed five times, has now operated more than a year past its originally planned shutdown.

Donald Trump, a climate denier who received support from the coal industry in the 2024 election, has championed coal as part of his larger push to support fossil fuel development and roll back clean energy initiatives.

Environmentalists argue the administration has illegally used emergency powers to extend the life of coal plants across Washington, Colorado, Indiana, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Florida, decisions the Sierra Club estimates have cost Americans more than $405 million so far.

Critics and some of the impacted states have sued to block the plant extensions.

open image in gallery The Trump administration has directed hundreds of millions of dollars to support the coal industry, while moving to slash regulations ( Getty )

“Abusing emergency powers in this way sets a terrible precedent for grid planning,” Ted Kelly, director and lead counsel for U.S. clean energy at Environmental Defense Fund, said of one such effort in May.

In addition to propping up aging coal facilities, the administration has worked to support new ones, announcing $700 million in federal funding in June, part of which will flow to the first new U.S. coal plants in more than a decade. The Trump White House has also opened more than 13 million acres of federal land for leasing by coal companies.

The Trump administration Environmental Protection Agency, meanwhile, has moved to roll back federal oversight of coal ash and wastewater, and it is working to repeal the 2024 updates to the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards regulation and carbon pollution standards.

“Many of the items that were on your wish list are now done,” EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin told members of the National Coal Council on Tuesday. “Over the course of the coming few months, hopefully [we get to] the remainder of those items, although I will not prejudge the outcome of any rule-making.”

The top federal prosecutor in Seattle who was fired last week less than an hour after being sworn in sued over his termination Tuesday, teeing up a legal challenge to the Trump administration's efforts to control who occupies the powerful Justice Department posts.

Roger Rogoff is the latest in a series of judicially appointed U.S. attorneys to be ousted by the Trump administration from their posts but is believed to be the first of that group to sue over the removal. His action creates a first-of-its-kind court case that will test the Justice Department's authority to fire federal prosecutors who are appointed by judges,

Rogoff was unanimously appointed to the job of U.S. attorney for western Washington by the federal judges in the district. But shortly after he was sworn in last Wednesday, he received an email from the Trump administration informing him that President Donald Trump had ordered his termination.

The lawsuit contends that the abrupt firing was unconstitutional and disregarded the authority of the judges of the district to name Rogoff to the job until the vacancy could be filled through a Senate-confirmed nominee. The complaint seeks a court order declaring that the firing “was unlawful and is void” and that Rogoff at least temporarily remains U.S. attorney.

“The President’s actions violate the law, and they ignore the protections of the Constitution of the United States," Rogoff said in a statement issued through the law firm representing him. "His removal of me, like his removal of other court-appointed U.S. attorneys across the country, is illegal and cannot stand."

US attorneys are typically nominated by the president

U.S. attorneys, top federal prosecutors who oversee regional Justice Department outposts across the country, are typically nominated by the president and then confirmed by the Senate.

In the case of a vacancy, attorneys general have the authority to name an interim U.S. attorney who can serve for 120 days, but when those temporary appointments expire, the judges in a judicial district are then empowered to name a U.S. attorney — as happened in Rogoff's case — who can serve until the selection of a Senate-confirmed appointee.

But under Trump, the Justice Department has sought to leave unconfirmed prosecutors in their positions indefinitely or has moved to fire prosecutors appointed by the courts.

The acting attorney general had foreshadowed the firing

Rogoff's district has not had a Senate-confirmed U.S. attorney since 2023. He submitted his name for consideration with the federal bench after the judges last January signaled their intent to fill a vacancy created by the end of the 120-day term of Charles Neil Floyd, who had been named to the job in an interim capacity last year by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi.

Even before Rogoff was appointed, the lawsuit notes, acting Attorney General Todd Blanche foreshadowed his plans to fire whomever the judges selected, writing on X after the court announced its appointment of a merit selection panel that the candidates did not have the president’s support, “and I expect they will suffer the same fate as others have when judges ignore Article II” of the Constitution.

After Rogoff was fired, Blanche posted: “District court judges can appoint a temporary U.S. Attorney, and POTUS can fire them.” Judges from the state’s western district, he said, “abandoned the time-honored process of consultation with the administration so that the selected U.S. Attorney is qualified to serve in the administration. Roger Rogoff has been fired by the President.”

The Justice Department said in a statement Tuesday that “the district court did not coordinate with DOJ on this selection. Consistent with other firings of this type, this is wholly within the President’s authority.”

Other jurisdictions that have seen tussles between the judiciary and the administration over the prosecution posts include New Jersey, where Trump's former personal lawyer, Alina Habba, resigned in December after an appeals court said she had been serving in the post unlawfully.

Lindsey Halligan, another of Trump's personal lawyers who was installed by the administration, left her position as an acting U.S. attorney in Virginia after a judge concluded her appointment was unlawful and that indictments she brought against New York Attorney General Letitia James and former FBI Director James Comey must be dismissed.

News.title: Private sector pay suffers worst growth since Covid
News.content:
Private sector wages are growing at their slowest pace since the pandemic, piling pressure on Andy Burnham as he enters Downing Street facing a fragile economy and strained public finances.

Salaries rose by 2.9pc in the three months to May, the first time growth has dipped below 3pc since October 2020 and only narrowly ahead of inflation at 2.8pc.

The slowdown was most acute in key industries, with wages in finance and business services up just 2.3pc, manufacturing at 2.5pc and construction earnings falling by 0.2pc over the year.

In contrast, public sector pay accelerated to 5.5pc after striking workers secured higher settlements, widening the gap between state and private sectors.

The cooling labour market came as borrowing overshot official forecasts, leaving John Healey, the new Chancellor, with a £2.7bn gap against expectations.

The Government borrowed £57.6bn between April and June – less than a year earlier but still ahead of projections – pushing public debt to nearly £3tn, or 94.9pc of GDP.

Mr Healey said: “The Prime Minister and I have talked about how we will work in lockstep to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty and how we’ll make life more affordable for working people right across the UK.”

However, Sir Mel Stride, the shadow business secretary, said: “If Andy Burnham and John Healey are really serious about the future of our economy then they must get borrowing under control.”

News.title: Scammers stole $114 billion as Southeast Asia’s crime gangs go corporate
News.content:
Scam gangs stole up to $114 billion from people in Asia-Pacific alone in 2025, the UN has warned, as crime syndicates rapidly professionalise their tactics to evade law enforcement in Southeast Asia.

By way of comparison, the sum dwarfs the $85 billion the UK spends each year on defence.

The Asia-Pacific region has emerged as an epicentre for massive cyber fraud operations since the Covid pandemic. Scammers – some willingly, others under duress – are now stealing billions from internet users across the world via fake romance and cryptocurrency investment schemes.

In 2025, these fraud operations stole between $88.3 and $114.1bn from just people across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand, according to a report on Tuesday from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).

Those figures are triple the estimated losses in 2023, between $18 and $37bn, and don’t account for victims in Europe or the US.

The scam centres – which began in fortified compounds but are now increasingly housed in innocuous office blocks and villas – are found across the region, but have especially exploited power vacuums caused by war, corruption and weak governance in Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos.

Although the scammers initially targeted people in China, they have dramatically expanded their ambitions. The UNODC said people from at least 80 countries and territories had been identified in compounds, with recruiters seeking people from outside Asia as they look to expand new markets.

News.title: UK borrowing costs rise at fastest pace in G7
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs rose at the fastest pace in the G7 after Andy Burnham said he would take a “flexible” approach to the UK’s fiscal rules.

In his maiden speech as prime minister, Mr Burnham on Monday signalled he could bend the rules underpinning Britain’s finances, spooking financial markets fearful of higher government spending.

UK gilts – a benchmark for how much the Government pays on its debt – saw yields rise 0.08 percentage points to an eight-week high of 5.03pc for the 10-year bond. Thirty-year gilts also pushed higher.

The rise was the fastest in the G7, excluding Japan, whose markets are closed for a national holiday.

After markets closed on Monday, Mr Burnham surprised the City by picking John Healey as his next Chancellor.

Mr Healey, who quit over defence funding rising too slowly, will now be tasked with finding billions of pounds in Britain’s stretched public finances.

Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, had widely been expected for the role. Ed Miliband, the former Energy Secretary, was also in contention.

Mr Healey will replace Rachel Reeves, who resigned on Monday.

The appointment of Mr Healey, a veteran of the Blair-Brown government, may calm fears in the City after Mr Burnham pledged to stretch the fiscal rules by using “flexibility” within them.

Speaking in Downing Street, Mr Burnham said: “I’ve said we’ll stick to the fiscal rules, and by that I mean the existing fiscal rules, and use obviously any flexibility within them.”

James Athey, a fund manager at Marlborough, said: “It’s not a good start because bandying around the words fiscal rules seems to be believed within government circles to be a sufficient condition to get financial markets on side, and that just misunderstands an element of the problem.”

He added that investors were watching closely for any signs that the Government will increase borrowing.

Matt Amis, investment director at Aberdeen, said Mr Burnham’s comments had “got the markets’ attention.”

He said “It just shows this week in particular the language from the Burnham administration, the new chancellor, is going to be key here. The gilt market is on edge.”

Mr Burnham, who has become the UK’s seventh prime minister in just a decade, has inherited a troubled economy as businesses grapple with low confidence and strained public finances.

Monday’s comment suggests the new prime minister will use measures to raise borrowing while keeping the additional sums off the Government’s book.

The Resolution Foundation, a think tank, said he could do this by expanding the remit of institutions like the National Wealth Fund, an arms-length government investment vehicle.

His plan to use “flexibility” in the fiscal rules comes after Ms Reeves altered the main indicator of government debt in 2024.

She tweaked the primary measure of the UK’s debt to Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities, meaning that when public financial institutions borrow to invest in a private business it does not count towards the government’s fiscal rules.

However, the think tank warned that boosting the financial capacity of public financial institutions like the National Wealth Fund by £16bn would cost around £400 million a year in debt interest.

Helen Miller, director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that challenging public finances will mean Mr Burnham will be forced to make tough choices on spending.

She said: “While chancellors come and go, the underlying fiscal constraints remain the same. Public debt, borrowing and debt-interest costs are all high. One in every £12 the government spends currently goes on debt interest.”

Higher borrowing costs threaten to increase the Government’s debt interest bill, which is already forecast to hit £111.2bn for the financial year - equivalent to 8.3pc of public spending.

Mr Burnham said he would announce a set of measures on Tuesday to give households “breathing space” to help with the cost of living.

“I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them,” he said.

“We will help more young people into education... and we will build more council homes. That is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down, to meet our fiscal rules and to honour our commitments on defence to our international partners.”

Mr Amis said: “Tomorrow we’re getting some cost of living news. [Burnham] said he was going to state where that funding’s come from. I think that’s key, any unfunded spending from here would get the market’s attention.”

News.title: India approves first dengue vaccine as cases surge in South Asia
News.content:
India has approved its first dengue vaccine as cases of the mosquito-borne disease surge in South Asia.

Japan’s Takeda Pharmaceutical’s dengue vaccine QDENGA has been approved by India’s drug regulator, the Centre Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).

The global threat posed by dengue has been rising for years, as climate change, urbanisation and international travel aid the spread of the mosquitoes that transmit it.

The approval comes as hospitals across South Asia grapple with a surge in dengue infections.

In Sri Lanka, health authorities reported 2,652 new cases on Sunday alone, taking the total to 76,044 dengue cases so far this year. At least 53 people have died.

Bangladesh is also suffering a major outbreak with over 9,000 cases and 30 deaths that has piled pressure on its health system even as it battles a measles epidemic.

Dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes.

Its symptoms include fever, severe muscle pain, and in severe cases, shock and internal bleeding that can be fatal.

Although mortality is relatively low, outbreaks place a substantial burden on health systems.

Takeda’s QDENGA jab is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. It can be given regardless of previous dengue infections.

“The approval comes at a critical time for public health, as reported dengue cases in India have increased 11-fold in the past two decades,” the company said in a statement.

News.title: Burnham’s plan to restore UK aid spending
News.content:
Andy Burnham is planning to reverse the cuts to Britain’s aid budget made by his predecessors Sir Keir Starmer and Rishi Sunak, according to reports.

A roadmap for returning the UK to spending 0.7 per cent of Gross National Income (GNI) on international aid will be drawn up as part of a major shake-up of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), The Independent reported.

Ed Miliband is set to be named Foreign Secretary and put in charge of overhauling Britain’s international development aims, as well as prioritising climate goals, senior Labour sources said.

The aid spending plan was absent from Mr Burnham’s brief first speech as Prime Minister, in which he pledged to end rough sleeping and bring down the welfare bill in order to fund defence and council housing.

But it follows anger within the Labour Party over what was seen as a broken manifesto promise, when Sir Keir and Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor, slashed aid spending to 0.3 per cent of GNI.

Senior Labour MPs have been lobbying for a return to the 0.7 per cent commitment, a target first established by the United Nations in the 1970s.

It has since become a key yardstick for international efforts to reduce poverty and tackle major health issues like the HIV/AIDS epidemic, vaccine access, and maternal mortality in poor countries.

News.title: The best bars and nightlife in Lyon
News.content:
While drinking in this gourmet city remains firmly rooted in the surrounding Rhône Valley’s ancient wine-growing heritage, new-gen addresses have embraced world cocktail culture in style. They’re using Lyon’s long-envied gastronomic know-how and rich bounty of local seasonal produce to create some sensational new drinks and food pairings as only the French can. Artisanal spirits meanwhile are increasingly fashionable: cornichon gin, Mezcal-fuelled soirées at chef Carla Kirsch’s gourmet tacos joint in Croix-Rousse, and the stunning Christian Drouin gin and pine-needle liqueur cocktail with stick of Comté cheese to stir I recently had at Hôtel Dieu’s Le Dôme bar all spring to mind.

Come the warmer days of spring and summer, the city’s fervent café-life spills onto pretty pavement terraces, while floating bars moored along Les Berges du Rhône (the landscaped river banks of the Rhône’s Rive Gauche or Left Bank) hum with after-dark dance parties and festivities. Clubbing remains fairly mainstream.

Sports.title: Alejandro Garnacho set to swap places with Morgan Rogers as Aston Villa eye swoop
Sports.content:
Alejandro Garnacho set to swap places with Morgan Rogers as Aston Villa eye swoop

Chelsea have completed a £117m deal for Aston Villa and England star Morgan Rogers with former Manchester United man Alejandro Garnacho expected to go the other way to the Midlands

View 2 Images Chelsea are happy to let Garnacho leave (Image: Getty Images)

Chelsea are set to get their wish for Alejandro Garnacho, with Aston Villa interested in signing the forward. The Blues only signed the Argentine frontman from Manchester United last summer in a £40m deal.

‌



But with Chelsea completing a £117m move for Villa and England star Morgan Rogers, the Blues are now happy to cut Garnacho adrift.

‌



Villa have already submitted a loan offer for him, with a conditional buy obligation attached and are close to finding an agreement. Chelsea initially wanted a permanent deal for the Argentine.

‌



Unai Emery is thought to be a big fan of Garnacho and is hoping to play a role in a career revival. Villa’s interest comes just days after new boss Xabi Alonso admitted that he was happy to let the forward leave.

He said: "Well the situation is that we have spoken with the sporting directors. There is an interest for him [Garnacho] from other clubs. So let's see how this develops. But hopefully, it finishes in the best possible way for other clubs."

West Ham strike £68m deal to sell Crysencio Summerville amid Man Utd interest READ MORE :

Man City to sign youngster from under Arsenal's noses after contract rejection READ MORE :

Garnacho, 22, signed a seven-year deal with Chelsea last summer following his arrival from Old Trafford. He made 43 appearances across his debut season, scoring just eight goals, only one of which came in the Premier League.

‌



Garnacho would arrive at Villa as Rogers’ replacement following his own move to Chelsea. The former Middlesbrough man scored 14 times last term but Paul Merson is not convinced his move to West London is the right one.

He said: “It's a lot of money. Crazy money. Bringing Morgan Rogers in for £117m isn't what Chelsea needed.

“They've got Cole Palmer! They play in the same position! Rogers went to the World Cup instead of Palmer, because they play in the same position.

‌



View 2 Images Garnacho only joined Chelsea last summer (Image: Getty Images)

“Unless Chelsea go for the almighty and sell Enzo Fernandez - and swallow the pill for him, because he's not worth £100m - and then play Moises Caicedo at the base, then Rogers and Palmer both ahead of him.”

He continued: “Rogers has got to carry that price tag around with him. He will sit there and say: 'there is no pressure on me, I didn't pay that fee'. But it's a load of rubbish. Everybody will look at that when you don't do well.

‌



“A lot of people were saying it was too much for Declan Rice and Moises Caicedo when they moved for £100m. But the biggest compliment I can give them is nobody ever mentions it. They were good signings. That's what Rogers has got to hope for.

“But he's got to make things happen, which is a harder position to be in than Rice and Caicedo were. In midfield, you can do this and that - but Rogers will be judged on scoring and creating goals. That's the hardest job in the world.

“I'm also sure that at the start of last season, he was atrocious for Aston Villa. I'm sure he was. Then he came good and then had a good second part of the season.

Sports.title: Morgan Rogers completes record-breaking £117m transfer to Chelsea
Sports.content:
Morgan Rogers completes record-breaking £117m transfer to Chelsea

Chelsea have completed the capture of Morgan Rogers after beating Arsenal to a whopping £117million deal for one of England's World Cup stars

View 2 Images Rogers has put pen to paper on a seven-year deal at Stamford Bridge (Image: Chelsea FC via Getty Images)

Morgan Rogers is officially a Chelsea player after finalising a transfer from Aston Villa which makes him the most expensive British footballer in history.

‌



The England star, 23, has put pen to paper on a contract until 2033 which includes an option for a further year. He moves to Stamford Bridge for a seismic £117million transfer fee, a figure which eclipses the amount Manchester City agreed to part with in order to acquire his World Cup team-mate, Elliot Anderson.

‌



Rogers was pursued for over two years by Chelsea, who beat off competition from Arsenal to sign the versatile attacking midfielder.

‌



Chelsea stole a march on Arsenal when the Gunners were unwilling to move from their valuation of the player, Mirror Football understands.

According to sources, the Gunners valued the England international at £80m, and were willing to pay a slight premium - but were left stunned when Chelsea agreed to pay a fee that makes Rogers' move the most expensive transfer of an Englishman in history - beating Anderson's move from Nottingham Forest to Manchester City by £1m.

His capture is a first major win for the Blues' new manager, Xabi Alonso, who held productive talks with Rogers to help entice the former Middlesbrough man to west London.

‌



Upon finalising his move, Rogers said: "I'm so excited. For me, Chelsea are the biggest club in London and a club I've always admired since I was a kid.

"I'm really excited about the project with the new manager, the players we've got and where the club is heading. That's why I'm here and I can't wait to get started.

“I’ve had a few conversations with him [Alonso] and I think it’s important for me to be here that I need to understand what the manager’s like, how he is and how he wants to operate.

‌



“It very much fits with the way I see the game, the way I want to play, and the way I want to be me, and be free and express myself. Him being a part of that was a massive factor in me being here.”

View 2 Images Rogers with new boss Xabi Alonso (Image: Chelsea FC via Getty Images)

Rogers came through the youth academy at West Brom before moving to Man City in 2019. He didn't make a first-team appearance for City and went out on loan to Lincoln, Bournemouth and Blackpool.

‌



He joined Middlesbrough for an undisclosed fee in 2023 scoring five times in their run to the League Cup semi-finals. He joined Villa in the following January for £8m, potentially rising to £15m.

In all, Rogers made 125 appearances for Villa scoring 31 goals and helping them to the Europa League title last term.

On the international stage, Rogers made his senior England debut in November 2004 in a 3-0 victory against Greece in Athens. He has played 22 times for England, including at the recent World Cup, scoring once.

Man City to sign youngster from under Arsenal's noses after contract rejection READ MORE :

Speaking earlier this month, Lille chairman Oliver Letang hinted at the price he wants. “When I see [Elliot] Anderson move to Manchester City for £116 million and [Sandro] Tonali to Tottenham for £100 million, and they don’t have the potential for development that Ayyoub has because he possesses unique qualities.

“I have a price in mind, and we’ll see what happens."

According to journalist Nicolo Schira, City have agreed a contract with the teenager that runs until 2031. The club will now continue talks with Lille to try and reach a club-to-club agreement over the transfer fee.

‌



It’s added that City expect two other ‘top European clubs’ to make a move, although it’s not said who those clubs are. Arsenal and United are two other clubs who have been heavily linked with an interest.

View 2 Images Ayyoub Bouaddi impressed for Morocco at this summer's World Cup (Image: Sathire Kelpa/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty Images)

Reports suggest that City see Bouaddi as someone who can go straight into Enzo Maresca’s starting line-up , despite the £116 million signing of England star Anderson earlier in the window. That may have given them the edge over some of their rivals.

‌



Former France international Emmanuel Petit has been full of praise about Bouaddi. "He's been one of the strongest young players in France,” he told talkSPORT

"We've seen that against Brazil. He's shown maturity and personality.

"I'm not surprised at all that he's been targeted for two seasons now with the big clubs in Europe, and it will be a fierce battle to get him."

Sports.title: West Ham strike £68m deal to sell Crysencio Summerville amid Man Utd interest
Sports.content:
West Ham strike £68m deal to sell Crysencio Summerville amid Man Utd interest

Manchester United were among the clubs linked with a move for West Ham winger Crysencio Summerville but it appears that the Dutchman is set to move elsewhere

View 2 Images Summerville is set to leave West Ham after two years (Image: Getty Images)

Manchester United are set to lose out on Crysencio Summerville, with the West Ham star on the verge of a move to Saudi Arabia. The Red Devils were linked with a swoop for the Dutchman this summer, following the Hammers’ relegation from the Premier League.

‌



They were interested in him alongside Mateus Fernandes, who eventually completed a big-money move to Tottenham Hotspur. But United are also set to be frustrated in their pursuit of the former Leeds man.

‌



The Londoners have agreed a £68m deal with Saudi Arabian side Al-Hilal. Italian giants Roma were also interested but were only willing to offer around £39m.

‌



Summerville, who scored five Premier League goals last term, is now expected to undergo a medical ahead of completing his switch to the Middle East. West Ham in the meantime will aim to re-invest the considerable fee as they attempt to earn promotion from the Championship at the first time of asking.

The only signing that the Hammers have made so far is a deal for Venezuelan international Keiber Lamadrid. But one considerable boost has been Jarrod Bowen’s decision to commit his future to the club.

FSG confirm Liverpool sale talks as billionaire family eyes deal after resignation READ MORE :

Man City to sign youngster from under Arsenal's noses after contract rejection READ MORE :

Speaking at the time, he said: "My main motivation is staying and bringing this club back to the Premier League where we belong. It was only right for me to speak at the right time. Ultimately it [relegation] hurt everyone and it should hurt everyone.

‌



"I flew out to Prague to meet (club directors) Daniel [Kretinsky] and Jiri [Svarc] and the ambition that I got from them, certainly in terms of the direction the club wants to move in, it interests me a lot. It didn't take a lot, because this club means a lot to me.

"For me, when you're here for a longer amount of time, you gain more affection, you grow into the club more, you grow into your role more and more, and I think that's what I've done.

View 2 Images Crysencio Summerville is expected to move to Saudi Arabia (Image: Getty Images)

‌



"I've been here six and a half years and transitioned from a boy to a man and I've never tried to hide away from anything.

"There are things you can do better, but certainly in my character on the pitch and off the pitch, I never try and hide away from anything and shift the blame.

"I always try and stand up for them and just kind of live my life as captain of West Ham and also as a fan as well.

Article continues below

"I see myself in years to come as a West Ham fan. So, I always think 'what would they want as a fan if they got the opportunity to play on the pitch?'. For me, I think I'm like that character as well, so I think that's the way."

Sports.title: Sepp Blatter blasts FIFA and Gianni Infantino and says World Cup 'lost its credibility'
Sports.content:
Sepp Blatter blasts FIFA and Gianni Infantino and says World Cup 'lost its credibility'

FIFA president Gianni Infantino has faced severe criticism during the World Cup for his close relationship with US President Donald Trump with controversial former chief Sepp Blatter among those to speak out

View 2 Images Sepp Blatter has taken a fresh swipe at Gianni Infantino (Image: Getty Images)

Sepp Blatter has once again called for ‘new leadership’ at FIFA in a brutal dig at Gianni Infantino. The current president has faced serious criticism for a number of decisions throughout this summer’s World Cup.

‌



Ticket prices, over-commercialisation, as well as his close relationship with US President Donald Trump have all been issues. Criticism then sharply increased after the decision to suspend Folarin Balogun’s red card following a phone call from Trump.

‌



Blatter tore into Infantino immediately after that decision. Taking to Twitter, he said: “Red cards are not overturned by political phone calls. They are overturned by rules, evidence and independent bodies.

‌



"If a U.S. President intervenes with the FIFA President — and a player is suddenly cleared before a World Cup knockout match — the question is unavoidable: Quo vadis, FIFA? Quo vadis means 'Where are you going?' in Latin. Football must never become a playground for political power.”

Blatter has now doubled down with a fresh post calling for change right at the top of the organisation just days after the World Cup final.

Lionel Messi sparks conspiracy theories as footage from World Cup final speech leaked READ MORE :

He said: “The longest World Cup has come to an end - with the right champions. But on the way to the final whistle, the tournament had lost its credibility. Politics must not be allowed to overshadow the game. Now it is up to the fans, players and national associations to reclaim football and bring it back to its roots under new leadership.”

‌



While Blatter has called for fresh leadership, it appears that is unlikely. La Liga president Javier Tebas has claimed that due to a lack of opposition, it appears that Infantino is set to stay in charge.

Asked if he should quit, Tebas replied: "In my opinion, yes, I think his time is up." He added: "There's no opposition candidate, nobody wants to stand just to lose. He shouldn't stay, but the current state of affairs means he won't leave.

View 2 Images Gianni Infantino has faced plenty of criticism throughout the World Cup (Image: Getty Images)

‌



"These past few days here in America, I've heard many people who are against Infantino, who disagree with what he's doing,

"They say it, but then they do nothing. I don't know what's worse, the silence or the complicity, because those who stay silent are perfectly aware of the damage football is suffering.

"The suspension of the American player's ban was absolutely serious. They were lucky that Belgium eliminated the USA, because otherwise a case could have arisen that might have cost Infantino his job. Since Belgium won, they managed to bury the matter. But these things are just the tip of the iceberg."

Sports.title: FSG confirm Liverpool sale talks as billionaire family eyes deal after resignation
Sports.content:
FSG confirm Liverpool sale talks as billionaire family eyes deal after resignation

Fenway Sports Group have confirmed that a consortium of investors, led by British-Indian businessman Amit Bhatia, have approached them about a significant minority stake in Liverpool

View 2 Images FSG are in talks over selling a minority stake in Liverpool (Image: Getty Images)

Liverpool's owners have confirmed that a consortium of investors, spearheaded by British-Indian businessman Amit Bhatia, have made an approach regarding a stake in the club. It is understood the group has the backing of the Mittal family, whose fortune was most recently estimated at more than £26billion by Forbes.

‌



No deal is currently in place and discussions remain at a preliminary stage, according to sources with knowledge of the situation. Bhatia was confirmed on Tuesday to have stepped down from his role as co-owner of Queens Park Rangers, with the London outfit announcing his exit on its official website.

‌



Bhatia is the son-in-law of Lakshmi Mittal, who heads up ArcelorMittal, the globe's biggest steel and mining firm, and Fenway Sports Group confirmed that active talks are underway over what has been characterised as a "significant minority stake".

‌



Kevin Keegan's final picture and brave public appearance before sad death aged 75 READ MORE :

Our sister title the Liverpool ECHO understand the discussions are being treated as comparable to the deal struck with Dynasty Equity in 2023, which was valued at between £82m and £164m. An FSG statement provided to the ECHO said: "An investment consortium led, managed and represented by Amit Bhatia has expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment in Liverpool Football Club."

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Mr Bhatia has thus far refused to comment on the developments but made public his decision to resign from QPR on Tuesday, having joined the club at Loftus Road almost two decades ago. Bhatia said: "Since joining the club in 2007, QPR has been a deeply important part of my life, and of my family's life. Over nearly two decades we have shared promotions, relegations, unforgettable highs and painful lows, and the memories we have made at Loftus Road alongside the supporters will stay with us forever.

‌



View 2 Images Amit Bhatia could soon have a stake in Liverpool (Image: Andrew Fosker/REX/Shutterstock)

"Being part of QPR has shaped me in many ways. It has taught me about resilience, responsibility and the importance of stewardship. I am especially proud of the work of QPR in the Community Trust, which reflects the best of the club and the extraordinary role it plays in the local community.

"I step back from my formal responsibilities with pride, gratitude and affection. I want to thank the players, managers, staff, the Community Trust, my fellow board members and, above all, the fans, who have made me and my family feel part of the QPR family for so many years.

‌



"I am grateful to my dear friend Ruben and his family for their friendship and partnership, as I am to Richard, Lee, Christian and everyone continuing to work on behalf of the club. QPR will always have a very special place in my heart."

FSG snapped up Liverpool for £300m back in October 2010. More than 15 years on, the 20-time Premier League champions have been valued at £5.2 billion by the prestigious American financial publication Forbes.

Earlier this year, the club recorded revenues exceeding £700m for the first time in their history.

Article continues below

In 2024, Fenway began exploring the possibility of establishing a multi-club ownership model, but have since put those plans on ice — a move that ultimately contributed to the departure of Michael Edwards, Liverpool's former sporting director, who had been appointed as FSG's CEO of football two years ago.

Sports.title: Hearts suffer chastening CL defeat in nightmare first game for Vrancken
Sports.content:
New Hearts head coach Wouter Vrancken endured a nightmare debut as his side's Champions League hopes all but vanished with a 4-0 defeat against Sturm Graz.

Hearts lost set-piece goals in the early stages of each half and conceded twice more during a torrid spell before the hour mark.

The visitors missed two excellent chances and played some good football in the first half but they are left with a mountain to climb ahead of next Tuesday's second qualifying round second leg at Tynecastle.

Hearts look almost certain to drop into the Europa League, where they would face Benfica or Swiss side St Gallen, with the winners of this tie facing Fenerbahce or Gornik Zabrze.

Vrancken passed up the chance of guaranteed Europa League football with Sint-Truiden to replace Derek McInnes at Tynecastle with key players Lawrence Shankland and Cammy Devlin following the manager to Rangers.

The Belgian named two debutants in his starting line-up, wide player Calvin Miller and centre-back Malachi Fagan-Walcott, while Jamie McCart was preferred to Stuart Findlay, one of Hearts' key players last season, in central defence.

Hearts also changed set-piece coaches in the summer with Liam Ross coming in for Ross Grant following his move to Celtic.

Set-plays were one of the team's strengths in their unlikely title challenge but they looked vulnerable from dead balls throughout.

Despite a promising start which saw Harry Milne force a save, Hearts conceded inside four minutes from a long throw. Jon Gorenc Stankovic ran away from his marker and outjumped McCart to head home.

Graz attacker Seedy Jatta headed off the post following a corner and Alexander Schwolow, who was selected despite sealing an imminent move to Mainz, saved an effort with his feet.

Hearts improved. Claudio Braga forced a save with a decent effort before Landry Kabore shot straight at the goalkeeper from 10 yards after a good run from Oisin McEntee. Alexandros Kyziridis soon missed an even better chance when he flicked the ball wide after good work from Braga.

The referee handed the Austrians a penalty for an extremely harsh handball decision against Milne before reversing the award following a look at his VAR monitor.

Graz dominated the opening stages of the second half and Jeyland Mitchell nodded home from close range after a 50th-minute corner. Schwolow seemed more concerned with pushing away an attacker than dealing with the inswinger, Kabore misjudged the flight and Mitchell shook off the attention of Braga.

Luca Weinhandl fired the third in off Milne three minutes later after the Hearts defence missed several chances to make a decisive challenge.

Schwolow stood motionless as Emran Soglo curled the ball off the inside of the far post and Jurgen Heil fired a shot through the goalkeeper at his near post after getting ample time and space to convert a return pass in the 59th minute.

Graz seemed to settle for four and Hearts could not get a lifeline.

McEntee made a mess of a free header, McCart failed to trouble the goalkeeper from a string of headed chances and Tom Renaud twice fired over from 22 yards.

Sports.title: Draper misses out on US Open main draw - will have to qualify
Sports.content:
Former British No 1 Jack Draper is set to have to qualify for the US Open this year as the 2024 semi-finalist missed out on a spot in the main draw.

Draper is poised to return to action at the DC Open in Washington from July 27 after missing Wimbledon due to a recurrence of bone bruising in his left arm.

The injury was the latest blow for the 24-year-old, who has managed only a handful of tournaments since first stepping away from the tour a year ago with the same issue.

Draper's ranking has taken a hit as a result, dropping down to 147th in the world, resulting in him having to likely qualify in order to play the fourth and final Grand Slam of the season.

Arthur Fery, the new British men's No 1, will feature at Flushing Meadows for the first time in his career after his remarkable run to the Wimbledon semi-finals as a wild card has seen his ranking soar to 36th in the world.

Both he and Emma Raducanu, the 2021 US Open champion, are just outside of the top 32 seeds, however, with Raducanu ranked 37th.

Image: Emma Raducanu is ranked 37th in the world, just outside of one of the top 32 seeds

They're joined by fellow British hopefuls Cam Norrie, Jan Choinski and Katie Boulter in the main draw for when the tournament gets under way on August 30 - live on Sky Sports.

Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka and Wimbledon winner Jannik Sinner will lead the fields for the respective women's and men's singles in New York.

Sabalenka will look to become the first woman to win three straight US Open titles since Serena Williams from 2012-14, while Sinner will be trying to regain the title that Carlos Alcaraz took from the 2024 champion when they met in last year's final.

Image: Jannik Sinner retained his Wimbledon men's singles title earlier this month

The top-ranked Italian is coming off his fifth major championship, after beating French Open winner Alexander Zverev in the Wimbledon final.

Alcaraz, who has missed the last two majors because of a wrist injury but hopes to return during the North American hard-court swing, is ranked as the third seed and entered in the field.

Sports.title: 'Rock star' Woad excited to return to scene of stunning pro debut win
Sports.content:
Lottie Woad returns to the scene of her stunning debut win as a professional this week when looking to defend the ISPS Handa Women's Scottish Open.

Last year, the then 21-year-old took a two-shot lead into the final day at Dundonald Links, managing to hold off Hyo Joo Kim and the chasing pack to take the title.

In doing so, Woad became just the third player in LPGA Tour history to win on her first professional start, following on from Rose Zhang in 2023 and Beverly Hanson in 1951.

"I didn't appreciate at the time, obviously being my first event," Woad said ahead of her return this week - the Scottish Open, live on Sky Sports Golf from 9.30am on Thursday.

"I didn't know what to expect. But now I've been playing every week and playing with the same people and obviously seeing how good everyone is, it definitely feels more special now.

"Very excited to be back. It's a little different to last year, I've got the family here as well. It will be a fun week."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lottie Woad reflected on her first LPGA Tour victory on her professional debut at the Scottish Open.

Woad's triumph in 2025 was exactly as she describes it, special, seeing her deliver immediately in the pro ranks on her long-touted talent that shone as an amateur.

Her name first floated onto the radar in May 2022 when making her debut on the Ladies European Tour in a 10th-placed finish at the Madrid Open, before she enrolled at Florida State where she would become WGCA Freshman of the Year, a junior FSU Female Athlete of the Year and ACC Golfer of the Year.

She continued her rise in April 2024 by winning the Augusta National Women's Amateur, while she'd later claim the No 1 spot in the World Amateur Golf Rankings and became the first English woman to win the Mark H. McCormack Medal as the leading amateur in the world.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from day two of the Amundi Evian Championship as Lottie Woad topped the leaderboard.

She was the leading amateur when she finished tied-10th at the 2024 AIG Women's Open, while her Scottish Open triumph last year followed a maiden LET victory at the KPMG Women's Irish Open and a narrow miss at making history as an amateur at the Amundi Evian Championship.

That tied-third finish has since been followed by further major top-10s at the 2025 Women's Open (eighth) and 2026 Chevron Championship (seventh), while she held the halfway lead at the 2026 Evian Championship two weeks ago before fading to a tied-16th finish.

The 22-year-old already sits a remarkable fifth in the Rolex Women's World Rankings, registering a second LPGA Tour win at the Kroger Queen City Championship in May.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the final round of the Queen City Championship, where Lottie Woad won her second LPGA Tour title.

"It's definitely been a long year," Woad reflected. "I've played a lot of golf, had a lot of new experiences.

"I've definitely learned some things as well in the year.

"It's nice to come back to where I guess it all started, my pro debut here. I've been happy with how I've been playing.

"At Evian, it wasn't the weekend I wanted there. But I'm trying to take what I can from that, still playing good golf but also learning too."

During Woad's Scottish Open victory last year that kick-started her pro career, she was grouped with world No 1 Nelly Korda.

"She's not afraid to compete against the biggest names in the game," Sky Sports Golf's Dame Laura Davies said at the time. "She has every part of her game, and her results already suggest she has all the qualities to become a rockstar of the future."

And 'rock star' Woad could well be the headline act this time round as she's again grouped with Korda and Hull for the opening two rounds of her title defence at Dundonald Links.

Not that the modest Woad sees it that way.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of Nelly Korda's US Women's Open win after a thrilling final round.

Speaking on Korda, who has doubled her career major tally to four with wins at the Chevron and US Women's Open this year, Woad said: "I think every event she's at, she's the person everybody is coming to see. She's No 1 in the world.

"Last year I was playing with her and we got a really big crowd. Playing with her again this year so I expect it to be the same.

"I hope it goes same as last year."

Sports.title: Curran, Pooran blast defending champs MI London past SunRisers in Hundred opener
Sports.content:
MI London began their pursuit of a fourth successive Hundred title with a commanding seven-wicket victory over SunRisers Leeds at The Kia Oval, as the new-look competition got under way.

The 2026 edition of The Hundred had a different feel to it with name and kit changes following heavy overseas investment but MI London, formerly known as Oval Invincibles, ensured some things remained constant.

Chasing 144 for an opening-night victory, Sam Curran (60no off 39) and Nicholas Pooran (58no off 22) produced a blistering 93-run fourth-wicket partnership as the defending champions weathered the early loss of Will Jacks and Jason Roy to cruise to victory with 16 balls to spare.

Score summary – MI London Women vs SunRisers Leeds Men Sunrisers Leeds 143 from 99 balls: Mitchell Marsh (41 off 27), Ryan Rickelton (25 off 16), Tom Alsop (31 off 18); Richard Gleeson (4-25), Sam Curran (2-27) MI London 144-3 from 84 balls: Sam Curran (60no off 39), Nicholas Pooran (58no off 22); Brydon Carse (2-18); Nathan Ellis (1-22)

SunRisers, who appeared in last year's competition under the Northern Superchargers name, had earlier been bowled out for 143 runs in 99 balls, with the big-hitting Mitchell Marsh (41 off 27) and Ryan Rickleton (25 off 16) top scoring before Richard Gleeson (4-25) ripped through the order.

Rickelton blasted three sixes as he put on 40 for the first wicket alongside Marsh before he was brilliantly trapped lbw by a trademark Sam Curran slower ball.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Six and out for Harry Brook! The England captain falls after scoring just eight runs for the SunRisers against MI London in The Hundred.

His replacement, England white-ball captain Harry Brook, lasted just seven balls, holing out to Rashid Khan on eight the ball after smashing Nathan Sowter for six.

Marsh steadied, striking three fours and three sixes before being undone by the Curran brothers, chipping a slower ball from Tom into the hands of Sam at cover.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Curran combo! Tom's 'beauty' of a delivery is rewarded with catch by his brother Sam.

With captain Zak Crawley (13 off 11) unable to kick the SunRisers into gear, it was left to Tom Alsop's 31 off 18 balls to help post a respectable total before Gleeson removed Nathan Ellis to wrap up their innings with a ball to spare.

Carse removed Jacks and Roy with the sixth and eighth balls of his opening spell as MI London suffered an early wobble in their run chase.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Outrageous! Abrar Ahmed hits Richard Gleeson's hat-trick ball for a massive six!

But after James Vince was bowled by Ellis, Pooran and Curran steadied the ship with a rapid-fire 50-run stand from 23 balls.

Curran brought up his fifty in 34 balls before Pooran reached his in 19, as the pair shared 10 fours and eight sixes to propel MI London to victory with plenty in reserve.

Captain Curran: I can read the game well

MI London captain Sam Curran:

"I did a little bit last year trying to work on things and it helps that I have captained for Surrey in the Blast and in the ILT20.

"I feel I can read the game quite well and that I can anchor run chases. I think I read the game well as I bowl.

"But I don't feel like a captain as there are so many good voices. I have so many great brains around and it is nice to start a tournament well."

Pooran: We just tried to stay positive

Meerkat Match Hero, Nicholas Pooran:

"I came in and did exactly what I needed to do.

"We just tried to stay as positive as we could. It was all about hitting a few boundaries and trying to take the partnership all the way to the end.

"Scoring runs gives you confidence but winning games is more important to me and I am happy we got off to the right start at home."

What's next?

Wednesday's Hundred double-header comes from the Utilita Bowl in Southampton as Southern Brave take on Welsh Fire. The women's game starts at 2.45pm, with the men's match under way from 6.30pm. Catch both fixtures live on Sky Sports.

Sports.title: Broad: England Test job less attractive than it was
Sports.content:
Former England bowler Stuart Broad says he understands Andy Flower's decision to turn down the England Test job, and is unsure over who the ECB turn to next, pondering whether the role has become "less attractive".

Brendon McCullum was removed as England's Test head coach after a run of seven defeats in nine and Flower, who led the team to victory in the three Ashes series during his previous spell in charge between 2009 and 2014, quickly emerged as the favourite to replace him.

But Flower cited his current coaching commitments with Indian Premier League franchise Royal Challengers Bengaluru, as well as The Hundred's London Spirit - which would overlap with the English cricket season - as a reason to rule himself out of contention.

Image: Andy Flower was previously coach of Trent Rockets in The Hundred but will be in charge of London Sprit for the 2026 tournament

"Andy Flower is one of the best coaches in the world," Broad told Sky Sports News. "He's done brilliantly with RCB to win back-to-back IPL titles. And he's now gone to the London Spirit from the Trent Rockets.

"I support his decision, really. He's got a very comfortable, steady job at the moment. He's got two brilliant franchises that he works with consistently and he's growing something very special.

"Would he want to leave that for the pressures of and the unknown of the ECB and the Test match job at the moment? Probably not."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Nasser Hussain and Michael Atherton discuss who they think should replace Brendon McCullum as the England Test head coach.

Broad added: "Five, 10 years ago, this was a very sought-after job. I think with the franchise world that surrounds cricket at the moment, it's less attractive.

"But it's still attractive to the right person, and there will be people keen to do that job."

Justin Langer, Darren Lehmann and Jonathan Trott are some of the other names to have been linked with the England Test job.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Southern Brave and Australia all-rounder Marcus Stoinis says Justin Langer's work ethic would make him a good choice if selected to be England's next men's Test head coach.

Broad has "absolutely no idea" who the ECB turn to next, but warned that the "grass isn't always greener" as they look to replace McCullum.

"I saw a very positive side to Brendon McCullum," Broad said. "I'm not saying that results were acceptable at all, in the last year really.

"But unless you get someone better than McCullum, then it's a poor decision. So I'm very interested to see what's coming.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player James Cole breaks down Brendon McCullum's departure from his role as England Test coach and looks into why 'something had to give' for the ECB.

"I don't know who's on their shortlist. I heard [ECB chief executive] Richard Gould talk about succession planning, that they have six to 10 names for every role.

"I don't know how true that can be if the first guy you go to says 'no, I'm not interested.'"

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Stuart Broad's reaction to news that Jacob Bethell will miss The Hundred due to a knee injury he picked up on England duty in the ODI series with India.

'Difficult for Brook to captain in all three formats'

England also have to name a replacement Test captain following Ben Stokes' retirement during the series-ending Test defeat to New Zealand at Trent Bridge in June.

Harry Brook was Stokes' vice-captain and is currently in charge of the white-ball sides, leading to workload concerns if he were to also take the Test job - along with how the move would look after Brook was disciplined during the winter following an altercation with a nightclub bouncer in New Zealand the day before captaining an ODI.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Harry Brook pays tribute to Ben Stokes following his retirement from international cricket and insists that he is up to the challenge of becoming the next England Test captain.

"I think [captaining] three formats is difficult depending on how long you do it," Broad said. "Ultimately, he's one of our best players, so you want him fulfilling his potential with the bat.

"He's done a brilliant job with the T20 side, particularly, and the question will be whether he wants to give that away with T20 World Cups that come around every couple of years?

"He's also got a 50-over World Cup next October in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, in what will feel like English conditions and will suit them.

"Does he want to give that away to then focus on the Test match job, which brings its own challenges and pressures? There's definitely more pressure in the Test match job than there is in white ball.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Eoin Morgan and Michael Atherton debate what the next steps are for England cricket after Ben Stokes' retirement.

"It's a really interesting call for [director of men's cricket] Rob Key. There's a lot on his shoulders at the minute.

"It's been a disastrous start to the summer from his and England's point of view after the so-called reset [following the 4-1 Ashes defeat in the winter].

"Really big decisions coming their way, and Harry Brook will probably have a decision to make at some stage."

Sports.title: Stokes scores century in first match for Durham after England retirement
Sports.content:
Former England captain Ben Stokes hit a match-winning hundred in his first appearance for Durham following his international retirement.

Stokes struck an unbeaten 108 off 123 balls, hitting 10 boundaries and three sixes, and suffered from cramp at the back end of his innings as Durham chased down 257 to beat Derbyshire by five wickets in the Metro Bank One-Day Cup.

It was Stokes' 10th List A century, and first for Durham since 2014, coming less than a month after he announced his retirement from England duty during the series-ending Test defeat to New Zealand at Trent Bridge.

Martin Andersson has top-scored for Derbyshire with 112 in their total of 256-9 after electing to bat first, Stokes (0-38) going wicketless from his nine overs with the ball.

He then arrived at the crease with Durham in trouble at 24-2 in the ninth over of their reply, but 50 stands with each of Will Rhodes (45), Colin Ackermann (28) and Ollie Robinson (23) helped push Durham towards their victory target.

When Stokes edged Nick Potts for four to reach his half century, he subsequently received treatment on his left leg, with Durham later confirming the issue was cramp.

Although restricted, Stokes smacked his former England team-mate Shoaib Bashir (1-56) for two sixes on his way through to a 116-ball hundred, with victory secured off the first ball of the final over of the match.

Sports.title: Could the World Cup be back in the US as soon as 2038? Absolutely
Sports.content:
As is often the case, it has been left to Donald Trump to say the quiet bit out loud. “We have to do this again and we have to do it while I’m around, you hear that Gianni?” the US president told Fox News in an interview broadcast in the buildup to the World Cup final.

An American bid for the 2038 World Cup has been the talk of the hotel lobbies populated by administrators from around the world over the past month, who have watched this country’s seemingly limitless appetite for major events and willingness to pay whatever it takes to attend them.

Fifa has been quietly, but actively encouraging a US bid for some time and in a meeting at the Waldorf Astoria on Park Avenue in New York on Saturday it became clearer why.

The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, told representatives of the governing body’s 211 member associations that its revenue projections for the current four-year cycle has increased from $11bn (£8.2bn) to $15bn, with the vast majority of the growth coming from an explosion in ticketing and hospitality revenue.

A Fifa source disclosed that such has been the demand in the US in particular that ticketing and hospitality sales have gone past $5bn, with that part of the market now worth more than the World Cup’s TV rights for the first time.

“Fifa will want to get back here as quickly as possible,” said a senior figure at one of its hospitality partners.

While ticket sales have exceeded expectations, helped by the dynamic pricing and secondary market resale models that are embedded in US culture, in one crucial respect Fifa left a huge amount of money on the table, another reason it is desperate to return.

In an extraordinary deal, Fox Sports was awarded English-language TV rights in the US by Fifa without a bidding process, a precautionary move by the world governing body to prevent a lawsuit when Qatar 2022 was moved to the winter after the TV contracts had already been signed, creating a direct clash with the US domestic sports season, particularly the NFL and NBA.

With no competitive tension, Fox was given a relative bargain, paying $485m for the 2026 rights, the same as in Qatar, despite the World Cup having an extra 40 matches and taking place on home soil. For context, the NFL’s domestic TV deal is worth $11bn a year, with the NBA bringing in around $7bn.

Fox has capitalised this summer as a result, on the back of bumper viewing, with industry experts predicting it will make more than $1bn from TV adverts, whose volume and value has increased due to the addition of hydration breaks.

Fifa is determined to recoup what many regard as lost income from the US market in future TV rights cycles.

Having watched with frustration as Fox has cashed in, ESPN and NBC are expected to bid for the 2030 tournament, while initial conversations have also taken place with Netflix about them joining in the auction.

View image in fullscreen High prices did not deter fans from packing out stadiums at the World Cup in the US. Photograph: Julio Cortez/AP

Netflix has already signalled its growing interest in football by buying American rights for the Women’s World Cup in 2027 and 2031, the latter being held in the US, and another men’s tournament seven years later would spark another boom.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

No country has hosted the World Cup twice in 12 years, but Fifa’s statutes and recent staging decisions give it the flexibility for this to happen.

By taking the 2030 World Cup to three continents and six countries – Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay – before Saudi Arabia hosts in 2034, a North American bid for 2038 is permitted under Fifa’s confederation rotation policy, along with one from Oceania.

Soccer Australia had wanted to bid for 2034, but after being given less than a month to formally register its interest by Fifa, withdrew its candidacy leaving Saudi Arabia to be selected unopposed, Infantino’s preferred method.

To complicate matters slightly, the North American confederation, Concacaf, is understood to have reservations about another US bid as it wants to give opportunities to other members.

Costa Rica, Jamaica and Mexico have been added to the 2031 Women’s World Cup bid and another joint endeavour could emerge, although unsurprisingly Trump would prefer the US to be sole hosts. “Based on the numbers we will be requesting it again immediately,” he told Fox.

Fifa’s timeline for opening the 2038 process is not yet known, but history suggests it could move quickly to secure the outcome it wants. The sudden opening of the 2034 bidding process in October 2024 took most confederations by surprise with Infantino announcing that Saudi Arabia would be the hosts just 25 days later, a decision ratified by all Fifa members at a bizarre virtual extraordinary general meeting two months later.

Infantino will be re-elected for a fourth full term at next year’s Fifa Congress in Morocco, almost certainly unopposed, and then all eyes will turn to the 2038 contest.

Barring what would be an unprecedented change to the US constitution to permit an additional term, Trump is due to leave office in January 2029, which may quickly become the deadline for Fifa.

Sports.title: Morgan Rogers ‘excited to join biggest club in London’ after making £117m Chelsea move
Sports.content:
Morgan Rogers has joined Chelsea from Aston Villa for a fee of £117m, signing a seven-year deal to become the Blues’ record signing.

A deal was agreed on Saturday for the 23-year-old to move to Stamford Bridge as the club stole in ahead of Arsenal, who had been in talks to sign the England international and had appeared to be favourites to secure his signature.

It is understood that the chance to work with the new Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso was a key factor in persuading Rogers, who has just returned from helping England to a third-place finish at the World Cup, to choose west London.

He started in the 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina in Atlanta last Wednesday as well as the 6-4 win over France on Saturday that earned the bronze medal. He told his new club’s website: “I’m so excited. For me, Chelsea are the biggest club in London and a club I’ve always admired since I was a kid. I’m really excited about the project with the new manager, the players we’ve got and where the club is heading. That’s why I’m here and I can’t wait to get started.”

A versatile forward who satisfies Chelsea’s need for a player that can play multiple attacking roles, he has enjoyed a rapid rise at Villa Park following his move from Middlesbrough in January 2024 and helped fire Villa to a top-four finish and the Europa League last season.

He leaves Villa having scored 31 times in 125 appearances under Unai Emery.

The deal represents one of the most significant buys of Chelsea owners BlueCo’s four-year reign. Co-owner Behdad Eghbali indicated towards the end of last season that the club had learned the lessons of an underwhelming campaign in which the team finished 10th and were thrashed in the Champions League last 16 by Paris Saint-Germain, and that they would be targeting players in the market that would be in a position to help them challenge for the title.

View image in fullscreen Rogers walks on the pitch at Stamford Bridge. Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty Images

The former Liverpool, Real Madrid and Bayern Munich midfielder Alonso, a two-time Champions League winner as a player, was hired partly in order to convince the right calibre of player to move to Chelsea.

The deal for Rogers is arguably the biggest the club have pulled off since Cole Palmer moved from Manchester City in 2023. Rogers becomes the fourth signing of the summer as the Blues overhaul their squad, following the arrivals of defender Marco Palestra, striker Emmanuel Emegha and winger Geovany Quenda.

In June, the club failed in an attempt to reunite Alonso with Sunderland’s Granit Xhaka, with Chelsea unwilling to meet the Black Cats’ valuation of a player who will turn 34 in September.

Sports.title: Iraola determined to keep Mac Allister and Alisson at Liverpool this season
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola has said he is determined to keep Alexis Mac Allister and Alisson for his first season as Liverpool head coach and must strengthen a squad that will be without Hugo Ekitiké and Conor Bradley for several more months.

The dust had barely settled on Argentina’s World Cup final defeat by Spain when Mac Allister was linked with a move to Real Madrid. Iraola, in Chicago for the start of Liverpool’s pre-season tour of the US, accepted the midfielder is unlikely to be 100% ready for the Premier League opener at Newcastle due to a post-World Cup holiday. But he allayed doubts over Mac Allister’s long-term future at Liverpool, where he is under contract until 2028, by insisting the 27-year-old is part of next season’s plans.

Iraola said: “I think Alexis has been one of the best players at the club for the last few years, and he has had a very good World Cup, so it is normal that other clubs want our best players. It always happens in other markets. But I want to keep my good players. I’m looking forward more to signing new players rather than losing the ones we have here.”

Alisson is another established figure whose Liverpool future has been questioned, with the Brazil international strongly linked with Juventus at the end of last season. Iraola has not met Alisson or Mac Allister in person due to their World Cup commitments but has spoken with both, and guaranteed the former will remain a Liverpool player next season.

“I am very happy with the situation we have right now in the goalkeeping area,” said Iraola. “We have Alisson, we have Giorgi [Mamardashvili]. Now we are going to send Armin [Pecsi] on loan but we have the guarantee of the three keepers here. Freddie [Woodman] played some games last season, I think it is a guarantee for us.

“Alisson is also someone in a changing room that has lots of references, in terms of experience. He is someone that definitely will help us in this process of adaptation of the new signings and the young players. We need the references like Virgil [van Dijk], Alisson, Joe Gomez; players that have been here for a long time, and I am sure we will have this help.”

Liverpool have brought a young squad on their US tour, which currently involves a training camp at Chicago Fire before the first game against Sunderland in Nashville on Saturday. Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Ryan Gravenberch will join the tour next week when Van Dijk, Cody Gakpo and Alisson will begin their pre-season training regimes back on Merseyside.

Iraola admitted Liverpool are “very thin” in terms of defensive numbers and while a fit Bradley would be considered first choice at right-back, his recovery from a serious knee injury sustained in January means the club could be forced into the market.
