By Ambassadors Emmanuel Mwamba

As Zambia counts down to the August 13 general election, a familiar contest is playing out, not over policies or crowds, but over what citizens are allowed to believe before they have seen the evidence for themselves.

An investigative report by Global Witness, the London-based anti-corruption group, is expected to examine influence in Zambia’s mining sector. Yet before the public has been able to read a single page, a campaign to shape how that report is received is already under way.

The clearest example is a lengthy article that appeared in the state-owned Zambia Daily Mail. Running ahead of the report’s release, it did not engage the substance of the findings so much as pre-frame the organisation itself: foreign, agenda-driven, suspiciously timed. It leaned on an anonymous ruling-party official, on attacks on Global Witness’s funding and the timing of its work, and even on the identity of the report’s sources, noting, for instance, that some are former associates of the late former President Rupiah Banda, as if old political connections settled whether a claim is true. These are the classic moves of “prebunking,” in which a story is discredited in advance so that, whatever it says, readers have already been told to dismiss it.

That would be concerning enough on its own but it is not the only manipulation in circulation. A document has also been spreading on social media under the letterhead of a “Washington Center for African Strategy” – an organisation with no verifiable existence: no website, no staff, no public record, a contact number drawn from a range reserved for fiction, and a name that closely imitates a real U.S. institution.

That fabricated document attacks the ruling party, not the opposition, and its true origin is unknown. But notice the effect: a flimsy, easily-debunked anti-UPND document surfacing just before a genuine, critical report muddies the water, letting the real thing be lumped in with “more forged foreign documents.” That plausibly serves the ruling party, whoever produced it.

The lesson for Zambians is not to decide in advance who is right. It is to refuse to let anyone else decide for them. When the Global Witness report is published, read it. Weigh its evidence. Note where it rests on named sources and documents and where it rests on anonymous ones that is fair scrutiny, and a genuinely credible report can withstand it. Then ask the same hard questions of those rushing to rubbish it before it appears.

Be especially wary of two tactics. The first is the pre-emptive dismissal that tells you a report is worthless before you can read it. The second is the fake “bombshell” that tries to stampede you into outrage. Both depend on you not checking. Both are defeated by a single habit: asking where a claim comes from, and waiting for the original source rather than the loudest summary of it.

Global Witness has spent decades investigating corruption and resource governance around the world; its work deserves to be read and tested, not pre-judged. So does every claim made about this election, from every side. In a democracy, that judgement belongs to voters not to whoever shouts first, or shouts loudest through the State and private media they control.

World.title: Time to plan for 2030 World Cup – Musonda  ‎
World.content:
Former Zambia international midfielder Charles Musonda says the focus for Zambian football must immediately shift to the 2030 World Cup, with a clear plan to strengthen local clubs and the national team.

‎

‎Musonda noted that most of Africa’s top players are professionals in Europe, while others gain valuable experience by going deep in CAF competitions, citing South Africa, Egypt, Tunisia, Algeria and Morocco. He added that all 10 African representatives at the last World Cup would want to return, and the number of slots for Africa will increase.

‎

‎“For Zambia, the priority is clear: help Dynamos and Arrows succeed in CAF competitions and produce more national team players,” the former Mufulira Wanderers star said.

‎

‎He called for foreign-based professionals to be selected on merit, regardless of the league they play in, and urged top Zambian clubs to recruit the best local talent.

‎

‎“South Africa’s leading clubs are built around their best local players,” he said.

‎

‎Musonda further proposed turning Heroes and Levy Stadiums into fortresses by winning every home game, and suggested a fan engagement initiative to boost atmosphere.

‎

‎“Give every fan a white ‘KK’ handkerchief at the gate and have them wave it whenever Zambia attacks. It creates atmosphere and puts pressure on opponents. ‘History helps’ – do not diminish it. We do remember him. After all, the team was KK. That would be a good gesture. Just imagine every Zambian waving white handkerchiefs before kickoff and during every attack. That would motivate Zambian players,” he said.

‎

‎He concluded by urging early planning and close player monitoring.

‎

‎“Plan now. Monitor players closely. Don’t wait until it’s too late. Even if a young Zambian is playing in Egypt, take him seriously. If he can improve the national team, give him the opportunity. That’s it,” Musonda said.

World.title: Govt.  committed to upholding rights of workers and employers
World.content:
Government says it is committed to upholding the rights of both workers and employers and creating industrial harmony, which is a cornerstone of the country’s economic resilience and national productivity.

‎Muchinga Province Deputy Permanent Secretary Brian Sichande underscored that a clear, equitable, and transparent mechanism for resolving workplace disputes is critical to protecting both workers and employers.

‎The Deputy Permanent Secretary made these remarks during a stakeholder engagement meeting on the Workers’ Compensation Tribunal and Draft Rules held at Elegant Triumph Lodge in Chinsali today.

‎Mr Sichande said industrial harmony cannot exist without accessible justice systems, especially for vulnerable workers in remote areas who remain unaware of their rights.

‎“Our duty is not only to adjudicate disputes but also to sensitize the public on the mandate of the Workers’ Compensation Tribunal,” he said.

‎Mr Sichande highlighted that the draft rules being reviewed are designed to streamline dispute resolution mechanisms, eliminate unnecessary bureaucratic delays, and ensure justice is administered swiftly and impartially.

‎He added that delays in resolving grievances, particularly for workers who have suffered workplace injuries or unfair compensation, add an unbearable burden to already difficult circumstances.

‎Mr Sichande has since called for the draft rules review process to be comprehensive and to reflect the realities in workplaces across the country.

‎And speaking earlier, Workers Compensation Tribunal Chairperson Maria Drass Neves stated that the vision for the tribunal is to build an industrial relations landscape where disputes are resolved swiftly, transparently, and fairly.

‎Ms Neves said the stakeholder engagement is a testament to a shared commitment to fostering a fair, balanced, and harmonious labour environment in Zambia.

‎” We want to ensure that every worker, union leader, and employer understands their rights, the remedies available to them, and how the Tribunal serves as a vital pillar in national labor relations as a unique alternative dispute resolution platform.

The engagement meeting brought together workers’ representatives, employers, government officials, and other stakeholders to input into the proposed rules that will govern the operations of the Workers’ Compensation Tribunal.

World.title: President Hichilema commissions Chisamba Phase II Solar Power Plant
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has commissioned the 100-megawatt Chisamba Phase II Solar Power Plant, describing the 75-million United States dollar investment as a major milestone in Zambia’s transition to clean and sustainable energy.

President Hichilema says the project demonstrates government’s commitment to achieving energy security while reducing the effects of climate change through increased investment in renewable energy.

The Head of State said the Solar Plant is contributing to government’s vision of generating 10,000 megawatts of electricity by 2030.

Speaking at the commissioning of the solar plant in Chisamba’s Chikokomena Ward, Mr Hichilema said he is optimistic that the 10,000 megawatt target of solar power generation is slowly being realized.

He disclosed that out of the 10,000 Megawatt target, ZESCO Limited only has so far produced 800 Megawatt of solar power energy generation.

President Hichilema commended ZESCO for undertaking the project works in seven months.

Mr Hichilema said the facility will increase power generation at the Chisamba Solar Complex from 100 megawatts to 200 megawatts, reinforcing government’s efforts to strengthen national energy security through increased investment in renewable energy.

He stated that the project demonstrates the importance of investing in renewable energy infrastructure as Zambia works towards achieving a diversified and sustainable energy sector.

And President Hichilema dismissed assertions by the opposition that load shedding has ended because of the forthcoming general election, saying government will continue to deliver development to the people with or without elections.

The President commended Chief Chamuka of the Lenje people for providing the land for the solar plant.

Speaking earlier, Central Province Permanent Secretary (PS,) Milner Mwanakampwe disclosed that the region has reached its target of providing 437MW of electricity above the 400 target.

ZESCO Managing Director, Justin Loongo revealed that 1,480 jobs were created in the second phase of the sole single largest solar generation in Zambia.

He said the additional 100 megawatts of solar power will be fed into the national grid, increasing the solar plant’s total generation capacity to 200 megawatts and improving electricity supply to households, businesses and industries

Chief Chamuka pledged to provide an additional 50 hectares of land for developmental purposes particularly, energy.

The traditional leader warned his subjects against vandalizing the facility emphasizing that the 200 MW power generation capacity will enhance electricity security and reduce the country’s dependence on hydropower.

He said developmental projects that uplift the livelihoods of the people should first benefit his subjects and the country as a whole.

Chief Chamuka said the project will create employment opportunities, promote technology transfer and support economic growth by providing reliable electricity to key sectors such as mining, manufacturing, agriculture and small-scale enterprises describing the project as a major milestone in Zambia’s energy sector.

The Head of State also toured and inspected the power control room, solar panels before he unveiled a plaque of the plant.

The Phase Two project has been developed by Kariba North Bank Extension Power Corporation Limited (KNPCL), a subsidiary of ZESCO Limited, while construction has been undertaken by Power China International Group Limited.

The commissioning of the Chisamba solar plant was witnessed by senior government, ZESCO and Power China officials, some traditional leaders, as well as Chisamba residents.

World.title: Lameck Banda goes AWOL at Italian club?
World.content:
Chipolopolo forward Lameck Banda is facing disciplinary action at his Italian Club U.S Lecce for late coming.

Lecce said in a statement that Banda has delayed reporting for pre-season ahead of the 2026/27 Italian Serie A campaign.

“U.S. Lecce announces that the player Lameck Banda, already called up for the resumption of sports activities, today represented the further delay in the logistical and bureaucratic issues that have, to date, prevented his return to Italy,” the club said.

Banda is a key member of the Lecce squad.

“U.S. Lecce will carry out the necessary in-depth investigations regarding the circumstances taken by the player, reserving any initiatives, even on a disciplinary level, that are aimed at the correct fulfilment of contractual obligations related to the employment relationship that expires on June 30, 2027,” Lecce stated.

Banda joined Lecce in August 2022 after leaving Israeli club Maccabi Petah Tikva.

He is the first Zambian player to ever feature in the Italian Serie A.

Locally, Banda has played for Nkwazi and Zesco United.

World.title: 8thAnnual Pensions awareness week launched
World.content:
Ministry of Labour and Social Security Permanent Secretary, Zechariah Luhanga has called on Zambians to take greater responsibility in planning for their retirement.

Mr Luhanga says a secure and dignified retirement depends on informed financial decisions and consistent pension contributions throughout one’s working life.

Speaking at the official launch of the 8th Annual Pensions Awareness week in Lusaka, Mr Luhanga said pension is more than deductions from workers’ salaries, describing it as an important financial tool that guarantees security, independence and dignity in old age.

He urged workers to join pension schemes early, make regular contributions and remain engaged with pension providers, adding that a strong pension culture reduces old-age financial vulnerability while easing the burden on families and government.

Mr Luhanga said government remains committed to promoting inclusive growth, decent work and comprehensive social protection through recent pension reforms.

He explained that the enactment of the National Pension Scheme Act No. 72 of 2026, the Public Service Pensions Act No. 73 of 2026, and the Local Authorities Superannuation Act No. 74 of 2026 has modernised Zambia’s pension legal framework, strengthened pension administration and enhanced protection of workers’ retirement benefits.

Mr Luhanga said government has also established a comprehensive four-pillar pension system comprising non-contributory social assistance, mandatory contributory pension schemes, voluntary occupational and private pension arrangements, and complementary social support services such as healthcare to promote active and dignified ageing.

He further said expanding pension coverage is a key pillar of the Second National Financial Inclusion Strategy for 2024 to 2028, as it promotes household resilience, long-term savings, wealth creation and reduces old-age poverty.

He added that a financially secure retired population contributes to stronger families, resilient communities and sustainable national economic development.

Mr Luhanga said the recently released 2025 FinScope Survey shows financial inclusion has increased from 69.4 percent in 2020 to 80.1 percent in 2025, while pension coverage has also grown from 8.2 percent to 14.6 percent over the same period.

He said the improvements reflect the success of government and stakeholder efforts to promote financial literacy and consumer education, while encouraging more Zambians to participate in formal pension schemes.

Speaking at the same event, Pensions and Insurance Authority (PIA), Registrar and Chief Executive Officer, Namakau Ntini revealed that the private occupational pensions industry recorded growth in 2025, with net assets rising to approximately K26.9 billion, representing a 29 percent increase from 2024, largely driven by gains in local equities and government bonds.

Ms Ntini added that membership in registered pension schemes increased to about 275,000 in 2025 from approximately 265,000 in 2024, largely due to the admission of new participating employers into existing occupational pension schemes.

World.title: RTSA calls for safer Munada transportation practices
World.content:
The Road Transport and Safety Agency (RTSA) Manager, Eugen Chisha, has called on drivers transporting Munada traders and goods to strictly observe the road traffic rules and regulations in order to help reduce road traffic accidents in Mpika District.

Mr Chisha expressed concern over vehicles that ferry Munada traders saying transporters frequently overload and disregard traffic regulations, particularly during night-time as they transport traders to various parts of the district, thereby putting their lives at risk.

He said such practices not only endangered the lives of traders and their property but also poses a serious threat to other road users.

Mr Chisha said this during a road safety sensitisation meeting for Munada traders and transporters in Mpika District.

“As people continue to travel using various modes of transport, road safety remains critical in preventing road traffic accidents,” he said.

Mr Chisha explained that RTSA had launched the sensitisation campaign to promote road safety awareness among Munada drivers and motorbike riders operating in the district.

He said the programme was intended to instil discipline, responsibility and compliance with road traffic laws among transporters.

Mr Chisha further urged motorists and motorbike riders to observe traffic regulations at all times, noting that adherence to the law would safeguard their lives and those of other road users.

He added that RTSA will continue engaging stakeholders in the transport sector to enhance compliance with road traffic regulations and curb accidents associated with Munada transport activities.

Meanwhile, Mpika District Munada Driver’s Association Chairperson, Simon Mwila, has welcomed the road safety sensitisation initiative, describing it as timely and important.

Mr Mwila said the programme would help reduce road traffic accidents in the district and urged his fellow drivers to take the messages seriously by complying with all traffic regulations whenever they were on the road.

And Mpika Traffic Motorbike Coordinator, Brain Malekani, has appealed to his fellow riders to strictly observe road traffic rules at all times.

Mr Malekani said motorbike riders have a responsibility to promote road safety and urged them to avoid reckless riding, especially when transporting passengers and goods to and from Munada markets among other areas.

World.title: Madagascar: One of the Most Important Places for Life on Earth - Madagascar
World.content:
guest column

Antananarivo — Has a chance to lead the world in conservation, and species protection, and we must not waste It.

Over 150,000 of the island's species exist nowhere else, including its famous lemurs. Its forests hold species still to be described for science. If Madagascar succeeds in protecting nature, the world keeps a living library of evolution, culture and possibility. If it fails, we lose ecological treasures forever.

If the effort to preserve a living library of evolution fails, we lose ecological treasures forever.

For years, those of us who care about Madagascar have known two things: 1) the country is almost unimaginably rich in biodiversity, and 2) conservation efforts have been beset by delay and instability.

That is why this moment matters. Madagascar has a real opportunity to reclaim its role as a global conservation leader. We should not downplay that. We should recognize it, support it and move quickly.

In the early 2000s, Madagascar seemed poised to show the world that conservation could protect natural heritage while improving the lives of people who depend on it. The government made an ambitious commitment to safeguard 10 percent of its land and territorial waters.

Protect natural heritage while improving lives.

There were challenges, of course. Conservation is never simple, especially in a country where rural communities under economic hardship rely on forests as their main source of fuel, food, land and income. But there was momentum, and there was a sense among conservationists that Madagascar could lead.

Then came political crisis. In 2009, the government was swept from power, and conservation entered a long and damaging period of uncertainty. Illegal rosewood harvesting surged. Deforestation climbed. Projects stalled. The trust and continuity between government and communities required for lasting protection were shaken.

Madagascar's parks and protected areas were caught in that instability. Local communities, conservation organizations and committed individuals in government continued to work, often with extraordinary persistence, but national progress was harder than it should have been.

Finally, a new administration made a clear commitment to 30x30, the global goal to protect 30 percent of land and sea by 2030, and this pledge has endured a transition to the current administration. In its first months, the administration moved quickly to unlock long-stalled protected area designations, including 21 new temporary protected areas covering over three million acres. In March 2026, 50 scientists, most of them Malagasy, from seven specialized fields completed the first full reprioritization of the country's conservation map since 1995, identifying roughly 44 million acres of priority land.

Rainforest Trust Ivohiboro, an isolated sub-humid mountain forest in Madagascar.

This effor is rooted in Madagascar's own institutions, science and communities.

Long-delayed designations are now moving because this effort is rooted in Madagascar's own institutions, science and communities — strong enough to carry forward no matter who governs. For a country of such global biological importance, this is not a bureaucratic footnote. It is a turning point.

Protected areas only endure when they are more than lines on a map. They need legal recognition, long-term financing, effective management and above all local support. They need to create tangible benefits for communities: secure rights, sustainable livelihoods, better fisheries, climate resilience, employment, education and pride. Protection endures when communities are recognized as both stewards and beneficiaries.

Madagascar has a plan. It has political will. It has local conservation leaders who have continued the work through years of difficulty. It has communities already proving that protection and prosperity can move together.

Madagascar needs partnerships at the scale of this opportunity.

What Madagascar needs now is partnership at the scale of this opportunity.

That means funding the full life cycle of conservation: designation, management, enforcement, restoration, monitoring and community livelihoods. It means investing in Malagasy institutions and local organizations, not just international intermediaries. It means moving quickly enough to overcome the pace of forest loss, but carefully enough to ensure that protection is durable, equitable and trusted.

Madagascar once inspired the world with its conservation ambition. Then it endured years in which that promise was delayed and, in many places, undermined. Now the country has a chance to lead again by building a 30x30 strategy grounded in science, community prosperity and national leadership.

There are moments when political will, community leadership and scientific urgency align. When they do, the conservation community has to be ready. This is one of those moments.

We should meet Madagascar's leadership with investment. We should meet it with trust. And we should meet it now.

Because if Madagascar succeeds, it will prove that even after years of setbacks, a country can choose a different future.

Liva Raharijaona is 30x30 Coordinator at Madagascar's Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development. James Deutsch is CEO of Rainforest Trust

World.title: Namibia: Windhoek Residents Brace for Higher Tariffs
World.content:
Thousands of Windhoek households are facing another financial blow after the City of Windhoek (CoW) confirmed last week an average 4% increase in municipal tariffs. Although minimal on paper, the increase means a larger share of household and business income will now be spent on basic services, risking weaker consumer spending, slower economic activity, and making it even harder for unemployed Namibians and young families to establish themselves.

While the city cites the measure as being necessitated by inflation, there is no doubt the single digit increase will add notable pressure to already constrained family budgets, which are reeling from higher borrowing costs, rising inflation and stubbornly high unemployment.

The CoW increases, which took effect retrospectively from 1 July 2026 and will first appear on municipal accounts on 31 July, apply to water, property rates and taxes, sewerage, waste management, refuse removal and fire brigade levies.

The CoW Council stated that the revised tariffs were approved under a Council Resolution and subsequently gazetted. According to the municipality, the increase is necessary to enable the city to continue maintaining essential infrastructure and delivering critical municipal services.



"We thank you for your continued support and understanding as we work together to build a sustainable Windhoek," the municipality stated.

However, while a 4% increase may appear modest on paper, economists warn that its cumulative effect could significantly deepen the financial strain on households already battling one of the country's toughest cost-of-living environments in years, thereby adding pressure to residents already stretched to breaking point.

Economist Abraham Eita believes the latest tariff adjustment cannot be viewed in isolation.

"The problem is not created by one factor only. It is the result of several pressures happening at the same time," he said.

In a recent opinion, Eita's warning comes as many homeowners are already paying more on mortgage repayments following recent interest rate increases, while inflation continues to erode household purchasing power.

Domestic inflation is currently hovering around 4.4%, while many workers have seen little or no corresponding increase in their salaries. For low-income earners, the mathematics are becoming increasingly unforgiving.

Namibia's minimum wage is approximately N$4 000 per month; however, transport costs alone can easily consume from N$700 to N$1000 monthly. Daily living expenses in Windhoek are estimated at between N$200 and N$450, meaning even the lower estimate amounts to roughly N$6 000 per month, which is well above the minimum wage before rent, school fees, medical expenses, or municipal accounts are considered.

"A 4% tariff increase may seem small on paper, but for a low-income household it can mean choosing between paying a municipal bill, buying enough food, or paying for transport to work," Eita explained, adding: "In economics, percentages can sometimes hide pain."

Meanwhile, Namibia continues to grapple with an unemployment rate of over 36%, with only about 867 000 people participating in the labour force out of a population exceeding three million. As a result, many households rely on a single income earner, informal trading or financial support from relatives.

As disposable income shrinks, economists warn that the impact extends beyond individual families. Higher municipal bills leave consumers with less money to spend in shops, restaurants and on discretionary purchases, putting further pressure on already struggling businesses.

"Families will now spend most of their income on survival... They will have little left to save, invest, educate their children properly or support small businesses. Businesses will also suffer because customers have less spending power," Eita stated.

Justifying the increase, the CoW argues that tariff adjustments are unavoidable if it is to maintain ageing infrastructure, expand services and ensure reliable water, sanitation and waste management.

However, the question increasingly asked by residents is whether consumers are receiving sufficient value for the steadily rising costs they are expected to absorb.

Municipal tariffs have risen regularly over the past decade as the CoW has sought to keep pace with escalating operating costs, bulk water and electricity price increases, infrastructure maintenance requirements and urban expansion. In recent years, annual adjustments have generally ranged from inflationary increases to above-inflation adjustments for specific services, steadily pushing up the fixed monthly cost of living for Windhoek households and businesses alike.

Critics argue that while residents are repeatedly being asked to pay more, the City itself has come under scrutiny over the remuneration packages paid to some of its senior executives. In recent years, public debate has intensified following disclosures that top municipal executives receive annual remuneration amounting to several million Namibian dollars when salaries, housing, vehicles and other employment benefits are considered. These exorbitant remuneration packages have repeatedly drawn criticism from residents and ratepayer groups, particularly as households have simultaneously faced tariff increases, weak economic growth and deteriorating disposable incomes.

Close 

The contrast has fuelled growing calls for restraint in executive remuneration, stronger financial accountability, and clearer evidence that additional revenue collected through tariffs is translating into tangible improvements in service delivery. Economists like Eita believe public acceptance of future increases will depend heavily on transparency.

"The City of Windhoek should communicate clearly how additional revenue will improve water supply, waste management, sanitation and emergency services," he said.

"People are more likely to accept higher charges when they can see better value."

He also cautioned that policymakers need to consider the cumulative burden being placed on consumers.

"When interest rates, municipal bills, food prices and transport costs rise together, the combined effect becomes too heavy for ordinary residents," Eita added.

World.title: South Africa: Ambassador Meyer Wants Trump Afrikaner Refugee Plan Stopped
World.content:
Roelf Meyer, South Africa's new ambassador to the U.S.

Donald Trump matters a lot to Mzansi and the rest of the world right now. Trump is changing the way America works - and how the world's most powerful country deals with the rest of the world.

We'll track what he does and connect the dots to your daily life.

Roelf Meyer wants Trump Afrikaner refugee plan stopped

South Africa's ambassador to the United States, Roelf Meyer, says he wants Donald Trump's Afrikaner refugee plan stopped.



Meyer said he is trying to get Trump's order cancelled. He said this would be difficult because Trump and the White House support it, Newsday reported.

Trump signed the order in February 2025. It allows Afrikaners who say they are being treated badly in South Africa to move to the US as refugees.

Trump has said South Africa is taking land and treating some people unfairly. The South African government says these claims are not true.

The first group of 59 Afrikaners arrived in the US in May 2025. Since then, many more people have applied.

Critics say white South Africans are still among the richest and most protected people in the country. They also say crime affects people of all races.

The Trump government says the plan will continue. The White House says Afrikaners are being attacked and forced off their land.

Meyer said it would be hard to change Trump's mind, but he would keep trying.

Trump says Iran strikes honour three dead US soldiers

US President Donald Trump says the latest American strikes hit Iran very hard.

He said the attacks were carried out in honour of three US soldiers killed in Jordan and Iraq.

The US military said it launched another wave of strikes across Iran for the ninth night in a row.

It said military sites and communication networks were targeted to reduce Iran's attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran said it responded with an attack in Syria and targeted US aircraft at an airport in Jordan. Kuwait also said it stopped Iranian drones.

Iranian media reported strikes in several cities. It also said two oil tankers exploded while trying to cross the strait, but the US disputed that claim.

Iran warned that the strait would remain unsafe for oil and gas ships while US attacks continued.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said America was still open to talks. But efforts to end the fighting have made little progress since Trump said a temporary agreement was over on 8 July.

Image source: File

Trump claims China targeted US election systems

US President Donald Trump has claimed that China tried to interfere in the 2020 election.

Trump made the claim during a speech from the White House, three months before the US midterm elections.

He said China had obtained 220 million voter files containing personal information. He claimed data from 18 states had been bought, stolen or hacked.

Trump did not provide evidence that China changed votes, hacked voting machines or affected the election result.

US intelligence previously found that China did not interfere in the 2020 election, which Trump lost to Joe Biden.

China also denied Trump's claims. Its embassy in Washington said Beijing had never interfered in US presidential elections.

Trump also said US voting machines were open to attacks from countries including China, Russia and Iran. He called for new voting rules requiring proof of citizenship and photo identification.

Democrats accused Trump of trying to make voters doubt the November elections. They said Americans should still trust the voting system and take part.

Image source: File

Trump gets his face on new US one dollar coin

The US Mint will soon begin making a new one dollar coin featuring President Donald Trump's face.

The coin will mark America's 250th birthday in 2026. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said it would be available later this year.

Trump's face appears beside the words "In God We Trust". The coin also includes the words "Liberty" and "1776 2026".

The other side shows an eagle holding arrows and olive branches. The coin is gold in colour but does not contain real gold.

The coin will be made in Philadelphia. It will be slightly bigger than a quarter and made from a metal called manganese brass.

Questions have been raised about whether putting a living president on US money is legal. US law says only dead people may appear on US currency and financial documents.

Bessent said the design was legal. He pointed to a coin made for President Calvin Coolidge while he was still alive.

Officials at the US Mint also said legal checks had been completed. They said the Trump coin did not break any laws.

Image source: File

Trump threatens to bomb Iran if talks do not restart

US President Donald Trump has threatened to bomb Iran's bridges and power plants unless it returns to talks.

Trump said the attacks could begin next week. His warning came as the US and Iran exchanged fire for a fourth straight day.

"We're going to knock out all their power plants. We're going to knock out all their bridges unless they get to the table and negotiate," Trump told Fox News.

Trump also restarted a US blockade of Iranian ports. A blockade uses military forces to stop ships from entering or leaving.

The US military said it struck dozens of Iranian military targets near the Strait of Hormuz. Iran said at least seven of its soldiers were killed.

Iran then fired missiles and drones at US targets in Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain. Kuwait and Bahrain said they stopped some of the attacks.

Trump dropped an earlier plan to charge a 20% fee on cargo moving through the Strait of Hormuz. He said Gulf countries would instead make large trade and investment deals with the US.

Iran said it would not return to talks because of US military attacks and the blockade. The renewed fighting has slowed shipping through the strait and pushed oil prices higher.

Image source: File

Trump tariff plan costs US billions in refunds

Donald Trump's tariff plan has forced the US government to pay back $81-billion to companies.

Tariffs are taxes placed on goods brought into a country. Trump has used them as a major part of his economic plan since returning to office last year.

But in February, the US Supreme Court ruled that many of Trump's extra tariffs were illegal. The government then had to return money to companies that had paid them.

Budget figures released on Monday show that $81-billion has been refunded since October 2025. Only $5-billion was refunded during the same period a year earlier.

A Treasury official said most of the increase came from the court ruling. Most refunds were paid in May and June.

Trump said tariffs would bring factories back to America, improve trade deals and help reduce government debt. But the US budget deficit has grown by 2% to $1.367-trillion.

The US also spent more than $1-trillion paying interest on its debt. Military spending rose by 5% because of the war in the Middle East.

Trump is still planning more tariffs. New taxes of between 10% and 12.5% could affect countries including the UK, Japan, India, Taiwan and China.

He has also threatened a 100% tariff on European countries that tax large US technology companies such as Apple, Google and Amazon.

Image source: File

Trump says US will destroy Iran if it tries to kill him

US President Donald Trump has warned Iran not to try to kill him. He said the United States would destroy large parts of Iran if there was an assassination attempt against him.

Trump said 1,000 US missiles were ready to hit Iran, with thousands more prepared to follow.

His warning came after mourners in Iran carried signs calling for the deaths of Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Trump also said talks with Iran would continue. But he said the ceasefire agreed in June was over.

The deal had called on both countries to stop fighting. Iran was also meant to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, an important route used to move oil and gas.

The US said it hit about 170 Iranian military targets this week. Iran then attacked US military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait.

Iran said it had followed the ceasefire deal. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused the US of breaking it by bringing in new sanctions.

Image source: File

Trump gets Florida airport named after him

A Florida airport has officially been renamed President Donald J Trump International Airport.

The airport was previously called Palm Beach International Airport. New signs went up on Thursday, but officials said the full change would take several weeks.

Its three letter airport code will also change from PBI to DJT on 18 August.

Trump said on Truth Social that the new name was a great honour. He also promised that planned renovations would make the airport one of the best in the world.

A Boeing 757 owned by the Trump Organization was the first plane to arrive after the name change. The aircraft is known as Trump Force One.

Trump's son Eric was on board. He said nobody had done more for Florida and the United States than his father.

Eric said he would be proud to see the letters DJT on his boarding pass when using the airport.

The Trump family often uses the airport when visiting Trump's Mar a Lago home in West Palm Beach. A road between the airport and the estate was renamed Donald J Trump Boulevard in January.

Image source: File

Trump declares Iran ceasefire over

The United States has struck Iran for a second day in a row after Donald Trump declared that the interim peace deal ending the war was "over," less than a month after it was signed.

Iranian state media reported explosions on Wednesday night in the port city of Bandar Abbas, in Sirik, and in Bushehr province, home to Iran's nuclear power plant. "This is in retribution for yesterday's bombing of ships by Iran. If it happens again, it will get much worse!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The strikes came after three cargo ships were attacked while passing through the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, the most serious clash between the two sides since the ceasefire deal was signed on 17 June. The US also cancelled a waiver that had allowed Iran to keep exporting oil.

Iran hit back at US military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait for a second day running. Sirens sounded in Bahrain, home to the US Navy's 5th Fleet. Kuwait said it was shooting down incoming drones and missiles.

Speaking at the Nato summit in Turkey, Trump said the US would "probably hit Iran hard again tonight" and suggested America might "just finish the job." He accused Iran of "behaving very badly."

Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf was defiant. "The era of bullying and extortion is over. It leads nowhere. We don't fold," he wrote on X.

US senator Bernie Sanders criticised Trump's decision to restart the war. "Restarting his reckless war with Iran won't make America stronger. It will cost more lives and waste more taxpayer dollars," he said.

Oil prices jumped more than 5% to close to $80 a barrel after the news broke, and US stock markets fell.

The fresh strikes came as Iranians prepared to bury their former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed on the first day of the war, following a funeral procession that drew millions of mourners.

Image source: File

Trump says Ukraine war is close to ending

Donald Trump has said the war in Ukraine is "getting closer than people realise" to being resolved, after speaking to both Russian president Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky over the weekend.

"I think we're getting much closer than people realise. President Putin wants it to end. I will tell you that very strongly," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday.

Trump gave no specific reason for his optimism. Overnight, Russia fired missiles and drones at Kyiv and the surrounding region, killing at least 28 people. He said he had a "good call" with Putin on 4 July that lasted 85 minutes, according to a Kremlin aide.

Zelensky described his own call with Trump as "very good." He told the Financial Times that Trump seemed to be viewing the war differently after recent Ukrainian successes, including a drone campaign that has caused fuel shortages inside Russia. "President Trump wants to be where there's success," Zelensky said.

Trump is due to meet Zelensky on Wednesday at the Nato summit in Turkey, where the war will be a major topic. A US official said Trump is likely to speak to Putin again after that meeting.

In Moscow, a Kremlin spokesman said Russia's position on the war had not changed, despite Trump's comments. "President Trump has a fairly consistent stance," he said, denying any suggestion Trump had shifted his views.

The war has now lasted more than four years. Trump's latest optimism comes after past comments in which he pressured Zelensky to strike a deal with Russia quickly.

Image source: File

Trump made calls to Fifa to get a US player's World Cup ban lifted

Donald Trump personally called Fifa three times to help get a red card ban lifted for US striker Folarin Balogun, clearing him to play in Tuesday's last 16 match against Belgium.

Balogun was sent off during the US win over Bosnia and Herzegovina on Wednesday after stepping on an opponent's ankle. On Sunday, Fifa suddenly announced it was suspending the ban. Sources told the Guardian that Trump had been calling Fifa since Wednesday to push for the change.

Trump thanked the organisation on Truth Social. "Thank you to Fifa for doing what was right, and reversing a great injustice!" he wrote.

Belgium's football federation was furious. It called the decision "astonishing" and said it went against Fifa's own rules, which normally make a one-game ban automatic after a red card. The federation said it was "investigating all potential options."

Belgium's manager Rudi Garcia was blunt. "I didn't know that 5 July was equal to 1 April at Fifa," he said, comparing the decision to an April Fools' joke.

US players said they found out about the decision from social media while sitting on the team bus on their way to training. "My family probably sent me eight tweets," said defender Chris Richards. "Nobody told us ahead of time that this was happening."

Balogun has scored three goals in three matches so far at the tournament and is seen as key to the US reaching the World Cup quarter-finals for the first time since 2002.

Image source: File

Trump plays doctor in fake AI video curing celebrities who criticise him

Donald Trump has posted an AI-generated video showing himself as a doctor who claims to have cured celebrities of what he calls "Trump derangement syndrome," a made up illness used to describe people who criticise him.

The video, shared on Trump's social media account on Thursday, uses fake footage of stars including Whoopi Goldberg, Edward Norton, Julia Roberts and Robert De Niro pretending to thank him for treating them. A fake version of De Niro says: "I couldn't eat, I couldn't sleep, constantly angry. I made everyone miserable around me."

In the video Trump wears a white coat and stethoscope. "They were so far gone, I wasn't really sure," fake Trump says, before giving his cure. He tells people to "turn off fake news, say your prayers, and if you ever feel anxious, just have a Diet Coke like me."

One of the celebrities featured, Rosie O'Donnell, made clear the video was not real. "He's quite ill and getting worse daily," she said in a statement. "The 25th amendment exists for exactly this reason. Remove. Impeach. Convict."

This is not the first time Trump has used AI to target critics or boost his own image. He previously posted an image of himself as Jesus healing the sick, which he deleted after Christian commentators called it blasphemous. He has also portrayed himself as the pope and as a king on a fake magazine cover. In February he shared a racist video showing Barack and Michelle Obama as apes, which he deleted but did not apologise for.

A White House spokesperson defended the latest video, saying posting it was Trump's "right" and calling the fictional illness "a crippling disease that has unfortunately rotted the brains of many people." Officials did not say whether the celebrities featured had given permission for their likeness to be used.

Trump made billions from a Bible, a perfume and crypto coins

The two-week ceasefire between the US and Iran agreed last week is now in serious doubt.

Image source: File

Trump accuses Iran of breaking ceasefire deal

US president Donald Trump has accused Iran of doing a "very poor job" managing oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, saying it was "not the agreement we have."

Trump posted on Truth Social that Iran appeared to be charging fees to ships passing through the strait. "They better not be and, if they are, they better stop now," he wrote. The strait is a narrow stretch of water through which about one fifth of the world's oil normally passes.

The ceasefire between the US and Iran, agreed earlier this week, has been shaky from the start. Iran and Pakistan said the deal included Lebanon. The US and Israel said it did not.

After Israeli strikes continued in Lebanon on Thursday, Iran said Israel was breaking the ceasefire. Iran then partly blocked the strait again and threatened further strikes.

Trump told NBC News he had spoken to Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and asked him to ease off. "I spoke with Bibi and he's going to low-key it," Trump said.

Israel and Lebanon are set to begin direct talks in Washington next week, focused on disarming Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group, and building peaceful relations between the two countries. Lebanon's president had called for a ceasefire before any talks begin. Netanyahu said: "There is no ceasefire in Lebanon."

Israeli strikes on Thursday were among the heaviest since the conflict began six weeks ago. At least 303 people were killed and 1,150 wounded on Wednesday alone, according to Lebanon's health ministry. More than 1.2 million people have been forced to leave their homes.

The head of the World Health Organisation warned that two major hospitals in Beirut, treating around 450 patients, were in an evacuation zone with nowhere to send patients.

Image source: File

Don't criticise your hosts, Ramaphosa tells ambassadors

South African president Cyril Ramaphosa has said ambassadors should never publicly criticise the countries they are sent to, in remarks made in front of the US ambassador to South Africa, Leo Brent Bozell III.

Ramaphosa made the comments on Wednesday after receiving credentials from 20 new ambassadors at the Sefako Makgatho Presidential Guesthouse in Pretoria. "Ambassadors should never criticise their hosts," he said.

Bozell was called in by the South African government last month after publicly criticising South Africa's policies at a business conference. He later apologised for his comments.

Ramaphosa said ambassadors should always raise concerns privately and in a constructive way, not publicly or in a confrontational manner. "It is this approach that I believe builds strong relationships between nations," he said.

South Africa has not had its own ambassador in Washington since March 2025, when the Trump administration expelled Ebrahim Rasool and gave him one week to leave the US.

Both leaders welcomed the two-week ceasefire agreed between the US and Iran on Tuesday.

Bozell said the ceasefire was "a good thing" but warned that Iran needed to stick to the agreement. Ramaphosa called for dialogue to bring about a permanent end to the conflict.

Image source: File

Trump backs down and agrees ceasefire with Iran

The United States and Iran have agreed to a two-week ceasefire after weeks of war, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the key route through which a large share of the world's oil passes.

Trump had threatened to bomb Iran's power plants and bridges if the strait was not reopened. He pulled back from those threats after Pakistan's prime minister Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Asim Munir brokered the deal.

"I agree to suspend the bombing and attack of Iran for a period of two weeks," Trump said in a White House statement. He said the US had already met all its military goals and was close to a long-term peace agreement.

Iran's foreign minister said Iranian forces would stop fighting if US attacks halted. He said ships could pass through the strait for two weeks, with coordination from Iran's military.

Iran claimed it had won a "historic victory." Trump called that claim "fake news." CNN said it had obtained the Iranian statement directly from official Iranian spokespeople.

Analysts said the ceasefire gave Iran more control over the strait than it had before the war started.

Oil prices, which had climbed to nearly $150 a barrel, fell after the announcement. Stock markets rose and bond markets rallied. Fuel prices had been rising around the world, including in South Africa.

However, Iran continued to strike Israel, Kuwait, the UAE and Qatar in the hours after the ceasefire was announced. Analysts said this was likely because the news had not yet reached Iranian forces on the ground.

Image source: File

Trump warns he can take out Iran 'in one night'

US president Donald Trump has warned that the whole of Iran could be "taken out in one night" if it does not reach a deal before his deadline to reopen a key oil route.

The deadline is set for 20:00 Washington DC time on Tuesday. Trump wants Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow stretch of water through which a large share of the world's oil normally passes. Iran has largely blocked it since the US and Israel began bombing the country in February.

"The entire country can be taken out in one night -- and that night might be tomorrow night," Trump said at a White House news conference on Monday. He warned Iran would have "no bridges" and "no power plants" if the deadline passed.

Despite the threats, Trump said he believed Iran's leaders were negotiating in "good faith." Iran has rejected a temporary ceasefire and is calling for a permanent end to the war and the lifting of all sanctions against it.

A regional official close to the talks told the BBC that progress is slow because of a communications blackout inside Iran. "To convey messages to Iran, getting a response in a reasonable time is not possible," the official said.

Legal experts warned that bombing Iran's power plants and bridges could be a war crime. "Those kinds of things are all flatly illegal," former US national security legal adviser Tess Bridgeman told CBS News.

Trump also hit out again at the UK, Nato and South Korea for not helping the US in the war. "That's a mark on Nato that will never disappear," he said. The US military said it has carried out more than 13,000 strikes on Iran since the war began.

Image source: File

Open the oil route or we bomb your power plants, Trump warns Iran

US president Donald Trump has threatened to bomb bridges and power plants inside Iran if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened by Monday.

Trump made the threat in a social media post on Truth Social on Sunday, using strong language to warn Iran of what was coming. "Tuesday will be Power Plant Day, and Bridge Day, all wrapped up in one, in Iran. There will be nothing like it," he wrote.

The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow stretch of water through which a large share of the world's oil normally passes. Iran has largely blocked it since the US and Israel began bombing the country on 28 February.

Trump told Fox News on Sunday that Iran was currently negotiating with the US and that he believed a deal could be reached before the deadline. Iran has denied this, saying it is not seeking to end the war.

Iran's mission to the United Nations condemned Trump's threats, saying they amounted to war crimes. "The international community must act now. Tomorrow is too late," it said.

An Iranian government official said the strait would only be reopened once Iran had been paid for war damages, possibly through fees charged to ships passing through.

Asked if he was worried about the effect of bombing bridges and power plants on ordinary Iranian people, Trump told the Wall Street Journal: "No, they want us to do it."

The US also confirmed it had rescued the crew member of an F-15 fighter jet shot down over Iran on Friday.

Image source: File

Tiger Woods told police he was on the phone with Trump after crash

Golf legend Tiger Woods told a police officer he had just spoken to US president Donald Trump on the phone, shortly after being arrested for drunk driving in Florida last week.

Bodycam footage obtained and published by TMZ on Thursday shows Woods walking back to the crash scene and telling the officer: "I was just talking to the president." Woods then told his manager that Trump "was very apologetic for what he did last night."

Woods, 50, was charged with driving under the influence after his Land Rover SUV clipped a truck's trailer in Jupiter, Florida on Friday. He was found with two opioid pills in his pants and showed signs of intoxication, according to police documents. He has pleaded not guilty.

Trump called Woods "a very close friend" shortly after the crash. "I feel so bad. He's got some difficulty," Trump told reporters.

The evening before the crash, Trump said during a Fox News interview that Woods would not be playing in the upcoming Masters golf tournament. Woods had not publicly ruled out playing before the crash.

On Tuesday, Woods said he was "stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health."

Woods is dating Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Trump's son Donald Trump Jr. This is not Woods's first run-in with the law. He was arrested for drunk driving in Florida in 2017 and was seriously injured in a car crash in California in 2021.

Image source: White House
