03 What moved it

The main driver of the session was not a sudden shift in physical steel demand but the continued bedding-in of tougher trade defences against cheap Chinese imports across Latin America. Alacero data show that after a record inflow of low-priced steel and finished goods in 2025, imports fell 8.6% year on year in March 2026 to 2.5 million tonnes, and were 1.2% lower in the first quarter at 7.6 million tonnes, as Brazil, Mexico and Chile increased tariffs and anti-dumping duties.

Brazil has imposed anti-dumping duties on Chinese flat steel, including cold-rolled and hot-dip galvanised products, for five years following complaints by domestic mills such as Usiminas, while Mexico has introduced broad tariffs of up to 35% on about 1,400 products from China and other Asian exporters not covered by free trade agreements. At the same time, the US and Mexico have agreed joint enforcement measures, including a strict ‘melted and poured’ requirement to prevent Chinese-origin steel from sidestepping US tariffs via Mexico, reinforcing the sense that regional trade policy is tightening around the sector.

04 The Latin American read

Regionally, the backdrop is one of near-stagnant demand and gently improving supply discipline, with Alacero describing 2026 as a transition year ahead of stronger growth in 2027. Apparent rolled steel consumption in Latin America rose just 0.1% year on year in March 2026 to 6.5 million tonnes, and the association forecasts apparent steel consumption to increase by only 0.5% for the full year to 75.6 million tonnes before accelerating to 2.5% growth and 77.5 million tonnes in 2027.

Crude steel output is inching higher, reaching 4.9 million tonnes in March, up 1.1% year on year, even though first-quarter production fell 1.9% to 13.9 million tonnes, reflecting a mix of cautious capacity use and selective cutbacks. Demand from cars and construction provides one of the few clear supports, with Latin American automotive output up 1.1% year on year in the first four months of 2026 and construction activity broadly flat, helping to stabilise order books even as broader industrial activity remains subdued.

05 The names to watch

Brazil’s trio of listed mills remains central to any foreign read on the sector, starting with Gerdau, a long-steel producer closely linked to construction and infrastructure, whose 4.64 $ close and -0.85% day-on-day move track the still-slow recovery in building activity. CSN, with a 1 $ close and -0.99% day-on-day change, is similarly hostage to domestic demand and the pace at which Brazil’s tariff shield and anti-dumping duties can rebuild pricing power in flat products.

Usiminas, while not on the board snapshot, sits in the middle of both tariff and corporate stories after Ternium completed the purchase of 153.1 million Usiminas ordinary shares from Nippon Steel and Mitsubishi for about 315.2 million dollars in cash on February 10, 2026, tightening regional strategic links. Mexico’s Ternium itself, closing at 44.84 $, up +0.74% day-on-day, offers exposure to North American auto and machinery demand and to Mexican flat-steel pricing, which Argus reports has been supported by recent increases that lifted HRC ex-works prices in northeast Mexico to around 760-762 dollars per tonne by late December.

06 The outlook

Looking ahead, the consensus is that 2026 will remain a year of consolidation rather than breakout for Latin American steel, with Alacero expecting only 0.5% growth in apparent consumption to 75.6 million tonnes and more meaningful 2.5% expansion pencilled in for 2027. Prices are likely to stay range-bound as long as demand growth is modest and imports continue to ease under the weight of higher tariffs, while sectors such as construction and autos keep providing a floor under volumes. For foreign investors, that argues for treating names like Gerdau, CSN, Usiminas and Ternium as policy-sensitive value plays, with upside tied to any acceleration in infrastructure spending or further strengthening of trade safeguards.

07 What to watch

Tariffs on Chinese steel: Policy changes in Brazil and Mexico will directly affect import volumes, local pricing power and margins at Gerdau, CSN, Usiminas and Ternium.

Policy changes in Brazil and Mexico will directly affect import volumes, local pricing power and margins at Gerdau, CSN, Usiminas and Ternium. Auto and construction demand: Latin American automotive output and building activity are currently the main supports for steel consumption, so any acceleration or setback here will shape volumes and utilisation rates.

Latin American automotive output and building activity are currently the main supports for steel consumption, so any acceleration or setback here will shape volumes and utilisation rates. Import volumes and safeguards: The pace at which steel imports fall from their 2025 peak and the strength of new safeguards will determine whether local mills can reclaim market share and firm up prices.

The pace at which steel imports fall from their 2025 peak and the strength of new safeguards will determine whether local mills can reclaim market share and firm up prices. Regional consumption trajectory: Alacero’s forecast of just 0.5% apparent consumption growth in 2026, followed by 2.5% in 2027, is crucial for understanding when steel equities may move from policy trades to genuine growth stories.

Frequently Asked Questions

How strong is current steel demand in Latin America?

Demand is barely growing, with apparent rolled steel consumption up only 0.1% year on year at 6.5 million tonnes in March 2026, and Alacero forecasting just 0.5% growth in apparent steel consumption to 75.6 million tonnes for the full year.

What role do Chinese imports still play in the market?

Imports from China and other low-cost producers were at record levels in 2025, prompting warnings about deindustrialisation, but by March 2026 overall Latin American steel imports had fallen 8.6% year on year to 2.5 million tonnes as tariffs and anti-dumping duties took effect.

How important are autos and construction for Brazilian steel?

Brazil’s steel market is structurally tied to construction, automotive and infrastructure, with automotive output across Latin America up 1.1% year on year in the first four months of 2026 and construction activity broadly flat, providing a crucial floor for demand.

Why does Ternium trade differently from Brazilian mills?

Ternium benefits from both Mexican tariff protection against cheap imports and its integration into the North American supply chain, with local flat-steel prices in Mexico supported by recent increases that lifted hot-rolled coil ex-works northeast Mexico to about 760-762 dollars per tonne, giving it a firmer pricing backdrop than some Brazilian peers.

03 What moved it

Verified data point to supply‑side constraints as the prime driver keeping zinc elevated rather than any sudden surge in demand: supply disruptions at smelters in Kazakhstan, the gradual recovery of Nexa’s operations in Peru, and lingering issues at European mines have collectively tightened refined metal availability even as global macroeconomic headwinds persist. This picture is echoed in company reporting, where Nexa’s Q1 2026 update highlighted that zinc prices advanced 4 percent during the period to 3,185 dollars per tonne, supported by concentrate tightness and low London Metal Exchange inventories that have left smelter margins severely compressed.

On the demand side, analysts still frame galvanised‑steel and construction as the key end‑uses to watch, with softer orders from consuming industries cited as a reason why zinc futures eased earlier in July despite the underlying tightness in supply. The international demand profile remains uneven: growth has been strong enough in China, India, the United States and Europe to push refined zinc consumption higher overall, but declines in Brazil and Peru show that Latin America itself is not immune to a softer construction and manufacturing cycle.

04 The Latin American read

Latin America continues to be central to the zinc story because of its mine supply footprint, with Peru, Mexico and Bolivia ranked among the world’s largest zinc producers by recent industry and survey data. Nexa Resources’ operations in Peru and Brazil and Buenaventura’s mines across Peru therefore offer foreign investors a practical way to gain exposure to the region’s role in the global zinc chain, from ore extraction through to smelting and sales into galvanising and construction markets.

Company disclosures underline how this regional production base is responding to current price signals: Nexa reported zinc mine production rising 18 percent year‑on‑year to 79,000 tonnes in Q1 2026, alongside a 13 percent increase in smelting zinc sales to 147,000 tonnes as Brazilian smelters recovered. Buenaventura, meanwhile, reported average realised Q2 2026 zinc prices of 3,451 dollars per metric ton, showing that Peruvian producers have been able to secure attractive terms even while managing mixed demand across metals and geographies.

05 The names to watch

Nexa Resources stands out as the purest Latin American proxy for zinc, with consolidated mining zinc production of 316,000 tonnes in 2025 and guidance that points to a further 6 percent increase at the midpoint in 2026, driven by higher output at Brazilian assets such as Vazante and Atacocha and expanding production at the Aripuanã mine. The company’s own outlook ties zinc’s price resilience to tight concentrate availability, low exchange inventories and demand linked to galvanising and infrastructure, reinforcing why its share price tends to respond quickly to any change in the physical zinc market.

Buenaventura offers a broader metals exposure while still providing a meaningful zinc read‑through: its latest filings show a diversified revenue mix, with Q2 2026 realised prices of 4,342 dollars an ounce for gold, 89.52 dollars an ounce for silver, 1,852 dollars per metric ton for lead, 3,451 dollars per metric ton for zinc and 14,029 dollars per metric ton for copper. For foreign investors, that means Buenaventura can benefit from zinc’s strength while being cushioned or amplified by moves in precious metals, making it a useful comparative name against the more zinc‑focused Nexa when gauging regional sentiment.

06 The outlook

Forecasts from macro and bank analysts suggest zinc is likely to remain elevated through the rest of 2026, though perhaps with less drama than earlier in the year: Trading Economics projects prices near 3,570.97 dollars by quarter‑end and 3,755.81 dollars in 12 months, while JP Morgan expects London Metal Exchange zinc to average between 3,400 and 3,500 dollars per metric ton for the remainder of the year. At the same time, broader research points to mine supply growth and new capacity gradually pushing the market toward a surplus of more than 270,000 metric tons in 2026, which would cap upside unless demand from galvanised‑steel and construction re‑accelerates in Latin America, Asia and Europe.

07 What to watch

Galvanised‑steel demand: Watch order books for galvanised‑steel makers in China, India, the United States and Latin America, because these flows into construction and automotive sectors will determine whether zinc’s multi‑year highs are sustained or fade.

Watch order books for galvanised‑steel makers in China, India, the United States and Latin America, because these flows into construction and automotive sectors will determine whether zinc’s multi‑year highs are sustained or fade. Smelter treatment charges: Track spot and benchmark treatment charges for zinc concentrate, which are currently near historically low levels and squeezing smelter margins; any rebound would signal easing supply tightness and could soften price support.

Track spot and benchmark treatment charges for zinc concentrate, which are currently near historically low levels and squeezing smelter margins; any rebound would signal easing supply tightness and could soften price support. Latin American mine output: Monitor production updates from key Latin American producers in Peru, Mexico and Bolivia, including guidance changes from Nexa Resources and Buenaventura, as any disruption or expansion directly feeds into the global mine supply story.

Inventory levels on exchanges: Follow zinc inventory data on the London Metal Exchange and other exchanges, because critically low stocks outside China have been a major pillar of price support and any sustained rebuild would point to a loosening market.

Frequently Asked Questions

How high are zinc prices compared with recent history?

London Metal Exchange spot zinc is quoted around 3,529.00 dollars per tonne, close to levels last seen four years ago, which places current prices in the upper band of recent trading ranges rather than at absolute record highs.

Is the global zinc market in surplus or deficit?

Preliminary data from the International Lead and Zinc Study Group show a global refined zinc deficit of 33,000 tons in 2025, down from a 69,000‑ton shortfall in 2024, even as mine production rose 5.4 percent and refined output grew 2.1 percent.

Why are smelter margins under pressure despite strong prices?

Smelter margins are being squeezed because treatment charges for zinc concentrate have fallen to historically low levels, with the annual benchmark for 2026 at just 85 dollars per tonne, reflecting tight concentrate availability even as refined prices stay high.

How exposed are Nexa Resources and Buenaventura to zinc?

Nexa Resources is heavily exposed to zinc, with 316,000 tonnes of consolidated zinc production in 2025 and guidance for higher volumes in 2026, whereas Buenaventura has significant zinc output but also large gold, silver, lead and copper businesses, making it a more diversified proxy for Peru’s mining sector.

01 The session in one read

The latest settled lithium session delivered a clear message to foreign investors: equities have turned up again, while the underlying commodity is merely pausing rather than collapsing. LIT, the Global X Lithium & Battery Tech ETF that bundles miners and battery-tech shares, closed at 69.08 dollars, up 3.23 percent day-on-day, underscoring renewed appetite for leveraged exposure to the sector’s earnings rather than a rush into physical lithium.

Albemarle, one of the largest integrated lithium producers, edged higher to 118.62 dollars, up 0.36 percent, and Chile’s SQM ended at 68.84 dollars, up 1.70 percent, after a previous session in which both had pulled back on profit-taking. This combination of modest share-price gains and almost flat spot prices suggests a market that is reassessing its fears of oversupply while still recognising that Triangle resources and EV demand keep the long-term story intact.

Assessment — Equities outrun cautious spot market MEDIUM Across today’s tape, lithium-linked equities look ahead to a world where electric vehicles and grid batteries keep demand expanding rapidly, while the spot market digests high inventories and new salt-lake output from China. That divergence makes this a session where investors in LIT, Albemarle and SQM are effectively betting that the structural story – especially in the Lithium Triangle – will overwhelm short-term wobbles in prices, with the variable to watch being how quickly new brine and hard-rock projects actually ramp up into meaningful supply.

02 The board

Reading the board that sits behind these moves, the first thing a foreign investor should note is that LIT is an equity fund that tracks lithium miners and battery-tech names, not the price of lithium itself, so its 69.08 dollars close and 3.23 percent rise measure confidence in corporate earnings and future volumes rather than today’s carbonate quote. Albemarle’s 118.62 dollars and SQM’s 68.84 dollars – both higher into the close – tell a similar story: investors are willing to pay slightly more for the biggest listed gateways into the Lithium Triangle and broader supply chain despite continued talk of oversupply in China’s futures market.

By contrast with these equity moves, global battery-grade lithium carbonate has only eased marginally, with recent readings around 22.38 dollars per kilogram worldwide and about 151,500 yuan per tonne in China, down roughly 0.20–0.33 percent after an earlier rebound. The board therefore shows share prices that have moved more than the commodity itself, pointing to positioning, sentiment and expectations rather than any overnight shock in physical demand or supply.

03 What moved it

The immediate driver of this session’s equity strength is a recalibration of the demand narrative: electric vehicles now account for roughly 63–70 percent of lithium use, and battery-grade carbonate prices have rebounded sharply from late-2025 lows as supply disruptions and stronger-than-expected orders from cathode and battery plants have bitten. Investors are also increasingly focused on stationary energy storage – large batteries for power grids and solar farms – with Macquarie forecasting global lithium demand growth of more than 20 percent per year through to 2030, even as EV sales growth slows.

On the supply side, the market is processing a short-term picture of high inventories and seasonal brine output from Chinese salt lakes, which recently nudged prices down only 0.20–0.33 percent, against a longer-term view that mine supply of lithium carbonate equivalent will have to almost double from 470,000 tonnes now to 875,000 tonnes by 2030. Rumours that big Chinese projects and a potential restart at a major CATL-linked mine could add substantial tonnage have weighed on futures, but several analyses still describe the market from 2026 onward as structurally tight, supporting today’s firmer tone in miners.

04 The Latin American read

For Latin America, the Lithium Triangle remains the gravitational centre of the story, with Argentina, Bolivia and Chile together holding about 53–60 percent of the world’s identified lithium resources and already providing close to a third of global supply. Argentina alone has more than 80 projects moving through exploration and construction and nine active operations, Chile has two major producing projects, and Bolivia – despite hosting roughly 23 million tonnes of resources and around 15 percent of global identified reserves – has only one significant producer and negligible output.

This imbalance between vast resources and uneven production is why foreign capital watches Triangle politics so closely: Chile’s debates on state control, Argentina’s efforts to stabilise its macro environment, and Bolivia’s hunt for technology partners all influence how quickly new brine projects can be financed and built. South America’s share of global supply is forecast to stay roughly around 28 percent between 2026 and 2035, implying that many of the tonnes needed to meet EV and storage demand must still come from these salt flats, keeping the region central to the lithium investment thesis.

05 The names to watch

Albemarle and SQM remain the flagship names for foreign investors seeking pure-play exposure to mining in the Lithium Triangle, with Albemarle active in Chilean brines and SQM deeply embedded in Chile’s salar de Atacama. Brokerage research still rates both as strong buys, noting that Albemarle’s earnings per share in 2026 are expected to rise almost tenfold year-on-year, while SQM enjoys higher return on equity and a portfolio that straddles fertilisers and specialty chemicals as well as lithium.

Beyond these giants, investors track LIT’s holdings list, which includes other Triangle players such as Allkem, Livent and Lithium Argentina, along with Asian and North American battery producers that translate lithium prices into cell margins. Given that LIT is a diversified basket, its movements provide a quick read on market sentiment toward the whole ecosystem – from evaporation ponds in Jujuy and the Atacama to gigafactories in China and the United States – making it a convenient barometer for regional and global lithium risk.

06 The outlook

Looking ahead, most specialised forecasters still expect lithium prices to remain elevated in the near term, supported by delayed supply growth, cautious project financing and robust demand from both EVs and energy storage, even if the headline balance for 2026 looks like a nominal surplus. At the same time, the Lithium Triangle’s long project timelines and Bolivia’s slow ramp-up mean South America’s contribution to supply will grow only gradually, so any disappointment on new tonnage could quickly tighten the market again – leaving investors fixated on permitting decisions, brine technology performance and the real pace of project execution as the variable to watch.

07 What to watch

Chinese lithium futures: Because sharp moves on the Guangzhou exchange, driven by oversupply fears or mine restarts, can quickly spill over into sentiment on LIT and Triangle miners even when physical demand is steady.

Because sharp moves on the Guangzhou exchange, driven by oversupply fears or mine restarts, can quickly spill over into sentiment on LIT and Triangle miners even when physical demand is steady. Triangle project approvals: Because environmental and political decisions in Chile, Argentina and Bolivia will determine whether the region can deliver the forecast 28 percent share of global supply through 2035.

Because environmental and political decisions in Chile, Argentina and Bolivia will determine whether the region can deliver the forecast 28 percent share of global supply through 2035. EV and storage demand: Because electric vehicles already dominate lithium use and energy storage is expected to maintain more than 20 percent annual demand growth, underpinning miners’ earnings and justifying today’s equity strength.

Because electric vehicles already dominate lithium use and energy storage is expected to maintain more than 20 percent annual demand growth, underpinning miners’ earnings and justifying today’s equity strength. Global spot carbonate prices: Because small percentage changes around the current 22.38 dollars per kilogram and 151,500 yuan per tonne levels can signal shifts in inventories and salt-lake output that precede larger moves in equities.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is LIT a direct play on lithium prices?

No, LIT is an exchange-traded fund holding shares in lithium miners and battery-tech companies, so its price reflects equity market sentiment and corporate earnings rather than the day-to-day spot price of lithium carbonate or hydroxide.

How important is the Lithium Triangle to global supply?

Extremely: Argentina, Bolivia and Chile together host roughly 53–60 percent of the world’s identified lithium resources and are expected to account for around 28 percent of global supply between 2026 and 2035.

Why did miners rise if spot prices barely moved?

Because investors are focusing on forecasts of strong EV and energy-storage demand, structural tightness in mine supply and improving earnings for major producers, rather than the small 0.20–0.33 percent dip in spot prices seen in recent sessions.

Is oversupply still a risk for lithium?

Yes, especially in the short term: Chinese futures have sold off on expectations of oversupply around 2027 and possible large mine restarts, but many analysts still see the market swinging back toward tightness or deficit as demand growth outpaces realistic project delivery.

03 What moved it

Gold’s modest climb is rooted in a delicate balance between safe-haven buying and the reality of high real interest rates, with US 10-year Treasury yields stuck in the mid-4% area after stronger employment data nudged the Federal Reserve into a more hawkish stance, raising the opportunity cost of holding a metal that pays no income.

Silver’s outsized move reflects that same macro backdrop plus its own dynamics: traders see repeated deficits in physical supply, strong demand from sectors such as solar panels, vehicles and electronics, and the metal’s tendency to respond more sharply than gold when investors rotate towards assets that can hedge both inflation and technological change.

04 The Latin American read

Mexico sits at the heart of this story as the world’s largest silver producer, with mine output of about 6,300 metric tons in 2024, even as the Silver Institute notes that Mexican production fell by roughly 5 percent in 2023, underscoring how hard it has become to grow supply at today’s prices.

Peru, the third-largest silver producer with around 3,100 metric tons of output in 2024 and estimated reserves of 91,000 metric tonnes, adds a second Latin American pillar, meaning that investors across the region are effectively living inside the global silver market’s supply-and-demand tensions.

05 The names to watch

On the corporate side, Mexican and Peruvian miners are obvious bellwethers: the Silver Institute points to Mexico, China and Peru as the top three mine producers, while company-level updates such as First Majestic’s 3.8 million ounces of silver in Q2 2026 show how operational performance and cost guidance can translate global price swings into local earnings and employment.

For silver-focused investors, national policy risk is just as important as geology: research highlighting resource nationalism in Peru and concerns over Mexico’s ability to sustain production suggests that any changes to tax regimes, environmental rules or export frameworks could have an outsized impact on market balances and, by extension, on regional currencies and equity indices.

06 The outlook

Looking ahead, the key question is whether high and possibly persistent US real yields keep gold in a sideways range while silver’s structural deficit, driven by industrial demand and constrained mine supply from countries like Mexico and Peru, forces the market to reprice the metal upwards again if any new geopolitical shock or policy change tightens the screws further.

07 What to watch

US real yields: Because firm inflation-adjusted Treasury yields raise the cost of holding gold and silver, any shift lower could unlock a more forceful safe-haven rally.

Because firm inflation-adjusted Treasury yields raise the cost of holding gold and silver, any shift lower could unlock a more forceful safe-haven rally. Silver supply from Mexico: Because Mexico is the top silver producer, further declines in output or policy moves that limit exports would deepen the global deficit and amplify price volatility.

Because Mexico is the top silver producer, further declines in output or policy moves that limit exports would deepen the global deficit and amplify price volatility. Peru’s mining policy and social stability: Because Peru is a key silver miner with vast reserves, renewed social unrest or regulatory tightening could constrain supply and push the market to reprice risk premia.

Because Peru is a key silver miner with vast reserves, renewed social unrest or regulatory tightening could constrain supply and push the market to reprice risk premia. Industrial demand for silver: Because demand from solar, automotive and electronics is growing, any acceleration in clean-energy and technology investment would widen the gap between silver’s physical needs and available mine output.

Frequently Asked Questions

How did gold perform in the latest session?

Gold closed at 4,101 $/oz with a 0.50% day-on-day gain, holding just above the 4,000 level as investors balance safe-haven demand against the drag from high US real yields.

Why did silver move more than gold?

Silver rose to 58.86 $/oz, up 4.45% on the day, because its market is facing repeated supply deficits and strong industrial demand, making it more sensitive than gold to shifts in risk appetite and macro expectations.

Why are Mexico and Peru so important for silver?

Mexico is the world’s largest silver producer and Peru is the third, together anchoring global mine supply, so any production change, policy shift or social unrest in these countries directly affects the balance of the worldwide silver market.

What should a foreign investor in Latin America watch next?

A foreign investor should track US real yields, silver supply data from Mexico and Peru, and policy or social developments in those mining jurisdictions, because these variables will drive both global precious-metal prices and local market performance in the region.

World.title: WEG Q2 Preview: Analysts See an 8% Profit Dip
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Net revenue estimate. Analysts project net revenue around R$ 9.97 billion (US$ 1.96 billion), a roughly 3% decline from a year earlier. —Net income forecast. Bradesco BBI sees net income falling 8% year-on-year to approximately R$ 1.47 billion (US$ 289 million). —Margin pressure. The EBITDA margin is expected to hover near 21%, squeezed by currency effects and factory expansion spending. —Release timing. WEG typically publishes second-quarter results in late July or early August, putting the report days away. —Share price context. Bank of America and Citi hold neutral ratings with target prices near R$ 50 (US$ 9.84), implying modest upside.

WEG, the Brazilian multinational that manufactures electric motors, generators, and transformers, is expected to report weaker second-quarter results within the next two weeks, according to estimates compiled from major financial institutions.

WEG manufactures electric motors and industrial equipment for global markets.

What WEG Makes and Why It Matters

WEG is one of Latin America’s largest industrial groups, producing everything from industrial electric motors and power transformers to automotive alternators and home-appliance components. Its equipment drives factory floors, wind turbines, transmission grids, and household appliances across more than 135 countries.

For Brazil’s export story, an electric motor maker carries outsized weight. WEG converts domestic engineering into high-value manufactured goods sold abroad, making it a bellwether for the country’s industrial competitiveness and a direct beneficiary—or victim—of currency swings.

To understand why a motor manufacturer matters so much, it helps to think of WEG as the hidden backbone inside other industries. When a mining company in Chile installs a conveyor belt, a water utility in the Middle East upgrades its pumps, or a wind farm in the United States raises new turbines, there is a good chance a WEG motor or transformer sits at the heart of that operation.

That reach means the company’s quarterly numbers are not just a report card on one firm—they are a temperature check on global industrial investment.

The Numbers: What Analysts Are Previewing

Bradesco BBI forecasts net revenue of R$ 9.97 billion (US$ 1.96 billion), down roughly 3% from the same quarter in 2025. Safra and Citi publish similar top-line estimates, while BTG Pactual’s consensus sits slightly lower at R$ 9.8 billion (US$ 1.93 billion).

Net income is expected to land near R$ 1.47 billion (US$ 289 million), an 8% year-on-year decline. EBITDA should reach about R$ 2.1 billion (US$ 413 million), implying a margin around 21%, a touch below last year’s level.

For readers less familiar with Brazilian financial shorthand, EBITDA stands for earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization. It is a widely used gauge of a company’s operating profitability because it strips out costs that can vary heavily depending on accounting choices and debt structure.

A 21% EBITDA margin means that for every R$ 100 of revenue, WEG keeps roughly R$ 21 as operating profit—a healthy level for a manufacturer, though the expected dip signals that costs are rising faster than sales right now.

Why WEG’s Results Are Under Pressure

A stronger Brazilian real is the main headwind. The exchange rate has hovered near R$ 5.05 per US dollar, reducing the local-currency value of revenue earned abroad by an estimated 3% to 5%.

WEG generates a large share of its sales outside Brazil, so a firmer real directly compresses reported top-line figures.

Costs tied to transformer factory expansion in Brazil are also eating into margins. While the new capacity should support future revenue growth, the near-term drag is showing up in analyst spreadsheets.

Slower domestic demand for industrial equipment adds a third layer of caution.

The currency effect deserves a closer look because it works in a way that can feel counterintuitive. WEG sells products in dollars, euros, and other foreign currencies, but it reports its financials in Brazilian reais.

When the real gains strength against those currencies—as it has done recently—each dollar of foreign sales translates into fewer reais on the income statement. The underlying business may be perfectly healthy in local terms abroad, yet the reported revenue and profit shrink simply because of the exchange-rate math.

That is why analysts and investors watch the real so closely when assessing Brazilian exporters.

The Bigger Picture: WEG’s Role in a Shifting Economy

WEG’s performance often mirrors broader trends in Latin America’s largest economy. When the real strengthens, Brazilian exporters across the board see their overseas earnings shrink when converted back to local currency, and WEG is no exception.

The company’s transformer expansion is a strategic bet on long-term electrification demand, both in Brazil and abroad. For foreign investors, this kind of capital expenditure signals confidence in future orders, even if it temporarily weighs on profitability and keeps the stock in a holding pattern.

That electrification trend is worth understanding on its own terMs Around the world, grids are being upgraded to handle renewable energy, data centers are multiplying, and industrial processes are switching from fossil fuels to electricity. Transformers are the critical link that steps voltage up for long-distance transmission and back down for safe use in factories and homes.

By expanding its transformer capacity now, WEG is positioning itself to capture orders that may take years to materialize fully—a classic case of short-term pain for long-term gain.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For expats and foreign investors holding Brazilian assets, a weaker quarterly report from a blue-chip industrial name like WEG can reinforce caution about the country’s near-term growth story. Currency volatility remains a double-edged sword: a stronger real helps your purchasing power locally but can hurt the companies in your portfolio that depend on exports.

Analysts at Safra and Itaú BBA note that as transformer capacity comes online and if currency pressures ease, revenue growth could reaccelerate in the second half of 2026. That potential recovery makes the current dip worth watching for those considering entry points into Brazilian industrials.

What Comes Next for Investors

WEG has not yet confirmed the exact publication date, but the company historically releases second-quarter figures between July 30 and early August. That puts the report roughly ten days away from the current date of July 21, 2026.

Despite the cautious preview, some analysts see a progressive recovery later in the year. Bank of America and Citi maintain neutral ratings with target prices near R$ 50 (US$ 9.84), implying modest upside from current levels.

The market will be listening closely for any update on transformer orders and export demand during the earnings call.

Beyond the headline numbers, several open questions will shape how investors react. Will management signal that the currency headwind is easing, or could the real strengthen further?

Are the new transformer lines already booking orders that will show up in the second half, or is the demand picture still uncertain? And how is WEG navigating the softer domestic market—through price adjustments, cost cuts, or a shift in sales mix toward export markets?

The answers to those questions, rather than the raw profit figure alone, are likely to drive the stock’s next move.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does WEG manufacture?

WEG produces electric motors, generators, power transformers, automotive components such as alternators and starters, and motors for home appliances and HVAC systems. The company sells to more than 135 countries and is a key player in industrial electrification.

Why are WEG’s Q2 2026 earnings expected to decline?

Analysts point to a stronger Brazilian real reducing export revenue, costs tied to transformer factory expansion, and softer domestic demand for industrial equipment. The exchange rate near R$ 5.05 per US dollar has trimmed the local-currency value of overseas sales by an estimated 3% to 5%.

When will WEG publish its second-quarter 2026 results?

WEG has not confirmed the exact date, but based on historical patterns the report is expected between late July and early August 2026. Investors typically receive the full earnings release and a conference call with management shortly after publication.

World.title: Argentina’s Javier Milei Heads to Brazil for Trade, Not Lula
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts —Primary event Milei will headline a campaign rally for presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro in São Paulo on July 25. —Blocked visit A Supreme Court justice barred Milei from visiting former President Jair Bolsonaro, who remains under house arrest in Brasília. —No Lula meeting The agenda includes no bilateral talks with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva or his ministers. —Trade mission Milei frames the trip as part of an outward-looking strategy to attract commerce and investment to Argentina. —Regional tour The Brazil stop precedes visits to Peru, Colombia, and Ecuador to meet conservative allies.

Javier Milei touches down in São Paulo on July 25 for what his team calls an investment and trade outreach mission, though the official agenda revolves around a single campaign rally for a key political ally.

Argentine President Javier Milei is a libertarian economist leading South America's second-largest economy.

A Campaign Stop With a Commercial Pitch

The Argentine president will headline an event backing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL), who is mounting a bid to unseat President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in next year’s general election.

Milei’s advisers insist the trip is not purely political. They describe it as one leg of an outward-looking tour designed to unlock more commerce and investment for Argentina’s struggling economy.

The rally is contingent on Flávio Bolsonaro’s formal anointment as the PL candidate at the party convention, a step that is scheduled for July 25 and would clear the way for the high-profile endorsement.

For foreign observers, the fusion of a campaign event with a trade mission reflects Milei’s unconventional diplomatic style, one that often blurs the line between statecraft and ideological alliance-building.

Why Javier Milei Is Betting on Brazil

Brazil remains Argentina’s largest trading partner, absorbing roughly 15 percent of its exports, from wheat and automobiles to natural gas.

Milei wants to deepen those commercial channels and has signaled he will use every foreign stop to pitch Argentina as a deregulated, investor-friendly destination.

Argentina’s economy has long relied on Brazilian demand for its manufactured goods and agricultural products, a relationship that becomes even more critical during periods of domestic recession.

By framing the São Paulo stop as a trade mission, Milei aims to reassure Brazilian business leaders that political drama will not derail the deep commercial interdependence between the two neighbors.

Mercosur Tensions Simmer in the Background

The trip highlights the awkward state of the Mercosur trade bloc, which also includes Uruguay and Paraguay. Milei has criticized the group’s protectionist rules and, as our reporting has shown, has repeatedly threatened to exit the bloc if necessary to pursue a free trade agreement with the United States.

Brazilian officials note that no Mercosur summit or formal negotiation session is scheduled during the visit, leaving the bloc’s reform debate for another day.

Mercosur has struggled for years to finalize a long-awaited trade agreement with the European Union, and Milei’s skepticism toward the bloc adds a new layer of uncertainty for investors watching the region.

For expats and companies operating across South America, any move to weaken Mercosur could reshape supply chains, customs procedures, and the ease of moving goods and personnel between member countries.

The Blocked Bolsonaro Visit and What Comes Next

As The Rio Times previously reported, Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes rejected Milei’s request to visit former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is confined to his Brasília home and barred from receiving political visitors.

The court ruling, issued on July 18, specifically prohibits visits of a “political-electoral nature” to the former president, who is already restricted to receiving only family, doctors, lawyers, and healthcare staff.

Milei had publicly stated his intention to greet Jair Bolsonaro personally, making the judicial block a symbolic setback that underscores the legal constraints surrounding Brazil’s former leader.

After São Paulo, Milei travels to Lima for Keiko Fujimori’s inauguration on July 28, then to Colombia in early August for Abelardo de la Espriella’s event, and finally to Ecuador to meet President Daniel Noboa, reinforcing his strategy of aligning with conservative leaders across the region.

What This Means for Expats and Investors

For foreign residents and investors in Argentina and Brazil, Milei’s trip signals both opportunity and political risk. His pro-market rhetoric may open doors for deregulation and foreign capital, but the absence of formal government-to-government talks leaves bilateral policy uncertain.

Brazilian companies with Argentine subsidiaries, and vice versa, should watch for any post-visit shifts in trade facilitation or regulatory tone, even if no agreements are signed this week.

The political polarization on display—Milei campaigning for Lula’s rival while ignoring Brasília—could also affect the mood in cross-border business forums and investor conferences in the months ahead.

The Broader Regional Picture

Milei’s multi-country tour reflects a deliberate effort to build a network of like-minded conservative leaders at a time when left-leaning governments still hold sway in several major Latin American economies.

By visiting Peru, Colombia, and Ecuador immediately after Brazil, Milei is stitching together a coalition that could influence regional policy debates on trade, security, and the future of multilateral blocs like Mercosur and the Pacific Alliance.

For tourists and short-term visitors, the political maneuvering is unlikely to disrupt travel plans, but those doing business across borders should monitor whether the ideological alignment translates into concrete bilateral deals down the line.

Background: Foreign Investors No Longer Fear a Lula Win — They’re Watching the Fed Instead.

Background: Brazil’s Own VP Calls Its Tax System a ‘Madhouse’ That Repels Investors.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Javier Milei meeting President Lula during this trip?

No. The agenda contains no bilateral meeting with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva or any Brazilian government minister. The visit is focused entirely on the campaign rally for Flávio Bolsonaro and Milei’s broader investment outreach.

Why was Milei barred from visiting Jair Bolsonaro?

A Brazilian Supreme Court ruling, issued by Justice Alexandre de Moraes on July 18, prohibits visits of a political-electoral nature to the former president. Jair Bolsonaro remains under house arrest in Brasília and is only allowed to receive family members, doctors, lawyers, and healthcare staff.

What is the main trade goal of Milei’s Brazil stop?

Milei aims to attract Brazilian investment and strengthen commercial ties by promoting Argentina as a deregulated, investor-friendly market. However, no formal trade talks or Mercosur negotiation sessions are scheduled during this visit, making the commercial pitch largely rhetorical for now.

World.title: Hattieville man fined $305 for $50 sledgehammer from employer who would not give him payment in advance
World.content:
Hattieville man fined $305 for $50 sledgehammer from employer who would not give him payment in advance

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Hattieville construction worker has been fined more than six times the value of a sledgehammer he admitted stealing from a man who hired him for a day’s work after he would not give him an advance in payment.

Forty-two-year-old Felix Larance Petillo appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday and was charged with stealing a red Truper-brand sledgehammer, valued at $50, from a construction worker who had hired him.

Petillo initially pleaded not guilty and was offered bail of $1,000. However, while waiting to secure bail, he returned to court and changed his plea to guilty.

Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison fined him $300, along with $5 in court costs. He was given until August 31, 2026, to pay or serve two weeks in prison.

According to the allegations, the construction worker hired Petillo on July 19 to assist with removing cement material from a demolished house on Locario Street in Hattieville.

Later that evening, Petillo reportedly asked for an advance payment for work scheduled for the following day. When the construction worker refused, Petillo allegedly threatened to take some of his tools.

The following morning, the construction worker discovered that his sledgehammer was missing and reported the matter to police.

Police later detained Petillo, who reportedly admitted placing the tool inside a mechanic’s vehicle. The mechanic subsequently handed the sledgehammer over to police and was not charged.

World.title: Businessman Miguel Guerra shot during armed robbery at Hand Money Loans; $80 stolen
World.content:
Businessman Miguel Guerra shot during armed robbery at Hand Money Loans; $80 stolen

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an armed robbery in Belize City that left a 67-year-old businessman injured on Tuesday morning.

The incident occurred at approximately 11:15 a.m. at Handy Money Loans on Handyside Street.

Police said the suspect entered the establishment under the pretense of pawning a cellphone before producing a firearm and demanding money.

The robber reportedly fled with approximately $80 in cash after firing a single shot at the businessman, Miguel Angel Guerra.

Guerra was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he is receiving medical treatment.

Police investigations continue.

World.title: Joseph Vaccaro receives disclosure in Gaston Barrow murder case
World.content:
Joseph Vaccaro receives disclosure in Gaston Barrow murder case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Thirty-year-old taxi operator Joseph Gabourel Vaccaro has received disclosure in the murder case stemming from the September 2025 shooting death of Gaston Barrow at Old Belize.

Vaccaro, a resident of Cumberbatch Street, appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday.

He was provided with 154 pages of disclosure, five compact discs and photographs forming part of the prosecution’s evidence. The matter was adjourned until September 7, 2026, when a preliminary inquiry is scheduled to begin.

Vaccaro was first arraigned for Barrow’s murder on October 6, 2025, and was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Police said Barrow and another man, Hank Carr, were shot at the Old Belize compound on the night of September 28, 2025. Barrow was pronounced dead on arrival at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, while Carr was treated and later released.

Investigators allege Carr was driving a vehicle with Barrow in the front passenger seat when a gunman near a taxi opened fire. The shooter reportedly entered the taxi and escaped towards the nearby police checkpoint.

Police later reviewed surveillance footage from the area, which reportedly led to Vaccaro’s detention and subsequent charge.
