World.title: Ministry of Sustainable Development and Statistical Institute of Belize sign 4-year MoU to strengthen coordination of National Development Data
World.content:
Ministry of Sustainable Development and Statistical Institute of Belize sign 4-year MoU to strengthen coordination of National Development Data

By Zoila Palma: The Sustainable Development Unit (SDU), under the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management (MSDCCSWM), and the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB) signed a four-year Memorandum of Understanding to strengthen the coordination, management, and dissemination of Belize’s national development data.

The agreement was signed during the National SDG and Statistical System Workshop at the Grand Resort Residences on July 16, 2026, by Milagro Matus, Chief Executive Officer of the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management, and Diana Castillo, Director General of the Statistical Institute of Belize.

“The partnership establishes a collaborative framework for coordinating the collection, validation, reporting, and dissemination of three important sets of development indicators: the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for Small Island Developing States (ABAS), and the #PlanBelize Medium-Term Development Strategy (MTDS) 2.0. These indicators will be made publicly available through the Belize National Statistical System (BNSS) Portal, providing policymakers, researchers, and the public with improved access to official development statistics,” the Ministry explained.

Through this Agreement, the SIB will collect the data from the respective producing agencies, validate the information, and publish the indicators on the portal. The SDU will lead national coordination for SDG and ABAS reporting, including Belize’s Voluntary National Reviews, while promoting stronger collaboration among ministries, departments, and agencies to improve data sharing, harmonize indicator frameworks, and encourage the use of the BNSS Portal as the country’s primary source of official development statistics.

The signing concluded a workshop during which participants approved the Interim SDG Progress Report 2025, the SDG Data Ecosystem Prioritization and Action Plan 2026-2030, and the Statistical Capacities and Needs Assessment 2026, all of which will guide future work. The workshop was supported by the Protected Areas Conservation Trust (PACT), the Green Climate Fund (GCF), and the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA).

World.title: Government of Belize and UNICEF launch landmark Climate Landscape Analysis for Children and Vulnerable Populations
World.content:
Government of Belize and UNICEF launch landmark Climate Landscape Analysis for Children and Vulnerable Populations

By Zoila Palma: On July 17, 2026, the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management, through its Sustainable Development Unit (SDU) and Climate Change Department (CCD), in partnership with UNICEF Belize, officially launched the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children Plus (CLAC+) Report.

The CLAC+ Report is the first comprehensive national assessment of how climate change, environmental, energy, and disasters (CEED) affect children and other vulnerable populations in Belize, including persons with disabilities, Indigenous Peoples, and pregnant and lactating women. It provides evidence-based recommendations to strengthen climate resilience and promote more inclusive policies and programmes that better address the needs of those most at risk.

The Ministry explained that the report offers a critical foundation for strengthening national policies, investments, and programmes that protect children and vulnerable communities from the growing impacts of climate change. Its recommendations encourage a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach to climate action by fostering stronger collaboration across sectors, including health, education, social protection, disaster risk management, environmental management, and sustainable development.

The official launch marks an important milestone in Belize’s efforts to advance evidence-based climate action and resilient development.

It brought together representatives from government, development partners, civil society, academia, youth organizations, and other stakeholders to share the report’s findings, discuss priority actions, and strengthen partnerships for implementation.

World.title: International News: Extreme weather raises concerns over commodity markets
World.content:
International News: Extreme weather raises concerns over commodity markets

By Zoila Palma: Commodity strategists are warning that financial markets may be underestimating the impact of increasingly volatile weather, as Europe experiences intense heat and forecasters raise concerns about a potentially powerful El Niño event later this year.

The World Meteorological Organization expects a strong El Niño to develop in the tropical Pacific between July and September, a climate pattern that can trigger shifts in temperatures and rainfall and contribute to extreme weather worldwide.

Agriculture is expected to be among the sectors most affected, with crops including corn, coffee, cocoa and wheat particularly vulnerable to heat stress, drought and changing rainfall patterns, CNBC reports.

Analysts say prolonged extreme weather could reduce crop yields and drive food prices higher.

The potential impact on commodities is expected to vary widely.

Bank of America analysts have identified corn as particularly vulnerable to weather risks in Europe, Brazil and the United States, while warning that sugar production in Brazil and Thailand could decline sharply due to El Niño-related conditions.

Meanwhile, milder winters could reduce demand for natural gas, potentially putting downward pressure on prices.

Extreme heat is also raising concerns for metals, with drought threatening water-intensive copper production and high temperatures increasing electricity demand for aluminum smelting.

World.title: International News: US urges isolation of Nicaragua after Ortega vows to end elections
World.content:
International News: US urges isolation of Nicaragua after Ortega vows to end elections

By Zoila Palma: The United States is urging countries across the Western Hemisphere to isolate Nicaragua after President Daniel Ortega vowed that his government would no longer hold elections.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Ortega’s declaration exposes the “true authoritarian nature” of his government and warned that Nicaragua cannot expect “business as usual” with other nations while rejecting democratic rule.

Rubio said Ortega and his wife, Vice President Rosario Murillo, have “abandoned even the pretense of popular consent.”

In a separate statement, the U.S. Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs called on regional partners to work together to ensure that Nicaraguans can eventually choose a future free from what it described as tyranny.

Ortega made the pledge during a speech on Sunday, saying elections would no longer be held because they could allow U.S.-backed movements to take power.

“There won’t be any more elections here for them to try to seize the government and seize power,” Ortega said, as he defended his government’s continued grip on power.

Ortega, 80, has been in power continuously since 2007, while constitutional reforms adopted last year established his wife as co-president and extended the presidential term to six years.

World.title: JLP condemns ‘vile’ alleged NaRRA voicenotes featuring PNP executives
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) says it has taken note of voicenotes leaked on traditional and social media in which two PNP executive members are allegedly heard confirming the PNP’s preparedness to implement delay tactics and use baseless allegations to smear “patriotic Jamaicans”.

In a statement on Tuesday, the JLP said media reports have indicated that the voicenotes were sent in a PNP executive WhatsApp group on May 27, 2026, shortly after Major General Antony Anderson was announced to head the National Resilience and Reconstruction Authority (NaRRA).

In the first piece of leaked audio the statement quotes, a PNP executive member whom it says may be heard stating:

“Bear in mind that the NaRRA is what the JLP sees as its glory and its saviour for a fourth term. So they see NaRRA as a saving grace and they are going to do everything in their power to try to get things done, which means bypassing, like all parish council, which, you know, we probably would do delay tactics, and they don’t get it, which is why they did it that way. But safety standards and these things is a concern. So let’s continue to play our ball game of politics.”

In the second piece of audio, which has gone viral in the public domain, a member of the PNP executive is heard referencing Major General Anderson’s appointment to lead NaRRA and saying:

“The concern I’m raising is that Anderson’s track record is not one full of blemishes that it will be so easy to attach certain things to him. The corruption argument is not going to be attached to him so easily, right? In my humble opinion, I think they’ve outsmarted us and put in this man to be a CEO and whatever reality is, we need to ensure that the average Jamaican is saying we don’t care who he is and him could have full integrity like, whoa, he could have been whatever. He’s the man who sorted out all of the hurricane relief that got it to Jamaica, whether we know it or not. So I would love for us to be able to put that information together, package it for the ground so that the average Jamaican can get that information.”

JLP Officer Corps member, Daryl Vaz, who co-chairs the Melissa Recovery and Relief Committee, says the revealing voicenotes disclose the PNP’s preparedness to implement delay tactics to slow down or block important national projects which NaRRA will pursue and to use baseless allegations to smear patriotic Jamaicans.

“What is particularly shameful is that the audio reveals that, despite the unprecedented natural disaster which devastated thousands of Jamaican lives and despite lamenting that the recovery effort should be faster, the PNP, at the highest level in their party, at the level of their executive, has been caught discussing ‘delay tactics’, which their executive member confessed they would probably implement. This behaviour by the PNP is most disgraceful but not surprising because we have seen these delay tactics implemented by the PNP before, to the detriment of Jamaicans.”

Vaz described the PNP executive member’s commitment to continue playing the political ball game concerning NaRRA as scandalous.

“Let us pause for a moment and recall that the Government has fast-tracked legislation to help rebuild communities and Jamaican lives in the aftermath of the devastating Category 5 Hurricane Melissa, and here is a PNP executive member caught on tape committing to ‘playing the ball game of politics’ with the people’s livelihood and the wellbeing of their communities. The obstructionist posture of the PNP on the issue of NaRRA and the Government’s bid to assist Jamaica to recover strongly and in a speedy manner is an utter disgrace,” he said.

He noted that the lamentation by another PNP executive member that corruption cannot be easily attached to Major General Anderson is also despicable and revealing, and confirms the PNP’s willingness to weaponise corruption without a credible basis and attempt to smear patriotic Jamaicans.

World.title: ‘Highway robbery’
World.content:
New toll fees affecting motorists using the North-South Highway are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

“HIGHWAY robbery” is how Noel Williams, president of the Kingston Chapter of Jamaica Union of Travellers Association (JUTA) Tours, has described the impending toll road rate increases, which transport operators fear could impact their operations. The increases prompted more calls on Monday for the Government to step in.

JUTA representatives, in collaboration with Jamaica Cooperative Automobile & Limousine (JCAL) Tours Limited and other transport organisations, gathered at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel in New Kingston for a meeting on Monday, hoping to get an audience with representatives of the Ministry of Transport and the Toll Authority of Jamaica to share pressing concerns.

But despite being invited, according to Williams, there were no representatives from either group.

Williams told the Jamaica Observer that their no-show was a clear indication of the scant regard which they have for transport operators.

“We are saying to the Government and the Toll Authority, that we cannot any longer absorb this toll increase, because we are of the opinion that this is the most expensive toll anywhere in the world,” Williams said, expressing that many operators already find it difficult to pay fees for certain categories of vehicles on the toll and cannot manage any upward adjustment at this time.

The new toll fees, to affect motorists using the North-South Highway, are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

The Government has published the proposed new rates with a capped toll of $2,610 each way for Class 1 vehicles. Operators of Class 2 vehicles would pay $5,220 one way, while the proposed toll for Class 3 vehicles, including larger trucks, is $7,830.

Williams recommended that the move be put on pause for a year, to allow for consultation among stakeholders.

“I think this is highway robbery by the Toll Authority, and the Government sits there completely complacent and they do nothing about it. With that said, we are asking the Government to have dialogue with the Toll Authority. We are having a serious issue already with what we are paying for one coaster bus to go from Kingston to St Ann and back. One round trip [now] costs bus operators $15,000. We will be asked to pay $15,680 when the new rate is introduced. If we are to do that, then we have to keep on passing on these increases to the passengers, who already have been complaining about what we are charging now,” he said.

The president said that numerous letters have been written to policymakers, but they have never responded.

He specifically referred to some representatives of the Toll Authority as being very disrespectful.

“We sent letters to the Toll Authority about another bus we have in the system, which is the new type of Hiace bus. It has a longer front than the older one, and hence when these buses go to the toll, they have to pay the same money as what the coaster pays,” he said.

“And when you question it, they are telling you that it’s because of the length of the bus. Nothing is put in place to accommodate the service that we provide in terms of transportation. And also the toll road barely has any lights. With all of this, we have to be paying so much money…

“We are definitely calling on the Government to sit and have a look at the situation and to renegotiate the contract so as to benefit the Jamaican people. A lot more people would use the toll as well, if it was much cheaper, but these people are just thinking about collecting money… they’re not thinking about us.“

Williams lamented that those operators who opt to take the alternative route from Kingston to St Ann cannot do so because those roads are deplorable. He appealed to the Government to have these alternative routes fixed.

“Right now, I believe it is a breach of people’s constitutional rights because they have been literally forced to use the toll, which is costly. The original roads are there, but they are not comfortable for people to drive on.

Meanwhile, Lorraine “Oscar” Finnikin, president of the All Voice Taxi Association, was among transport association heads present at the meeting.

He told the Observer that he attended to show solidarity with the JUTA president.

“They have tried their best over the years to not pass on the cost to their passengers but as it is now, they don’t have any choice,” he said.

“There are a lot of overhead expenses facing the public passenger vehicle sector. One is the cost of gas due to the situation in the Middle East, then there are overall expenses through maintenance, operational costs and service parts. With the increase in the toll fees, it has reached a stage where it is just too much for the sector to bear anymore.”

In a statement last Thursday, Minister of Transport Daryl Vaz acknowledged the concerns expressed by motorists, but explained that the concerning toll rates were yet another example of the former People’s National Party Administration entering into a less than favourable toll deal, which does not yield any tangible advantages for the Jamaican populace.

Vaz said the toll agreement binds current and future governments to its terms, but said the Government was moving to have discussions towards arriving at a more favourable and affordable toll cost for Jamaicans.

“However, the binding agreement entered by the former administration has put us in a position where the concessionaire has to agree to whatever we suggest in order for it to be implemented,” Vaz said.

He also said suggestions that Government pay off the toll operators in an effort to discontinue the unsustainable rise in rates, were impractical.

The Concession Agreement for the North-South Highway (Caymanas to Ocho Rios) was executed in June 2012 under a 50-year Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer arrangement.

World.title: Sweltering heat threatens egg industry
World.content:
President of the Jamaica Egg Farmers Association Mark Campbell on his egg farm in Trelawny on Monday. (Photo: Horace Hines)

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — President of the Jamaica Egg Farmers Association (JEFA) Mark Campbell is urging members to protect their flock from an ongoing heatwave that is taking a toll on the industry, even as it recovers from the double whammy of hurricanes Beryl and Melissa.

Speaking with reporters on his farm in Trelawny Monday afternoon, Campbell noted that prolonged high temperatures have been especially hard on farmers along the island’s south coast, where laying hens have died from heat stress. He said farmers have reported losses of hundreds of birds, representing millions of dollars in replacement costs, plus income lost from reduced egg production.

“This year, 2026, the egg industry has come under sweltering heat, and a number of farmers, particularly those on the south side of the island — St Elizabeth, and Clarendon — they have suffered heavy losses. One farmer over there told me that he has lost over 700 chickens because of the heat that is on the land. And another farmer on the same south side of the island lost over 600 chickens. Now, those two figures run into millions of dollars just in the cost to purchase these chickens. And then the opportunity that has been lost is significant,” said Campbell, who is also operator of Campbell’s Egg Farm Limited in Trelawny.

He explained that laying hens perform best at temperatures between 60 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit and become increasingly vulnerable as temperatures approach about 106 degrees Fahrenheit, which is their body temperature.

The JEFA president is recommending that farmers install irrigation systems or lawn sprinklers on the roofs of bird houses to help reduce temperatures during the hottest part of the day, between 10:00 am and 2:00 pm.

“The heat that radiates off these roofs and goes down to the chickens is what really hurts them. Once the temperature comes up to the body temperature of the chicken, the bird is going to die,” he explained.

Campbell pointed out that while temperature-controlled poultry houses provide greater protection, many local producers may not be able to afford them. To compensate, he encouraged farmers constructing new poultry houses to incorporate adequate roof height and insulation.

Other advice provided by the JEFA president involve feeding birds during cooler hours of the morning, adjusting lighting schedules to encourage earlier feeding, and providing vitamin supplements to help maintain feed intake.

“We have to start looking at how we are going to prepare for periods of elevated heat because laying birds cannot deal with heat at all,” he urged.

Campbell said chickens experiencing heat stress often reduce their feed intake, resulting in lower egg production. He added that production losses could range from 50 to 70 per cent if birds remain exposed to excessive heat. He said farmers in cooler, mountainous areas have not reported similar levels of losses because of lower temperatures and stronger winds.

Despite the challenges being faced by some farmers, Campbell cautiously said he does not expect any scarcity of eggs this year as replacement birds are entering production.

“I hate to make forecasts about production because so many I have made in the past have been wrong. But this is the period between now and the end of the year where a significant number of new birds are going in the field, and if the farmers pay attention to good practices, I do not see a shortage because of the heat at the moment,” he said.

World.title: Supporting acts, fireworks fuel A Taste of Sumfest
World.content:
A section of the Sumfest crowd at Plantation Cove in St Ann.(Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Although thousands of patrons from across Jamaica and the Diaspora travelled to Plantation Cove in St Ann to witness the highly anticipated reunion of dancehall rivals Vybz Kartel and Mavado on the same stage at A Taste of Sumfest, the night’s supporting acts proved they were more than capable of delivering memorable moments of their own.

From explosive pyrotechnics and dazzling fireworks to energetic choreography and crowd-pleasing performances, the annual Reggae Sumfest warm-up event transformed Plantation Cove into a pulsating celebration of dancehall culture long before the night’s main attraction.

The night’s entertainment included music from selectors Code Red Sound, C Note Sound, DJ Mac and Baba, Boom Boom, DJ Ashile, DJ Tom & Reavers, and Ricky Platinum, who kept the energy high with a carefully curated mix of dancehall anthems that had patrons dancing from the early hours of the evening.

One of the standout performances came from Ayetian, whose appearance was especially significant as it followed his impressive seven Caribbean Music Awards nominations. Clearly determined to celebrate the milestone with fans, the artiste delivered an energetic set featuring crowd favourites Wah Yo Deh Pon, Tip, and Balance, with the audience enthusiastically singing along to every word.

Recording artiste Marcy Chin also commanded the stage with a bold and unapologetic performance that reaffirmed her place among dancehall’s elite. Addressing critics who questioned her repeated appearances at Sumfest, Chin declared that, “Sumfest is my home,” before reminding patrons that, “It nuh tek bwoy fi do music,” earning loud cheers for her statement celebrating women’s place in the male-dominated genre.

Dressed in a striking red velvet, long-sleeved monokini emblazoned with her name on the sleeves, sheer fishnet stockings, and thigh-high boots, Chin captivated audiences from the moment she stepped onstage. She was joined by a dancer from France and a male performer during Gimme More, creating one of the night’s most visually engaging performances. She also drew laughter and applause after delivering a cheeky freestyle playfully addressing long-standing rumours linking her romantically to Downsound Entertainment CEO Joe Bogdanovich.

Dancehall artiste Shawn Storm was equally well received, earning several pull-ups for his hit Itch Scratch, originally released in December 2025. The humorous track, which marked a departure from his usual catalogue centred on women and relationships, has grown into a fan favourite, with patrons repeatedly demanding rewinds.

He also performed songs including Empire and My Life, while encouraging fans to continue representing Gaza, reaffirming his unwavering loyalty to the movement that has defined much of his career.

Shauna Controlla, Youngwildapache, and Jamal each maintained the night’s momentum, delivering energetic sets that kept patrons engaged.

Veteran deejay Harry Toddler delivered one of the night’s most emotional moments as he paid tribute to late reggae artiste Fantan Mojah, who died on July 14 at age 49. The heartfelt tribute prompted patrons to observe a moment of silence, creating a touching contrast to the night’s otherwise high-octane energy. It marked the first of two tributes to the late singer during the event.

Another memorable appearance came from cultural icon Queen Ifrica, who explained why she was included on a show centred on Gaza founder Vybz Kartel.

Reflecting on the height of the infamous Gully-Gaza rivalry, she reminded the audience of the role she played in promoting peace.

“Me a the bravest fi stand up inna the middle of the war and tell dem fi look out fi the children, and we still a dweet in 2026,” she said, drawing loud applause from sections of the crowd.

The event attracted visitors from several countries, many of whom described the experience as unlike anything they had witnessed before.

“I flew from Toronto just for Sumfest, and every performer gave us a reason to dance. The energy, the music, the fireworks — it wasn’t just a concert; it was a celebration of who we are,” one patron told the Jamaica Observer.

First-time visitor Marcus Bennett from London, England, said the event exceeded his expectations.

“I’ve watched dancehall online for years, but nothing compares to seeing it in Jamaica. The passion of the performers and the connection they have with the crowd is incredible. This culture is alive, authentic and unforgettable,” he added.

World.title: World Cup champs Spain get heroes’ welcome home
World.content:
Spain fans pack Cibeles Square in Madrid on July 20, 2026, as they await the arrival of Spain’s players one day after the national football team won their second FIFA World Cup title with a 1-0 victory against Argentina. Spain’s World Cup winners come back home to a heroes’ welcome in Madrid where a reported one million fans showed up to greet them after a night of raucous celebrations across the country. (Photo: AFP)

MADRID, Spain (AFP) — New World Cup champions Spain began their celebration parade on an open-top bus through the streets of Madrid on Monday, early evening.

Local authorities told AFP that a jubilant crowd of over a million people turned out to celebrate.

The players, some shirtless, others holding drinks, set off on their procession under a blazing sun, along the main arteries in the city centre where a sea of fans in red and yellow were waiting, with the destination Cibeles square.

After flying back from the United States to Madrid, the players were received by King Felipe VI and the royal family, and then Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, before kicking off the parade.

Players passed around the gleaming World Cup trophy and waved to a sea of delighted Spain fans in red and yellow, the day after defeating Argentina 1-0 in extra-time in New Jersey.

Ferran Torres’s strike in extra-time was enough to bring Spain their second World Cup, following a first victory in 2010.

“You have shown your grit, your resilience and your courage, always backed by your technical skill, your control and command of the game, combining head and heart,” the king told La Roja’s stars, who were dressed in suits but changed to more casual clothing for their parade on a hot summer’s day.

“Kings of the world” ran the words on the front of their vehicle, with fans chanting “champions” to their heroes.

Spain captain Rodri held the World Cup trophy aloft at the top of the stairs as he descended from the Iberia plane that flew the team home after clinching their second star.

Later at Moncloa, Rodri said this was the crowning achievement of his career.

“I’ve always said it, winning with your country is the most beautiful thing there is, above all a World Cup,” he said.

“This generation grew up watching [Iker] Casillas and [Andres] Iniesta lift the cup and that we can do it today is the biggest thing you can do in football.”

Many younger supporters were not yet born when Iniesta’s extra-time goal against the Netherlands secured Spain’s first World Cup in South Africa 16 years ago.

Match-winner Torres joked he was “flying, literally” after the team returned from the United States after beating Argentina in New Jersey.

“I’m very happy to see how excited all of the children are… [and] to have the parade and celebrate with all of the Spaniards,” he said.

Spain’s World Cup winners bus parade started at Moncloa before heading towards Cibeles square, where hordes of fans had reserved their spots hours in advance.

A ceremony involving the players and a concert will then be held at the square, the traditional gathering point for celebrations by the Spanish national team and its supporters. Over 120,000 people were estimated to be waiting there.

Spain’s women’s side won the World Cup in 2023, meaning for the first time a country has both trophies at the same time.

In 2030, Spain will defend their crown on home soil, as one of the World Cup hosts along with Portugal and Morocco.

“It’s two for two,” said Prime Minister Sanchez, of Spain’s record in World Cup finals. “Why not dream of a third in 2030, especially with Spain as hosts?”

The Spanish press was running out of superlatives to describe its heroes after they overcame favourites France in the semi-finals before downing Argentina.

“The kings of all-time!” wrote Marca, celebrating a “second star that will now be stitched onto the Spanish jersey after yet another masterclass in collective play”.

Argentina, despite the presence of all-time great Lionel Messi, failed to create clear chances against Spain’s well-organised and more positive side in the final.

Messi had a sensational World Cup but drifted through the final like a ghost, shedding tears at the end.

“The pain is immense, and it’s going to be hard for this wound to heal,” Messi wrote on Instagram.

In Madrid, tears also flowed on Monday night, but they were tears of joy.

World.title: A host of concerns
World.content:
An architectural design of the National Stadium redevelopment project unveiled by the Sports Ministry in 2025.

DESPITE FIFA expressing concerns about Jamaica’s readiness to host matches at the Women’s World Cup in 2031, Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts says he’s confident the country will secure hosting rights, with an official announcement expected in November.

Last October, Jamaica joined the USA, Mexico, and Costa Rica in launching a joint bid to host the 2031 tournament, which would mark the first time a FIFA World Cup would be staged across four countries.

A FIFA delegation visited the island in February, inspecting facilities including the National Stadium and meeting with representatives of the Jamaica Football Federation and the Government. Hosts were initially expected to be confirmed at the FIFA Congress in Canada in April, but the world governing body postponed the announcement until November 23.

Despite the delay, Sports Minister Olivia Grange told Parliament last month that Jamaica had been selected as one of the hosts, although FIFA has yet to officially confirm the successful bid.

FIFA Consultant and Women’s Football Division Advisor Jose Andres Portabella told the Jamaica Observer that while FIFA is enthusiastic about Jamaica hosting matches, there is no guarantee the country will be selected.

“I couldn’t be more excited about the possibility of the World Cup coming to Jamaica in 2031,” he said. “FIFA wants to see football all over the world. Next year, the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup will be held in Brazil, which shows the first time ever that the World Cup goes to South America. It’s going to be a fantastic performance by players, by fans, incredible stadiums, so why not Jamaica in 2031 with the US, and Mexico, and Costa Rica?”

“There’s a lot of work to be done, let’s be clear. We have had a delegation that’s come here to visit already [so] you (Jamaica) know what you need to do. The infrastructure is a key component of hosting the Women’s World Cup so we’re hopeful, we’re excited, and we’re looking forward to seeing what Jamaica does to bring this tournament to the island.”

It’s understood that USA and Mexico are almost guaranteed to host the tournament given their established infrastructure, some of which was on display during the recently concluded FIFA Men’s World Cup. Costa Rica is also reportedly well positioned, having hosted FIFA youth tournaments including the Under-20 Women’s World Cup in 2022.

Jamaica has never hosted a FIFA tournament but it has staged several Concacaf competitions, most notably the 2019 Concacaf Gold Cup, becoming the first Caribbean nation to do so.

Although the country faces a nervous four-month wait for the Women’s World Cup decision, Ricketts told the

Observer he’s optimistic Jamaica will host matches after seeing the level of work and commitment that has gone into the bid.

“When the FIFA team came here we had intense discussions with the contractors who would be doing the renovation and the refurbishing of the National Stadium, and they would have done a presentation which, based on the body language from the FIFA reps, we’re pretty satisfied and pretty confident that we will be in a position to host the Women’s World Cup in 2031,” he said.

“Minister Grange did make an announcement in Parliament. She was pretty confident and so am I, and I want to believe that we will be one of the four countries that will be hosting the 2031 Women’s World Cup.”

The redevelopment of the National Stadium, which is intended to meet FIFA standards, is expected to begin in July or August 2027, with United Kingdom-based Ryder Architecture and global consulting firm CAA Icon currently completing the detailed design phase, after the feasibility study and concept design.

Last summer Grange said the redevelopment would be completed in 2029. However, during World Athletics President Seb Coe’s visit to Jamaica in January she said she could not provide a completion date, although she was “conscious that we have to be finished by a particular time”.

Ricketts says FIFA would still allow Jamaica to host the World Cup even if the National Stadium’s full upgrade isn’t completed by 2031.

“I would want to think that even if — and I’m hoping that it doesn’t happen — the stadium is not completely refurbished we still would be in a position to host,” he said. “Of course our stadium is, maybe, archaic but when you look at some other stadiums around Concacaf, it is still not the worst. And I would think if we can’t get it fully refurbished and we can do minor repairs and minor adjustments, we still would be in a position to host the World Cup.

“It’s unfortunate that we really do not have options like some countries do but this is our main stadium — and, of course, it’s probably the only stadium that could really host a World Cup game — but it’s not that bad. And I don’t think FIFA would come down [hard, even though] they would not be totally happy if the stadium was not refurbished and ready, because they were given some kind of a guarantee from the contractors.

“It’s out of the hands of the JFF and out of the hands of even Concacaf but the Government has given an indication. And, having had discussions with the contractors who did a presentation to the FIFA group in the presence of the IPL [Independence Park Limited] personnel, persons representing Minister Grange’s office, the JFF and Concacaf… we are pretty confident that we will host this major tournament — probably the biggest thing ever to happen in local football, maybe in local sport.”

World.title: More Than Practice: Why Your Wedding Rehearsal Matters
World.content:
More than a run-through, the wedding rehearsal is a chance to gather loved ones and savour the moments before “I do.”

When couples think about wedding planning they often focus on the venue, flowers, menu, music, and décor. The wedding rehearsal, however, is sometimes treated as an optional extra or simply another item to check off the list. In reality, it is one of the most meaningful moments of the entire wedding journey.

A wedding rehearsal is about much more than practising how to walk down the aisle. It is an opportunity to slow down, gather the people who matter most, and prepare emotionally and practically for one of life’s biggest milestones.

For many couples the rehearsal is the first time everything begins to feel real. The ceremony space is set, family and friends have arrived, and suddenly the months — or even years — of planning come together. It becomes a quiet pause before the excitement of the wedding day. As you stand where you will exchange your vows, the reality often sinks in: Tomorrow, you begin a brand-new chapter together as husband and wife.

It is also a rare opportunity to spend quality time with your closest family members and wedding party before the celebrations become a whirlwind. Wedding days move incredibly quickly. From hair and make-up appointments to photography, greeting guests, speeches, dancing, and countless other moments, couples often find they have very little uninterrupted time with the people they love most.

The rehearsal creates a more intimate setting in which conversations are unhurried, laughter comes naturally, and emotions can be shared without the pressure of a full schedule. Parents offer words of wisdom, siblings share stories, lifelong friends toast the journey ahead, and everyone has the chance to simply be present together before the festivities begin.

Beyond the emotional value, a rehearsal is essential for ensuring your ceremony runs smoothly.

Every member of the wedding party should know exactly where to be, when to move, and where to stand. From the procession order to the recessional, everyone should understand their role. This eliminates uncertainty and helps avoid awkward pauses, confusion, or unnecessary delays during the ceremony.

The rehearsal also allows everyone to become familiar with the venue. Questions such as where parents will be seated, how the bridal party will enter, where the officiant will stand, how bouquets will be handed off, and where readers or musicians will be positioned can all be answered ahead of time.

For couples who are nervous about speaking in front of a crowd, rehearsing provides confidence. Walking through the ceremony once beforehand helps reduce anxiety because the setting already feels familiar. Instead of wondering what comes next, you can focus on the moment itself.

Your wedding planner and officiant also benefit from the rehearsal. It gives them the opportunity to coordinate timing, fine-tune logistics, answer last-minute questions, and identify any adjustments before guests arrive. A small issue discovered during rehearsal is far easier to resolve than one encountered during the ceremony.

One of the simplest pieces of advice I give every wedding party is this: Please pay attention during the rehearsal.

It may seem obvious, but conversations, mobile phones, and side discussions can easily distract everyone. The more focused the group is during those 30 to 60 minutes, the more relaxed and seamless the ceremony will feel the following day. Listen carefully, ask questions if you’re unsure, and remember where you’re meant to stand and when you’re meant to move. Those few moments of attention make an enormous difference.

If you’re planning a destination wedding, rehearsals become even more valuable. Many guests and members of the wedding party may be unfamiliar with the venue, so walking through the ceremony helps everyone feel comfortable and confident in the space.

When the wedding day finally arrives, you’ll be grateful you took the time to rehearse. Everyone knows where to go, transitions happen naturally, and the ceremony flows effortlessly. Instead of worrying about logistics, you can focus on what truly matters — looking into the eyes of the person you’re about to marry and embracing one of the most unforgettable moments of your life.

A wedding rehearsal is not simply a practice session. It is the bridge between planning a wedding and beginning a marriage — a chance to reflect, connect, prepare, and fully appreciate the incredible journey that starts the very next day.

World.title: Jamaica received more than 1,300 deportees in 2025, says PIOJ
World.content:
The majority of the deportees, also referred to as involuntary returned migrants (IRMs), came from the United States.

The survey also found that the total number of voluntary returned migrants (VRMs) stood at 852 in 2025, an increase of 52.1 per cent when compared with the 560 who returned home in 2024.

VRMs are individuals who choose to return to their home country or place of origin due to personal decisions, economic opportunities or family reasons.

Conversely, IRMs are those who are forcibly returned or repatriated to their country of origin due to legal reasons such as immigration violations or criminal activities.

In the meantime, the number of Commonwealth Citizens who migrated to Jamaica in 2025 decreased by 3.8 per cent to 3,491 from 3,630 in 2024.

The PIOJ said there was also an increase in the number of aliens registered in 2025, with the figure jumping to 11,029 when compared to the 2024 figure, which stood at 10,146, an 8.7 per cent increase.

The planning institute said that at 49.0 per cent, Asians accounted for the largest share of individuals who requested extension of stay beyond six months, followed by Caribbean nationals at 19.4 per cent, and Africans at 11.4 per cent.

World.title: Ukraine’s drone strikes pile pressure on Russian economy
World.content:
The central bank has had to keep interest rates painfully high to keep a lid on inflation, at a time when the budget deficit is widening sharply. Its key rate currently stands at 14.25 percent.

Businesses typically have to pay well above that rate for credit, and things aren’t made easier by the Kremlin competing for the same, limited pool of savings.

Moscow had originally budgeted to cut military spending this year, Janis Kluge, an analyst with the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, said. Instead, it has ballooned and accounted for nearly half of government spending in the second quarter, he estimates.

Kluge said the bond market standoff doesn’t herald any imminent collapse, but is consistent with other signs of strain in Russia’s financial markets. The benchmark stock index, dominated for years by the oil and gas industry, has fallen 30 percent in the last two months as Ukraine has shown its ability to hit important economic infrastructure as far afield as Omsk in Siberia.

Ukraine has broadened its drone offensive in spectacular fashion during that time. In addition to the refinery attacks that have caused long lines for fuel up and down the country, its armed forces claim to have struck 183 ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, severely disrupting Russia’s attempts to resupply a beleaguered Crimea with fuel, as well as hampering its exports of grain to world markets.

Wild fires

But even that has been overshadowed by attacks in recent days on the fulfillment centers of Wildberries, Russia’s biggest e-commerce company and an essential part of the supply chain for thousands of small businesses.

World.title: 7 times Andy Burnham flirted with Nigel Farage’s voters
World.content:
1) Staying out of the EU

Last year, the then-Greater Manchester mayor said he’d like to rejoin the European Union within his lifetime. But then reality struck.

At the outset of his by-election campaign in Makerfield — which voted heavily for Brexit — this May, Burnham said reentering the Brussels orbit is a battle he wouldn’t fight.

Despite calling Brexit “damaging,” he stressed “the last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments.”

Burnham said his own calls to strengthen democracy would be undermined “if we don’t respect that vote.”

2) Slamming the Whitehall ‘blob’

Burnham has attacked the British state, arguing real power is vested in around 50 people with “London-centric views” at the heart of officialdom.

Though praising the civil service as “full of good people,” Burnham has said they’re held back by a “structure and the culture” which is “too adversarial.”

World.title: Post-Orbán sanctions showdown exposes EU capitals’ red lines
World.content:
A deal is still broadly expected, but more concessions may be needed before ambassadors can get it over the line. Seven people working on the package told POLITICO that several measures had already been weakened or dropped altogether.

The package, presented by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in June, is the 21st since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. After 20 previous rounds, diplomats say the EU is running out of easy targets and increasingly colliding with powerful national interests. Sanctions require the unanimous backing of all 27 EU countries.

“There’s no more low-hanging fruit, with 20 packages done. You’ll bump into individual member state interests more, so you have to find a balance,” said an EU diplomat involved in the discussions, granted anonymity to discuss the confidential talks, like others in this article.

Greece has so far refused to support the 21st package because of a ban on EU companies shipping Russian liquefied natural gas to third countries. Athens oversees the world’s largest merchant fleet and is concerned about the impact on a Greek company that operates ice-breaking tankers that export Russian LNG.

Greece’s ambassador warned that the measure could prompt vessels to reflag and move to jurisdictions where the rules would be even harder to enforce, according to two further diplomats involved in the discussions.

“We’re trying to find a way out of this, but what this [issue with Greece] shows is that we’re starting to collide with some key economic interests,” said a fourth diplomat.

World.title: Lifting Russian athletes ban only helps Putin, Ukraine tells IOC
World.content:
“Why now? I have no answer on this question. I can’t see any reason for it,” said Bidnyi, a former bodybuilder. “Undermining the collective pressure that the international community has been building against the aggressor … it’s not a very honorable role for this organization.”

The IOC said that the reversal did not represent any change in its view of Russia’s war in Ukraine, which it still condemns. However, it said the ban was relaxed because the Russian committee removed regional sports organizations ​from Russia-occupied Ukrainian territories from its membership, which was the reason it was sanctioned.

Bidnyi said the IOC had fallen for a “primitive legal trick” and that Russia had simply restructured its Olympic committee to circumvent the IOC’s ban.

“We do not believe the IOC fails to understand this,” he said. “This is a deliberate decision to ignore reality, which completely ruins their own credibility.”

Moscow has repeatedly used international sport to maintain a foothold in Western institutions despite its broader diplomatic isolation since the war in Ukraine began. That has included influencing the world of chess, international fencing and lobbying for the gradual return of Russian athletes to global competitions.

European sport ministers have also reacted with anger to the IOC’s decision, with ministers from nine countries — Sweden, Estonia, the Netherlands, Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, Romania, Finland and Denmark — calling for the EU to cut funding for the Olympics.

World.title: Zelenskyy fires top army commander amid nationwide protests
World.content:
"We will jointly determine an updated strategy of our defense [and] steps to continue the reform of the corps system, to fulfill the supply requests of combat commanders," Zelenskyy said in an address to the nation on Tuesday evening.

He also expressed gratitude to Syrskyi for previous successful operations in 2022 in Kyiv and Kharkiv and the 2024 incursion into Russia's Kursk region.

Joint Forces Commander Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi will become the Ukrainian Army's new commander-in-chief, Zelenskyy said in his speech.

Drapatyi is an experienced field commander who successfully organized the protection of Kharkiv in 2024 from a Russian counteroffensive. He was among the first of Ukraine's top commanders to openly support Fedorov last week.

Ukraine has seen nationwide protests since Zelenskyy ousted Fedorov, and it's far from certain that Syrskyi's ouster will suffice to quell them.

Fedorov has refused to take any post besides his old job as defense minister, two officials familiar with the talks told POLITICO. It's not clear whether he has accepted Zelenskyy's latest offer to return to government.

He congratulated Drapatyi, however, describing him as a "breath of fresh air." He also called Syrskyi to thank him for his successes in Kyiv and Kharkiv, calling them now "part of history."

"But we need to move even faster and write new chapters, correcting all previous mistakes," Fedorov said.

World.title: Zelenskyy replaces Oleksandr Syrskyi with Mykhailo Drapatyi as Ukraine's commander-in-chief
World.content:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has dismissed four-star General Oleksandr Syrskyi as commander-in-chief and appointed Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi to replace him, well into the fifth year of Russia's all-out war against Ukraine.

 

Zelenskyy announced the decision after days of mass protests across the country, triggered by the dismissal of Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov over what he said was an increasingly fiery clash with General Syrskyi.

Zelenskyy said that after numerous consultations with the military command over the past few days, it has been “determined how the structure of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine is to be reorganised.”

Zelenskyy also praised General Syrskyi for his contribution to Ukraine’s defence.

“It is a fact that Oleksandr Syrskyi ensured Ukraine’s success in the defence of Kyiv, in the Kharkiv offensive and in the Kursk operation,” Zelenskyy said.

“The defence of Ukraine continues, and every soldier deserves to be treated with respect,” he added, referring to widespread criticism of Syrskyi's military management style and lack of support in the military.

“We all share the same desire, to defeat the enemy and to create conditions on the front line and exert sufficient pressure on Russia to force it to make peace.”

FILE: Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left, listens to Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi's report during his visit in Izium, Kharkiv region, Ukraine, Wednesday, Sept. 14, 2022. AP Photo

General Drapatyi previously praised Fedorov’s six-month tenure at the defence ministry, saying he saw a genuine effort to change long-standing military rules and tackle problems the system had grown used to ignoring.

Supporting Fedorov’s push for faster decision-making and a change in approach, Drapatyi, like Fedorov, has called for a systematic overhaul of the army.

“The military needs change, but without justice, no change will make sense to the people who carry this war on their shoulders every day,” the general said in a Facebook post last Thursday, backing Fedorov the day after his dismissal.

“A commander has no right to remain silent about problems, especially when their cost is measured in lost opportunities, time and human lives," Drapatyi said.

"Silence does not protect the army, it only allows mistakes to accumulate until they become much more difficult to correct.”

Who is Ukraine’s new commander in chief?

Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi has built a reputation as a favourite among civil society activists and many in the military.

He had been leading the Joint Forces, the newly-created command covering the front line in and around the northeastern Kharkiv region.

Since taking charge of the area in autumn of last year, Ukrainian units, including the Khartiia Brigade, have recaptured swathes of territory around Kupiansk, which had been under threat from Russian troops.

Before that, Drapatyi led the Dnipro operational-strategic group (OSUV), a wider eastern command that Syrskyi dissolved in October 2025.

As Russia’s initial invasion of eastern Ukraine escalated in 2014, Drapatyi, then a major and battalion commander in the 72nd Mechanised Brigade, was sent into the battle for Mariupol, which was briefly occupied by Moscow's army.

An armoured vehicle from his unit later gained lasting fame after breaking through a barricade erected by Russian forces on one of Mariupol's main streets.

What about Fedorov?

Last week's decision to dismiss Defence Minister Fedorov has turned Zelenskyy’s latest wartime reshuffle into a political crisis of his own making.

The removal of the reform‑minded, tech‑savvy minister — widely supported by civil society and within the armed forces — immediately sparked a wave of anger, with critics accusing Zelenskyy of siding with Syrskyi and entrenched military hierarchies over a figure associated with transparency, cleaner procurement and better conditions for soldiers.

Dmytro Koziatynskyi, a military veteran and protest organiser on Monday has set out a list of demands to the president.

These include dismissing Syrskyi as commander‑in‑chief and reinstating Fedorov as defence minister.

“If by Friday, 24 July, Syrskyi is not dismissed and Fedorov’s candidacy for the position of minister of defence is not submitted, we will begin a general indefinite protest,” he warned.

Zelenskyy made no further comment on the possible return of Fedorov to the defence ministry after announcing his decision to let go of Syrskyi.

World.title: Trump promises US support for Lebanon in White House meeting with president
World.content:
US President Donald Trump pledged to help Lebanon “a lot” during a White House meeting on Tuesday with his Lebanese counterpart, Joseph Aoun, who travelled to Washington seeking US support for long-term stability following months of war between Israel and the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group.

 

“It’s been a very badly treated place and country and we’re going to have it properly treated and treated with the respect it deserves,” Trump told Aoun.

“We’re gonna help it a lot," he said, without giving concrete details.

Aoun thanked the US President for his support, writing in the White House guest book that he felt "deep appreciation for President Trump's friendship and for the support the United States of America provides to Lebanon, its sovereignty, its legitimate institutions, and the Lebanese Armed Forces".

Asked about a full Israeli military withdrawal from Lebanon, Trump said: “They’re in the process of doing that. They’re in the process of redeploying,” but did not elaborate.

Aoun praised Trump’s approach, telling him: “Your vision is peace,” and describing it as his “legacy.”

“I do agree with that,” Trump joked. He then called Aoun handsome and said he “knows how to get to me,” adding: “Now he can have anything.”

President Donald Trump meets with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun in the Oval Office at the White House, Tuesday, 21 July, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein) Pro AP Photo

The US has pushed for peace in Lebanon but has become increasingly focused on a new escalation in the war with Iran, which has further destabilised the Middle East. On Wednesday, Trump said he had little interest, at least for now, in holding talks with Iran’s leader to end the conflict.

Lebanon hopes the talks result in Israeli troops withdrawing from large swaths of southern Lebanon that they currently occupy, and the Lebanese military receiving support to assert full control in areas where Hezbollah militants had held sway.

Meanwhile, the US said operations had begun in three villages under a pilot plan aimed at facilitating the deployment of the Lebanese army as Israeli forces prepare to redeploy from parts of southern Lebanon.

World.title: US appeals court rejects Biden bid to block release of memoir ghostwriter recordings
World.content:
A federal appeals court has rejected former US President Joe Biden's bid to block the release of audio recordings and transcripts of interviews he gave to a memoir ghostwriter before he was elected president.

 

In a 2-1 ruling issued late Monday, the panel found there is a "substantial" public interest in disclosing the material Biden wants to keep under wraps, adding that redactions to the recordings would help protect his privacy.

“We conclude that any remaining incursion on personal privacy from disclosure of the now-redacted materials likely does not outweigh the public interest in disclosure,” the ruling said.

The recordings stem from interviews conducted by Mark Zwonitzer at Biden's home in 2016 and 2017 while they were working on his books. Biden's lawyers argue the conversations were candid, personal and intended to remain private.

The recordings were obtained by special counsel Robert Hur, who investigated Biden's handling of classified documents from his time as a senator from Delaware and as Obama's vice president.

Related Former President Joe Biden to publish memoir after November US midterm elections

Republicans in Congress demanded the material after Hur declined to file charges against the then-president.

Judge Florence Pan, who was nominated by Biden, wrote a dissenting opinion arguing that the former president has a "substantial privacy interest" in keeping the material hidden.

“The conversations at issue took place in Biden’s home, and the recordings of them were obtained by the government in the course of a criminal investigation that did not lead to an indictment,” she wrote.

Biden sued to stop the Trump administration's Justice Department from releasing the recordings to Congress and the conservative Heritage Foundation, but appealed after US District Judge Dabney Friedrich ruled in June that the public interest in the material outweighed his privacy rights.

In her dissent, Pan said the majority's decision effectively clears the way for the recordings' immediate release, making the case "moot."

World.title: Aliyev visits Berlin to deepen energy and trade ties with Germany
World.content:
Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev arrived in Berlin on Tuesday for his first state visit to Germany, with energy security and the Middle Corridor trade route at the top of the agenda as Europe continues to reduce its dependence on Russian fossil fuels.

 

Aliyev met Chancellor Friedrich Merz for bilateral talks before a wider meeting with cabinet ministers.

The two sides signed a joint declaration on a strategic partnership and a series of agreements covering energy, transport, infrastructure, trade and investment, and science and technology — with Germany becoming the second European country after Italy to sign the same agreement with Azerbaijan. A joint business forum ran alongside the talks.

“I would like to express my gratitude to President Ilham Aliyev,” Merz said. “You are creating an opportunity for us to receive larger volumes of gas from Azerbaijan. This issue is also reflected in the Joint Declaration that we signed today.”

“Azerbaijan can supply the required volume of oil,” Aliyev said. “This can be done both through domestic sources and through the trading division of SOCAR.”

Germany has become one of Baku's newest gas customers, after Azerbaijan's gas began flowing to Germany in 2024 via the Southern Gas Corridor and onward connections. Aliyev said he expected annual deliveries to reach 2 billion cubic metres by next year.

Merz described the Southern Gas Corridor as a reliable supply route and said Germany intended to build a long-term relationship with Azerbaijan.

Azerbaijan currently supplies around 12 billion cubic metres of gas per year to Europe, with Italy, Greece, Bulgaria and Hungary among the largest recipients.

"Azerbaijan is ready to increase energy supplies to Germany and other European Union countries as Russia’s energy infrastructure continues to suffer damage from the war in Ukraine," Aliyev said.

Berlin's decision to diversify away from Russian energy after Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022 has increased the strategic value of the Southern Gas Corridor for EU member states.

The Middle Corridor, linking China to Europe through Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey, also featured prominently. Aliyev said Azerbaijan had invested heavily in expanding its port capacity at Alat on the Caspian Sea and that freight volumes through the corridor had grown significantly.

Germany, as one of Europe's main industrial economies and a major importer of Asian goods, has a direct interest in reducing dependence on trans-Russian routes.

Aliyev separately addressed the ongoing war between Iran and the US, which has disrupted regional energy and trade flows and increased the importance of overland and Caspian routes as alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz.

He said Azerbaijan had maintained a balanced position throughout the war and was ready to support any diplomatic efforts to restore stability.

In turn, Merz lauded the Armenia-Azerbaijan peace process, expressing support for a lasting settlement and calling on both sides to finalise the peace agreement.

Europe's reliable partner

According to Orkhan Yolchuyev, director and co-founder of the CASPIA analytical think tank in Baku, the significance of the visit lies in the wider range of sectors included in the new strategic agenda.

“For the first time at such a high level, bilateral cooperation includes green energy, low-carbon hydrogen, digital transformation, industrial modernisation, transport connectivity and innovation,” Yolchuyev said.

“Germany increasingly sees Azerbaijan not only as an energy supplier but also as a partner for new industrial and logistics projects linking Europe, the South Caucasus and Central Asia.”

Yolchuyev said the newly established Business Council could help turn political agreements into practical cooperation, while the inclusion of education, science and cultural exchanges gives the partnership a broader foundation.

Shahin Ismayilov, a member of Azerbaijan’s parliament and chairman of the Youth and Sport Committee, said the agreements reached in Berlin could strengthen cooperation in energy, trade, transport and investment.

“President Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Germany marks an important step in further strengthening the strategic partnership between Azerbaijan and Germany,” he told Euronews.

“Azerbaijan remains a reliable partner for Europe, particularly in ensuring stable energy supplies and advancing the Middle Corridor initiative.”

Aliyev further discussed bilateral cooperation between the two countries in a one-on-one meeting with German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier later on Tuesday.

Steinmeier, who previously served as Germany's foreign minister, described Azerbaijan and Germany as “islands of stability” amid ongoing global conflicts and broader challenges.

World.title: Spanish singer Julio Iglesias sues Spain's deputy PM Yolanda Díaz, demands €50,000
World.content:
Spain’s Deputy Prime Minister, Yolanda Díaz, has been sued before the Supreme Court by singer Julio Iglesias, who accuses her of "unlawful interference with his right to honour and privacy" after two former employees came forward in January with allegations of sexual abuse.

 

Iglesias has asked the judge to order the Sumar leader to pay him €50,000 in compensation over remarks she made on her Bluesky account and on RTVE’s programme ‘La Hora de la 1’ at the start of the year, which he argues amounted to “unlawful interference with his right to honour”. The lawsuit also calls on the deputy prime minister to issue a public retraction.

According to Iglesias’s complaint, Díaz voiced “clear prejudices”, alleging that “sexual abuse was taking place in his home, that staff were kept in conditions akin to slavery and that their fundamental rights were systematically violated”.

The deputy prime minister had previously rejected a conciliation bid, arguing that her remarks had not harmed the artist’s reputation, prompting Iglesias to take the case to the Supreme Court through civil proceedings.

Iglesias has also filed a criminal complaint in a Madrid court against several journalists from Diario.es, the outlet that first reported the former employees’ allegations, accusing them of insult, slander and violating his moral integrity.

The singer’s defence argues that the publication’s editor, Ignacio Escolar, along with several of its reporters, published “false and defamatory” statements intended to “undermine” his public image.

In January, two women who had worked for the Spanish artist at his mansions in Punta Cana, Dominican Republic, and Lyford Cay, Bahamas, came forward alleging that Iglesias had sexually assaulted them.

The investigation, carried out by Diario.es in collaboration with Univisión over three years and based on additional testimonies and documents, alleges that one of the former employees was forced to have sexual encounters with the artist. She claims that during those encounters Iglesias slapped her and penetrated her without her consent.

Shortly after the allegations came to light, journalist Paloma García-Pelayo, who is known for her closeness to Iglesias, said the artist was “worried”, believing his image had “absolutely” collapsed. She added that he was living through the situation “as if he had been killed internationally because of his image.”

Ultimately, the National Court prosecutor’s office decided to shelve the proceedings against Iglesias over the alleged sexual assaults. The prosecutor’s office based its decision on the court’s “lack of jurisdiction” to hear the case, as the alleged incidents took place at the artist’s residences in the Caribbean.

World.title: France becomes the first country in Europe to officially ban social media for under-15s
World.content:
French lawmakers have adopted a bill banning children under 15 from using social media, making France the first country in the European Union to approve a blanket ban on platforms as concerns grow worldwide over the harmful effects of digital content on kids.

 

Both chambers of the Parliament voted Tuesday in favor of the measure, a flagship initiative of French President Emmanuel Macron’s second term. The bill also bans the use of mobile phones in high schools.

The legislation is one of the final major measures adopted under his presidency before he leaves office next year. Macron wants the law to take effect at the start of the new school year in September. However, a review to determine whether the bill complies with the French Constitution is likely to take place and could delay its implementation.

The compromise text was approved behind closed doors by MPs and senators in a joint committee on Monday. Only the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) opposed the text, while socialists abstained.

"Do we decide to impose a blunt, blanket ban on all social media for minors, or do we instead decide – as the European Commission is actually advocating – to ban only the harmful features of social media? We’re more aligned with the latter position", socialist MP Arthur Delaporte said.

Other EU countries such as Greece, Slovenia and Sweden are planning to restrict minors' access to social media: Spain considers banning social media for children under 16 and Austria for children under 14.

In parallel, the President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen called earlier this month for "phased and gradual access for different age ranges" to digital platforms.

Children under the age of 13 would have time-limited access to social media under the supervision of parents, caregivers or teachers. From the age of 13 on, there would be gradual access provided platforms can prove they are age-appropriate and safe for teenagers.

In addition, the European Commission advocates a ban on screens for toddlers.

Von der Leyen said the European Commission would present a proposal on the matter "after summer".

World.title: Russia at Venice Biennale, Brussels cuts €2 million in EU funds: appeal planned
World.content:
The European Commission has confirmed the withdrawal of the €2 million grant earmarked for the La Biennale di Venezia Foundation, opening up a new front of tension between Brussels and one of Italy's most important cultural institutions.

 

The decision, formalised on Tuesday by the European Education and Culture Executive Agency (Eacea) after a legal assessment and on the Commission's recommendation, is linked to Russia's controversial participation in the 2026 Art Biennale.

According to the EU executive, cultural events supported with Union funds must promote and uphold democratic values, dialogue, diversity and freedom of expression, principles that 'are not respected in today's Russia'. This is the reasoning with which Brussels has justified cutting off the European contribution.

Why Brussels decided to cut the funding

The affair stems from Russia's return to the Venice Biennale for the first time since the start of the invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The Russian pavilion, owned by the Russian state, hosts the performance and music project 'The Tree Is Rooted in the Sky', created by around fifty artists selected by the Moscow authorities. Although the pavilion has remained closed to the public, the installation has been made visible from outside via a large screen.

The choice prompted strong protests from Ukraine and from numerous artists, curators and cultural professionals from around the world, who accused Moscow of using its presence at the Biennale as an instrument of cultural propaganda and 'hybrid war'. Kyiv also challenged the alleged ties of the pavilion's curator with the Russian arms industry.

In recent months the European Commission had already warned the Foundation that the choice could lead to the suspension of EU funding. After deeming the explanations provided by the Biennale insufficient, Brussels has decided to proceed with the definitive withdrawal of the contribution.

The Biennale: 'We will defend our position'

The La Biennale di Venezia Foundation has announced that it will lodge an appeal against the decision.

In a statement, the institution stresses that the move had 'long been signalled' and reiterates that it is ready to defend its position before the competent authorities.

The Biennale also points out that the European grant did not concern the artistic event at the centre of the controversy, but activities in the Cinema Sector, in particular Biennale College and the Venice Production Bridge.

'The grant co-funded activities that have nothing to do with Russia's participation in the Art Biennale,' the Foundation says, specifying that the decision 'has no significant impact on the budget, the accounts or the planned activities, which remain fully confirmed'.

Government reaction: Borgonzoni hits out at Brussels

The Italian government responded immediately. Undersecretary for Culture Lucia Borgonzoni expressed full support for the Biennale's decision to challenge the European measure.

'In Eacea's reasoning, no grounds are set out that would justify a decision of this magnitude. This is yet another shameful political and ideological attack on an institution that creates culture and refuses to bend to become a tool for those who like to throw their weight around in the European Union,' she said.

In recent days other centre-right figures have also criticised Brussels' choice. The president of the Veneto region, Luca Zaia, described the withdrawal of the funding as 'unacceptable', arguing that artists cannot be treated as 'soldiers' of their respective governments and that culture must continue to provide a space for discussion and dialogue even in times of international crisis.

A dispute set to continue

The Biennale case is one of the most delicate entanglements between foreign policy, culture and EU funding since the start of the war in Ukraine.

Brussels reiterates that Union funds must be consistent with the EU's founding values, while the Foundation insists on its cultural autonomy and contests the link between the European contribution earmarked for film activities and the participation of the Russian pavilion in the Art Biennale.

The clash is now set to shift onto the legal terrain, with the appeal announced by the Biennale which could open a new chapter in the dispute between the Venetian institution and the European Commission.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.
