World.title: ‘We sent the tech bros to Mars’: the story Anna Funder most wants to tell
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Acclaimed author Anna Funder this month embarks on an Australian tour for a series of unscripted conversations exploring history, power, democracy and other stories the Miles Franklin Award winner has touched on in her bestselling books Stasiland , All That I Am , and Wifedom. “I think the organisers looked at my work and thought, ‘Here’s someone who’s got something to say about what’s happening in the world now’,” Funder says, referring as much to her books as to her recent lobbying of MPs around the work of artists being ingested into AI programs without consent or payment. During her tour, she plans to discuss her books, the reactions to them, and the parallels between them and the present political landscape. “It’s a little bit behind the scenes and a little bit about how to take these human values, and look at them in our world now.” Anna Funder kicks off a national speaking tour this month. Michele Aboud Worst habit?

I have a lot to choose from, but I think one of my worst is that I’m not very good at filing. I’ve got this screen here so that you can’t see my floor – whatever I’m working on, I have in piles of paper around the place. Greatest fear?

That I will find myself in a situation, like one of my characters, where I will be required to say or do something out of fear of the consequences, and that will bend me morally out of shape. My fear is that I would not have the courage and I would be … morally unrecognisable to myself. It’s very hard to know what you’re going to do until you’re in a very extreme situation. The line that stayed with you?

Last year, I gave the closing address at the Sydney Writers Festival and I adapted a quote I really love from American novelist Richard Powers. He has a character in his novel Plowing the Dark (2000) who says, “belief is not the form my astonishment takes”. I said in my speech, “writing is the form my astonishment takes”. He’s writing about a character who experiences the wonder of our planet and people, but doesn’t express that in a religious way – it’s a secular expression of wonder, and I feel that very strongly.



Biggest regret?

One of my biggest regrets in recent times has been that when my book All That I Am came out, there was a lot of film interest and there were competing companies, in the UK, Australia and Germany, and I didn’t go with a very famous icon, (German filmmaker) Margarethe von Trotta, to make it into a movie. Out of some kind of … patriotism, I went with the Australians and I really regret that because she would have made an amazing film – and the Australian thing fell over. Funder beside the Berlin Wall in 1988, the year before it came down. Courtesy Anna Funder Tell us about your turning point.

When I was 20 I went to West Berlin, which was surrounded by a wall, so it was a city deep inside the Eastern Bloc. I was a student at the Free University [of Berlin] doing German studies, film studies and fine art. That was a turning point for me because I had known since I was six that I wanted to be a writer – whether I could do it or not, I didn’t know. And that was when I got to know some people who were exiles from East Germany – they were writers and painters, and they had been kicked out of their country. Funder alongside fellow creatives calling on the federal government to uphold copyright law and Australians’ right to decide how their work is used by AI companies. Alex Ellinghausen For me, that sort of aligned all of my artistic and aesthetic interests, and this political fascination: what it is to be human, how some humans will continue to make up or speak out in a totalitarian environment and then what it feels like to be kicked out and to be on your own. It was also about what it’s going to be to live an artistic life because that always puts you on the outside of things. And then what it is also to look at these terrible totalitarian systems. Out of that later, I came to write Stasiland and then All That I Am and then Wifedom. The artwork or song that you wish was yours?

I don’t know that I’d be able to choose just one, but I am really obsessed with the Aboriginal artist Sally Gabori. I look at her canvases, and I am overwhelmed by them and I love them. There’s something particularly about the ones that are in pinks which is a lot of them. Her work is sort of … coming deep from her psyche, and it so speaks to my psyche. It’s massive and bold and feminine at the same time. If I ever win Lotto, I’ll go and get myself a Sally Gabori.

World.title: ‘I’m gonna die of this’: The hidden cost of former Socceroos captain’s greatest gift
World.content:
SportSoccerAustralian soccer ‘I’m gonna die of this’: The hidden cost of former Socceroos captain’s greatest gift Vince Rugari July 22, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For as long as he can remember, former Socceroos captain Paul Wade has had a gift. When he was 11 years old, newly arrived in Australia from England, he realised he could head a football harder, cleaner and more accurately than the other kids he would play with. Paul Wade at his home on the Central Coast. Wolter Peeters “Goalkeepers always kicked the ball into the air back then. Nobody threw it out,” he said. “And because I was in midfield, I was probably one of the very few that was willing to head it. Right from the start, I knew I could head a ball - even if it was on the top of my head, where it hurt.



“I just felt that this was something I can do. And as I got older, the more I did it, the more accurate I got with my headers, the more people went: ‘Yeah, Wadey can head a ball. This is really cool.’ And then I just loved it.” Wade would go on to win 84 caps for the Socceroos, wear the captain’s armband more often than almost anyone, and build a reputation as one of Australia’s most fearless competitors. He retired in 1997, but continued to endear himself to generations of Australian soccer fans through his work in the media, becoming one of the game’s most recognisable faces and voices. Diego Maradona (right) and Socceroos captain Paul Wade walk onto the Sydney Football Stadium for the first leg of a World Cup qualifying tie in 1993. Getty Not that he thought much about it at the time, but Wade’s willingness to put his body - and his head - on the line was the foundation for his legendary career. Every time he was split open by a stray elbow in an aerial contest, Wade could feel the adulation from supporters, teammates and coaches, and it made him walk taller. “It was a badge of honour. And I fed off it,” he said.



“They cheered for me and they had respect for me when I went back into the dressing rooms. And for the rest of my career, I didn’t mind getting it done: stitches at halftime, coming off concussed and then saying, ‘Right boss, I’m ready to go back on.’” Wade, now 64, cites the motto that he and so many footballers of his vintage used to live by: never let them know you’re hurt. Former Socceroos captain Paul Wade has been diagnosed with probable CTE. Wolter Peeters “That’s what kept me out there,” he said. “And it didn’t matter what happened, who hit me, if I fell on somebody - I didn’t make it an issue.” Little did he know his greatest attribute would cause him so much grief later in life.



These days, Wade’s memory is not as good as it once was. It has never been great: he was diagnosed with epilepsy during his playing career and underwent brain surgery in 2002 to remove a scarred section of his temporal lobe, and that history made it easier for him to dismiss the concerns of those closest to him whenever he forgot an appointment, or couldn’t find something he had put down only 30 seconds earlier. Related Article Concussion crisis ‘My brain was smashed’: Knocked unconscious for nine minutes, this ex-Socceroo is living a nightmare But there were also changes to Wade’s behaviour which didn’t track with the person they knew. Eventually, those changes became serious enough for his family and friends to intervene. “There were a couple of incidents where Paul’s behaviour was not appropriate,” said his wife, Val. “And when I say not appropriate … he spoke to people and did things that were just not OK. We nearly lost a friendship over it. That was the turning point. That’s when we sat him down and said, ‘You’ve got to go and see a neurologist. There’s something wrong, this is not you.’



“It still took probably a year to get him to do it, because he still didn’t think that there was something wrong with him, and he just kept putting it off.” After speaking to his GP, Val began researching his symptoms and saw signs consistent with CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a degenerative brain disease associated with prolonged exposure to repeated head impacts. Definitive CTE diagnoses can only be made after death. But late last year, Wade was told by Dr Rowena Mobbs, one of Australia’s leading concussion experts, that he had probable CTE - the highest level of diagnostic certainty possible in a living patient, based on his history as a footballer, neurological symptoms and specialist assessment. Wade can’t point to a single, major concussion incident which changed everything for him, like his former Socceroos teammate Warren Spink. But CTE is also associated with prolonged exposure to repeated head impacts, including sub-concussive blows that may not produce immediate or obvious symptoms. In football, that has focused attention on the cumulative effect of heading the ball over the course of a career, or lifetime. “When I found out, the girls [his daughters] were very concerned. I said, ‘Don’t worry. I haven’t changed. It’s just that they’ve given me a headline,’” Wade said.



Related Article Analysis

FIFA World Cup Spanish domination shows the limitations of ‘suffering’ in football “But when the neurologist said, ‘It’s terminal. Go and make some memories,’ that’s when reality kicks in. All my mates have been going, ‘Yeah, but we’re all terminal, Wadey.’ But I’ll never forget those words when she said them, that it’s terminal. “I’m gonna die of this. I might not die for 20 years, I might get hit by a bus, but there is no cure. And that was the moment I thought, people have got to understand … you don’t have to have a concussion to have CTE.” Wade doesn’t blame anyone and has no regrets. That’s just what he and so many others who loved football did, and still do. But he is hopeful that, by going public with his story, greater awareness of the dangers of heading the ball can be raised, and the risks can be mitigated. England has prohibited deliberate heading in matches for children aged under 12, while limiting heading in training for older junior age groups. Mobbs wants Australia to introduce similar restrictions, and Wade would also like to see that happen.



“I just want people to know that if you want to continue to do thousands of headers, these could be the consequences,” Wade said. “And for those who are making the rules or should be applying the protocols, do it. Do it now. Don’t think about the consequences of that if you can save a few thousand lives. “Because if I die in the next five years, all those doubters will go, ‘Wow, we’ve just wasted five years.’” Loading

World.title: Cruise boat captain sacked after sleeping in front of passengers
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesUnfair dismissal Cruise boat captain sacked after sleeping in front of passengers Millie Muroi July 22, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A cruise tour boat captain has failed to win back his job after being sacked for unsafe and “cavalier” behaviour including sleeping and snoring in front of guests and leaving unqualified staff to steer the boat. The man, who worked for Queensland business SeaLink Whitsundays on their “Wildcat” vessels from June 2024 to June 2025, was employed as a casual master — responsible for the safe operation of the boat — and was found by the Fair Work Commission to have been validly dismissed. The cruise captain was found to have dumped food into the water while guests were snorkelling nearby. In June last year, one of SeaLink’s deckhands made a complaint about “very unsafe behaviour” from a “current skipper within the company”. The allegations included the man sleeping on the vessel and snoring in front of guests to the point where they asked “what’s wrong with the skipper?”, constantly vaping on board, and making other crew members drive the boat despite their lack of qualification.



Related Article Unfair dismissal ‘Evasive’ postie who drove to KFC on lunch break loses job Several other staff deckhands also gave evidence against the man. Fair Work Commission deputy president Nicholas Lake said that during the hearing, while the man was “perhaps not deliberately dishonest”, he often deflected and blamed others when asked about his own behaviour. “He appeared to enjoy the theatrics of being on the witness stand,” Lake said, adding the man tried to dismiss the evidence of the young women involved in the investigation, calling them “a junior group of girls who have nothing better to do than gossip”. The man also compared a girls-only group chat for women working on the boat to the movie Mean Girls.



Lake said the man’s suggestion that the witnesses were less reliable because they were allegedly gossipy young women was “condescending at best and sexist at worst” and noted he was the least credible witness of all the witnesses who gave evidence. The man admitted to falling asleep on multiple occasions but said it was common practice in some instances such as when the boat was moored and guests were on the beach, and that in another instance, he had taken sleeping tablets before his shift and in retrospect should not have gone to work that day. The man worked for Queensland business SeaLink Whitsundays on their “Wildcat” vessels from June 2024, was employed as a casual master Getty Images/iStockphoto The man also admitted he vaped on board occasionally, but said he did it to help him quit smoking after seeing a hypnotherapist. One deckhand alleged the man said, “I just don’t give a f---, let them die,” in response to a conversation about snorkel control measures, but he denied this and the commission found there was inadequate evidence to prove this had occurred.



Related Article Unfair dismissal Chauffeur who agreed to retire at 65 to be paid $40,000 after ageist dismissal The commission also said the man asked his deckhands to take the helm without supervision despite them not having the appropriate qualifications to drive the vessel, although the man argued he hadn’t put them “in control” of the boat. “They were following direct orders from me to drive in a straight line,” he said. “There were no manoeuvres, they were not asked to change direction, they were not asked to change engine speeds.” The man admitted he had thrown a tray of rice salad overboard during one trip out of frustration with the crew and acknowledged this was an error in judgment as it breached marine pollution regulations. However, one witness alleged it was a more significant amount of food including bread rolls, meats and salads, thrown into the water while guests were snorkelling, and that the man had said he did not want to carry heavy bins of food at the end of the day. The man argued that his conduct amounted to “a number of rather innocuous indiscretions”, but the commission ultimately found there was a pattern of inappropriate behaviour.



However, the commission noted there was some doubt about whether the man had a fair opportunity to respond to the company’s allegations before a conclusion had been reached on them and to have his say on whether the conduct warranted dismissal. “I consider the rushed and appended disciplinary process in this matter was unreasonable and, as a result, caused some unfairness,” Lake said, ordering $5000 in compensation to be paid to the man. World.title: Miners and energy stocks push ASX higher; Lynas, tech stocks decline
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets Miners and energy stocks push ASX higher; Lynas, tech stocks decline Staff writers Updated July 22, 2026 — 11:58am ,first published July 22, 2026 — 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket advanced in early trade on Wednesday after Wall Street was pushed higher by gains in makers of computer chips and other winners of the artificial-intelligence boom, shrugging off another jump in oil prices amid the hostilities in the Middle East. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 25.3 points, or 0.3 per cent, at 8818.60 as of 11.22am AEST, boosted by the energy and mining sectors. The local bourse closed flat on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US$70.07. AI stocks once again were at the centre of the action on Wall Street, and they rose for a second straight day after tumbling the week before. AP Energy and materials stocks pushed the ASX higher in early trade, thanks to higher prices for oil, copper and gold overnight. Brent crude oil briefly got near $US92 per barrel for the first time in more than five weeks because of continued attacks between the US and Iran. It later pared its gain to 2 per cent and settled at $US91.01. That’s up from less than $US72 in early July, which is roughly where it was before the war with Iran. US President Donald Trump played down the prospect of immediate talks with Iran as the two sides exchanged strikes near the Strait of Hormuz, while Houthi militants in Yemen threatened shipping in the Red Sea.



Local oil giants Woodside and Santos rose in early trade, up 0.6 and 0.8 per cent, respectively, while local refiners Ampol and Viva Energy both added 1.2 per cent. Coal producer Yancoal gained 1.7 per cent as higher oil prices boost demand for coal as a fossil fuel alternative. Mining heavyweights BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue jumped 3 per cent, 2.4 per cent and 2 per cent, respectively, after copper futures jumped 3.3 per cent. After demand for iron ore peaked, the mining giants have pivoted to the red metal to become their main earnings driver. Related Article Opinion

Online shopping $900 million fines look like the cost of doing business for giant shopping apps Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Meanwhile, gold prices held their gains as traders monitored the war-induced threats to energy supply routes that risk stoking inflation and putting pressure on the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates. Bullion was trading at about $US4080 an ounce, after gaining almost 2 per cent the previous session. Northern Star Resources rose 2.5 per cent, while Evolution Mining jumped 4.2 per cent. South32 climbed a further 3.7 per cent, adding to its 6.6 per cent rally on Tuesday. The mining outlier this morning was Lynas Rare Earths, which slumped 6.2 per cent after the company revealed in a trading update a more than 10 per cent slump in its output of NdPR – an important alloy blend of rare earths elements crucial for making the strong magnets that power the traction motors used in electric cars and wind turbines – in the June quarter compared to a year ago, due to issues at its new Mount Weld water recycling plants and ore concentrate quality issues.



While rising oil prices boosted energy stocks, the flip side is threatening a re-acceleration of inflation, which in turn could push the US Federal Reserve and other central banks to raise interest rates, slowing economies and undercutting prices for stocks and other investments. Real estate investment trusts, which tend to suffer when rising rates boost the returns of bonds, were trading lower, with warehouse and AI data centre owner Goodman Group down 1.2 per cent, Westfield shopping centres landlord Scentre down 0.5 per cent and Vicinity down 1.1 per cent. Healthcare stocks also declined, with biotech giant CSL down 1.9 per cent and Chemist Warehouse owner Sigma Healthcare slipping 1.42 per cent. Tech stocks gave back their gains from Tuesday, with software makers bearing the brunt of the losses. Xero, the nation’s biggest tech stock, lost 4 per cent. WiseTech fell 2 per cent after saying it bought a developer of AI-powered supply chain risk and compliance intelligence technology for $10 million and shares. Technology One slid 3 per cent. Wesfarmers slipped 0.7 per cent after the conglomerate said it would spend between $645 million and $715 million to expand the Mount Holland lithium mine and concentrator with its partner, Sociedad Quimica y Minera de Chile. It will pay for the investment using existing cash and debt facilities.



The big four banks were slightly higher in early trade. CBA was up 0.3 per cent, Westpac and National Australia Bank both rose 0.4 per cent and ANZ Bank edged up 0.1 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump wants to make his trade wall bigger and better than ever before Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist On Wall Street overnight, the S&P 500 climbed 0.9 per cent. The Dow Jones added 385 points, or 0.7 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 1.3 per cent. AI stocks once again were at the centre of the action, and they rose for a second straight day after tumbling the week before. After rocketing higher because of the boom in investment in AI chips and data centres, they’ve come under pressure in recent weeks on worries that they shot too high. Concerns are also weighing that investment in AI may fall off if it doesn’t produce as much profit as hoped.



Micron Technology jumped 12.2 per cent and added to its 1.9 per cent gain from the day before, coming off its 13.3 per cent drop from last week. Nvidia added 2 per cent; they were the two strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. On Wall Street, several stronger-than-expected profit reports from big US companies also helped the market higher. 3M climbed 7.3 per cent after topping analysts’ expectations for both profit and revenue in the latest quarter. It also raised its forecast for profit over the full year of 2026. Hasbro rallied 8.8 per cent after the toy maker said its Magic: The Gathering game topped $US500 million in revenue for a quarter for the first time. It also raised its revenue forecast for the year. General Motors cruised 4.9 per cent higher after the automaker’s profit and revenue for the latest quarter beat analysts’ expectations and CEO Mary Barra said demand in North America remains strong. Alphabet slid 1.5 per cent after Google released a trio of cheaper versions of its Gemini AI model, but shared no timing updates for the flagship Pro model that has already delayed its launch by several weeks.

World.title: The real oil shock from the Iran war might be just beginning
World.content:
BusinessMarketsMiddle East at war Opinion The real oil shock from the Iran war might be just beginning Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist July 22, 2026 — 11:57am

July 22, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A new front has opened in the war in the Middle East, global oil and refined product inventories are tumbling and oil and gasoline prices are spiking again. So much for all that winning. After the 60-day ceasefire agreement was signed by the United States and Iran last month and the Strait of Hormuz reopened, shipments of crude oil from the Gulf recommenced and oil and gasoline prices fell sharply, with Brent crude trading (briefly) below $US70 a barrel. Maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has ground to a halt yet again, raising concerns of another supply shock. AP The oil market, which had been helped by the release of about 300 million barrels from strategic reserves and China’s halving of its imports, appeared to be recovering rapidly. Global oil inventories rose by 21 million barrels in June, the first increase since the outbreak of the war in February. The breakdown of the ceasefire late last month initially had only a modest impact on oil prices, which edged up towards, and then above, $US80 a barrel as the hostilities resumed and intensified.



On Monday, however, with the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed again, the Iran-aligned Houthis emailed most of the world’s major shipping companies, threatening to attack ships attempting to export oil from Red Sea ports via the Bab el-Mandeb strait. The Saudis have been using their pipelines and their port at Yanbu to ship about 4 million barrels a day – compared with only about a million barrels a day before the war broke out – via the Red Sea, with about 2.5 million barrels a day heading south, via the Bab el-Mandeb, to Asian buyers and the rest travelling the far longer route via the Suez Canal (which can’t handle the larger tankers) at the northern end of the sea. The oil price immediately broke through $US90 a barrel. The world is now far more vulnerable than it was in the earlier phase of the war.



The International Energy Agency’s July oil market report said that about three quarters of the 400 million barrels of strategic oil reserves that its members agreed to release in March have been released. What’s left of that commitment could be exhausted within weeks. The oil shock definitely isn’t over and, indeed, with no obvious way for the US to gracefully retreat from the conflict it chose to start, the real shock might just be getting underway. The ceasefire did produce a surge in oil “on the water” for the first time since February, but it also produced a revival in demand, which had previously been reduced as the war pushed up prices. Both OECD and non-OECD oil stocks fell again last month – by a combined total of roughly 100 million barrels – and Washington’s strategic reserve has fallen to its lowest level in more than 40 years. More threatening is the position in refined products. Businesses and consumers don’t consume oil, but its derivatives like petrol, diesel jet fuels and fertilisers.



The margins on refined products hit four-year highs earlier this month, even when crude was trading just above $US70 a barrel. Exports from the Persian Gulf of refined products were less than half their prewar levels last month, even as crude flows were running at about 75 per cent of prewar levels again. That disparity is partly due to the combination of Iranian attacks on Middle East refineries and the depletion of their inventories. But stocks have also been hit by the success of Ukraine’s targeting of Russian refineries and oil industry infrastructure, which has forced Russia – previously the world’s second-largest exporter of diesel – not just to halt exports of diesel refined products, but to start importing them. That has subtracted supply and added demand to the market for refined products, as has a shift in China’s energy security strategy. During the war, China nearly halved its imports of crude, taking about 5 million barrels a day of demand out of the market while restricting exports of refined products.



With a strategic reserve of its own estimated at more than 1.2 billion barrels, it was better positioned than any other economy to ride out the war. With the ceasefire, however, it resumed purchases of oil to rebuild its depleted reserve. Related Article Updated

Middle East at war Trump to bomb Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site ‘soon’, appears to blame Jordan for US deaths The released strategic reserves and China’s withdrawal from the market are probably the two major factors in oil prices failing to reach the $US150-a-barrel prices that were predicted early in the conflict, which the IEA described as the biggest energy shock in history. The price peaked at about $US126 a barrel in late April. Those buffers, however, have been run down and, with the Strait of Hormuz again closed and the Houthis threatening to shut the Bab el-Mandeb, supply is under an even more significant threat than it was during the first phase of the conflict. The most acute threat to the global economy remains the supply of refined product.



Gasoline and diesel inventories around the world are at or close to record lows – US diesel stocks are, for instance, at 20-year lows and gasoline stocks at their lowest level since 2012 – and global refining output, which didn’t surge like crude oil flows during the ceasefire, is around 5 million barrels a day lower than it was a year ago. An oil tanker struck by the Houthis in the Red Sea in 2024. The rebel group is threatening to strike tankers attempting to export oil from Red Sea ports via the Bab el-Mandeb strait. AP The US had boosted exports of refined products to record levels (with record profits for US refiners) as Middle East supply fell away, but the decline in domestic stocks has seen its refiners’ output redirected to the domestic market, with export volumes falling back quite sharply. With no obvious ability to bring back refined product supply to prewar levels quickly while the conflict continues – the damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia will take months, at least, to repair and ramp up their output – it is demand destruction, driven by price spikes, that will have to drive a rebalancing of the supply-demand equation. Ominously for US President Donald Trump’s Republicans facing midterm elections in November, US petrol prices rose back above $US4 a gallon this week. This time last year, the average US petrol price was $US3.14 a gallon. Diesel is selling at about $US5.14 a gallon, compared to $US3.72 a year ago.



Related Article Oil These are the corporate gamblers who never waste a good energy crisis The oil shock – and more particularly the downstream effects of that shock on refined product prices and supply – definitely isn’t over and, indeed, with no obvious way for the US to gracefully retreat from the conflict it chose to start, the real shock might just be getting underway. That has implications for global economic activity and for inflation rates around the world. The drop in the US inflation last month from 4.2 per cent to 3.5 per cent as the ceasefire took hold and oil and gasoline prices fell illustrated how significant the impact of the war has been on businesses and households. Trump, of course, says he isn’t worried about the escalation and broadening of Middle East hostilities, even as he professed no interest in restarting negotiations with Iran.



And if the Houthis do close the Red Sea? “If something like that happens, we take care of it,” he said. “We’ll take care of it”: Donald Trump says he isn’t worried about the escalation and broadening of Middle East hostilities. AP The US has done such a great job of taking care of the Strait of Hormuz that less than a handful of tankers now risk the passage each day. “If we left tomorrow, we had a big, we had a big success. But we’re not leaving tomorrow,” Trump said this week. Trump defines success and winning differently to the rest of us.



Every day that the two straits remain closed and oil and refined product prices stay elevated underscores how unsuccessful – and humiliating – Trump’s excursion in the Middle East has been, and how costly it is – not just for the US, but for the rest of the world. World.title: Eight editorial jobs on the line at news website Stuff
World.content:
Stuff Digital has confirmed that up to eight journalism jobs could go as it pursues a "simplified structure" in its editorial team.

In a statement, the media company said it had begun consultation with some of its editorial team across its national newsrooms.

If the proposal goes ahead, it may result in the loss of eight staff, from a total Stuff Group editorial headcount of more than 300.

"The proposal is to invest in new roles in our In-Depth journalism team and in our specialist content areas," said the company.

Members of Stuff Digital's live news and commissioning teams were called into meetings today regarding the proposed changes.

It's understood the staff involved were emailed on Tuesday advising them of a meeting on Wednesday with HR, Stuff Digital editor in chief Keith Lynch and an E tū union rep.

Those invited included members of Stuff Digital's live news and commissioning teams from across the country.

RNZ has approached Stuff Digital and E tū for comment.

In 2024, the media company was divided in two - Stuff Digital and Masthead Publishing which runs newspaper brands and their own websites.

Last year, Trade Me announced it was taking a 50 percent take in Stuff Digital.

Stuff Group owner and chief executive Sinead Boucher bought Stuff from its Australian owners Nine Entertainment for $1 in 2020.

Stuff Group owner and chief executive Sinead Boucher supplied by Stuff.co.nz

In an email that was sent to staff, seen by RNZ, staff were told that at the meeting they would be provided with "information and details on what is being proposed and why".

"After the meeting you will receive documentation outlining the proposed changes for your consideration. We will then commence a period of consultation with you, where you will be able to ask questions, provide feedback, and seek advice, before any decisions are made.

"You're welcome to ask questions at the meeting, or simply listen and take the information away to consider in your own time."

The email said no decisions had been made.

World.title: Vector's majority shareholder says electricity market 'failing consumers'
World.content:
The majority shareholder of Auckland's lines company says the electricity market is failing consumers and is calling for more competition and regulatory reform to address market shortcomings.

Entrust, which owns just over 75 percent of Vector on behalf of 372,000 customers, said the government's proposed Winter Energy Reliability Obligation policy was an indication New Zealand's electricity market was failing consumers.

The obligation put forward by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) was meant to address dry year risk by ensuring major generators and users secured sufficient supply to meet peak winter demands.

"The whole reliability obligation that the government's putting in is actually the indication that the market is failing consumers, and something needs to happen," Entrust chair Denise Lee said.

"The current system is failing to deliver reliability or affordability. Under-investment in new and backup generation has left the country vulnerable to supply shortages and sharp price spikes during dry years."

Lee said the Electricity Authority had been too cautious in addressing structural failings in the market, which had resulted in the need for government intervention.

She said new obligations should be applied to the four large incumbent gentailers - Contact, Genesis, Mercury and Meridian - as well as Tiwai Smelter.

"These parties have the scale and market power to meaningfully address dry-year risk."

She said Entrust considered dry-year risk to be part of a broader competition problem in a market dominated by four large, incumbent gentailers.

"If we do have a genuinely competitive market, why are we seeing persistent under-investment and lack of building that generation capacity much later than we all should. That's the very definition of keeping a market perennially tight.

"There needs to be a stronger focus on reducing barriers for smaller and independent generators."

Lee said the electricity market appeared to lurch from one energy crisis to the next, which was an unacceptable situation for a country with New Zealand's natural resources.

"The result has been higher wholesale prices and annual increases in gentailer profits, which is not a good outcome for households, businesses, or the wider economy."

She said New Zealand had the natural resources to deliver reliable, affordable electricity and support energy-intensive industries on the world stage.

World.title: Petition opposes Christchurch council's extra funding for cathedral
World.content:
More than 18,600 people are calling for the Christchurch City Council to reverse its plan to spend an extra $15m on the city's iconic cathedral.

The council agreed in May to contribute the additional money from its $44m surplus towards Christ Church Cathedral's rebuild, as long as central government and the Anglican Church do the same.

The rebuild of the earthquake-damaged building has been on hold since 2024 because of a $45m funding shortfall.

The council money depends on the government also contributing at least $15m and the church showing it can complete the project, after its budget was revised to $219m when costs blew out to $248m.

A petition by local James Pawson is calling for the city council's decision to be revoked and this year's 7.35 percent rates rise to be revisited.

"The restoration of the cathedral is indeed an important cultural and historical project yet it raises critical questions around funding priorities and equity, especially in an economic climate where many residents are already facing financial hardships," the petition said.

"The decision to allocate $15 million of ratepayer money to a project that should arguably be funded by the Anglican Church sends the wrong message to the people of Christchurch who are directly affected by this rates increase."

On Wednesday morning the petition had received 18,650 signatures.

The Christchurch City Council said it would not comment as it had not formally received the petition.

Christ Church Cathedral Reinstatement Ltd chair Steve Wakefield said a range of views existed regarding the cathedral's future including strong support for restoration.

"A common theme is that [Cathedral] Square cannot be revitalised without the cathedral being reopened. The council has considered community input and made its decision, which is contingent on central government support for the reinstatement, and we are all working toward that outcome," he said.

Only 14 percent of submitters supported further funding for the cathedral during annual plan consultation.

The city council has already committed $10m to the project via a ratepayer levy.

In May, 12 councillors voted in favour of the extra $15m of support. Two abstained and three councillors - Celeste Donovan, Yani Johanson and Andrei Moore - voted against it.

At that meeting, Cr Moore accused other councillors of ignoring public feedback.

"Fourteen percent of the respondents supported funding the cathedral and our response to that has been not only to fund $15 million to the cathedral but also to expedite that to the annual plan rather than the long-term plan that we asked them about in the first place, which will leave many wondering what the point was in having their say in the first place," he said.

The council also voted to support two other projects - $15m for upgrading and quake-strengthening Canterbury Museum, and $4m for the Christchurch School of Music.

World.title: PNG's East New Britain province devastated by unfolding maritime tragedy
World.content:
People in Papua New Guinea's East New Britain province are coming to terms with an unfolding maritime tragedy that could be among the country's worst ever.

As hopes fade for the rescue of any of the 27 people missing at sea after their two boats capsized over the weekend, authorities are pleading with the public to take heed of weather warnings before going to sea.

The group set off in two boats on Saturday from the Duke of York group of islands to Kokopo, the capital of East New Britain province on Saturday.

The Provincial Disaster Committee said the vessels capsized that afternoon during rough seas and bad weather, and a search was immediately initiated, using both air and sea capabilities.

One of the boats was located off the west coast of neighbouring New Ireland province, far off the intended journey's course.

"That's when they found the first body, the other day, and then this morning (Wednesday) they found a second body there," local MP Jelta Wong of Gazelle Open said.

"So we've come to realising that we are now going to search for the bodies, just to give closure to the families of East New Britain."

Up to 17 children involved

Two survivors, who the provincial government says were skippers, are reported to have made it ashore on the mainland at Baii Village, Kombiu, on Saturday night.

Police took the pair to Kokopo Police Station, where they were kept and interviewed as part of the ongoing response.

Despite some disruptions due to ongoing bad weather, the search has continued, with as many as 17 children understood to be among the missing.

"The devastation and realisation that children were involved, it really affects us," Wong told RNZ Pacific.

PNG recently strengthened its maritime regulations so that basic precautions and safety standards are in place on boats travelling by sea, but Wong said they were not being adequately enforced or adhered to.

"This is what we as a province have to look at, to try and implement them and make sure the new regulations are enforced for the good of the travelling public.

"With the new regulations, GPS will be compulsory, life-jackets will be compulsory, and there'll be heavy penalties and fines (for non-compliance)."

Weather and maritime warnings

In recent months, local authorities have increased their advisories on weather and maritime conditions, particularly as sustained stronger winds have increased in the developing El Nino weather phase.

PNG's Disaster and Emergency Office had warned about sea travel in their advisories over the recent bad weather in the region, which Wong said he'd sent to his network to raise awareness.

Wong said people must take heed of them before travelling by sea.

"Sometimes because we are complacent in our thinking and how we travel. Every day our people travel by sea. They kind of ignore the warnings and look at the weather themselves and then they think it's okay," Wong said.

"But you don't realise the weather can change automatically, quickly. That's how we get these tragedies."

Meanwhile, three people are missing in a separate boating incident in the same Niugini Islands region.

World.title: Wait times for young people seeking mental health support to be made public
World.content:
The mental health minister says the government will begin publicly reporting wait times for young people accessing mental health support.

Matt Doocey said he had listened to calls for greater transparency, and the next quarterly report on mental health targets would include youth wait times.

"When I introduced these targets, I was clear that their purpose was to improve transparency and accountability," he said.

"There is nothing that holds me more accountable than publicly reporting how we are tracking for everyone to see."

He said including this metric was "common sense", alongside regional and ethnicity data.

"We know mental health is one of the biggest challenges facing young New Zealanders today, and I am determined to pull every lever available to ensure they can get the support they need."

It comes after a public call from the Mental Health Foundation in June for data to be collected on youth access to services.

"For Māori and young people, their mental health is getting worse, and we are losing ground," it said. "That's why we're disappointed the results have no data on access to services for young people."

Meanwhile, a recent survey had shown only 3.7 percent of young people who needed support said they struggled to access it because they couldn't get an appointment.

Twenty-nine percent said they did not know where to get help, and more than 35 percent said they were too embarrassed to seek it.

"That tells us our work must go beyond increasing access," Doocey said. "We also need to make sure young people know where to go for help and feel confident asking for it."

"I want to especially thank the Mental Health Foundation for their advocacy in ensuring the youth data is publicly released."

As of the most recent quarter the below is how youth are tracking against the targets:

77.3 percent of young people accessing specialist mental health services within 3 weeks

79.5 percent of young people are accessing primary mental health support within 1 week

73.1 percent of young people are being admitted, transferred or discharged from an emergency department within six hours

Chief executive of the Mental Health Foundation Shaun Robinson. Chris Skelton / Stuff

Shaun Robinson, chief executive of the Mental Health Foundation, said this was good news.

"The system has had a long-term blind spot around responding to young people's health needs, which has been enraging me and many people in the mental health sector, because in fact, young people are experiencing some of the worst mental health issues."

He said close to one in four young people were experiencing significant mental distress.

Producing quarterly stats "makes this issue really visible".

"The system can no longer be blind to it, and there will be a lot more pressure to actually respond."

World.title: Lack of progress on abuse prevention akin to a crime, government told
World.content:
A survivor of abuse in state care says the government's lack of progress towards preventing further harm is bordering on a crime.

But the minister in charge says the government's committed to change, and it will take years to make things right.

Survivors gathered outside Parliament on Wednesday to hand ministers and opposition MPs bouquets of flowers gathered from institutions where people were abused.

Survivors gathered outside Parliament on Wednesday. RNZ / Lauren Crimp

The ceremony marked two years since the release of the Abuse in Care Royal Commission of Inquiry's final report.

It made more than 100 recommendations, but survivors and the Human Rights Commission told politicians only a fraction had been delivered and some had been rejected.

As survivor Keith Wiffin handed a bouquet to the minister responsible for the government's response, Erica Stanford, he shared a few quiet words with her.

"I told the minister that the Royal Commission's work, its findings, its recommendations has a legacy," he told reporters afterwards.

"It's not going away until justice is delivered."

Wiffin was disappointed and frustrated about what he believed was slow progress on those recommendations, saying the Royal Commission's work should have been a catalyst for change, but it had not happened.

"For me, that is bordering on a crime," he said.

"That is the biggest Royal Commission we've had in our country's history, representing the biggest human rights issue to affect our country.

"Not only is there slow progress and stall around that, things are moving in the wrong direction."

He pointed to the government's actions like introducing youth boot camps, and repealing a section of law which bound Oranga Tamariki to the Treaty of Waitangi's principles.

Wiffin said a redress system should have been implemented by now, and he was concerned that [. https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/community/588539/survivor-angry-and-saddened-as-number-of-young-people-abused-in-care-increases abuse in state institutions continued].

RNZ / Lauren Crimp

'We stand by our apology' - Stanford

The minister for the government's response to the inquiry, Erica Stanford told survivors many of the recommendations required funding and drastic changes to how government departments operated.

She said the government in recent years had committed nearly three quarters of a billion dollars towards compensation, as well as building systems to prevent further abuse.

"I work closely with my Cabinet colleagues to make sure that through each agency we're changing how we care for people," she said.

"We stand by our apology. We're listening. We're making changes."

The government's work continued, but it would take time, she said.

The minister in charge of the government's response to the inquiry, Erica Stanford told survivors many of the recommendations required drastic changes to how government departments operated. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Wiffin did not buy it.

"Things can move quite quickly if there's a will to do it, and that is the secret here, there isn't that will to do it," he said.

With the election looming, Wiffin said he would be speaking with opposition parties about how they would approach implementing the inquiry's recommendations.

Labour's Willow-Jean Prime and the Greens' Marama Davidson also spoke to survivors, saying they would honour the government's promise to prevent further abuse, and to ensure survivors would get justice and redress.

Minister moved to tears

Tears rolled down Children's Minister Karen Chhour's face throughout the ceremony, and she told survivors to keep up their advocacy.

Chhour herself is a survivor of abuse.

"I'm eternally grateful for all of those who are brave enough to tell their story," she said.

"Whilst I myself didn't tell mine, those who did, did on behalf of myself as well, which I'm eternally grateful for."

Children's Minister Karen Chhour RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Chhour later told reporters the ceremony brought back [ https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/533547/the-full-text-of-christopher-luxon-s-crown-apology-to-abuse-survivors

memories of the government's apology in 2024].

"I was sitting, watching the stage and listening to that apology, and kind of a bit confused within myself because I was part of the apology, making the apology, but also the one being apologised to," she said.

"It reminds me each and every day of the burden on my shoulders to, kind of, be that advocate in that space."

She said law changes would not be a "magic wand".

"It shouldn't just sit with the state," she said.

"Community knows what the issues are within their community, and they're wanting to step up, and we should be enabling that."

Chhour said she had been working with iwi and hapū to ensure they can look after their people, the way they want to.

Human Rights Commission urges government to listen to survivors

Human Rights Commission chief executive Meg de Ronde accepted the level of change required would take time.

But she said the government had not listened to survivors who warned policy settings were perpetuating harm.

"Almost 3000 people came forward and they told you their stories of abuse and neglect," she said.

"They gave many reasons for coming forward, but the most common was they said this abuse and neglect should never happen again to tamariki in Aotearoa, and so we say it is now the government's turn to carry that responsibility on their shoulders."

De Ronde said the Royal Commission's recommendations had offered the government a clear roadmap, but politicians had not committed to it.

World.title: Pride, money and professionalism: Pacific's rugby reality check
World.content:
Opinion: The first leg of the 2026 Nations Championship and World Rugby Nations Cup competitions was completed over the weekend.

Pacific teams featured in both events. Fiji joined New Zealand in the Nations Championship, the first such Tier 1 competition the Flying Fijians have been included in apart from the Rugby World Cup.

This came after both Fiji and Japan were granted Tier 1 status by World Rugby last year, elevating them to the top tier of world rugby status and joining world champs South Africa, Australia, Argentina and the Six Nations teams England, France, Italy, Scotland and Wales.

Samoa and Tonga competed in the Nations Cup, which also featured Tier 2 teams from Asia, Africa, the Americas and Europe.

Other teams competing at the event included Chile and Uruguay from South America, Canada and the United States, Portugal, Spain, Georgia and Romania from Europe, Hong Kong China from Asia, and Zimbabwe from Africa.

So, how did our Pacific sides fare on the global stage? And more importantly, what key lessons can they carry forward into the rest of 2026 and towards the 2027 Rugby World Cup?

Fiji's flanker Lekima Tagitagivalu (C) and teammates huddle after conceding a sixth try during the Rugby Union Nations Championship match between Fiji and England at Hill Dickinson Stadium in Liverpool on 11 July 2026. AFP / Oli Scarff

Flying Fijians

The Fiji Rugby Union (FRU) moved the Flying Fijians' three home matches against Wales, England and Scotland to Europe for the July series.

They used the tour as an income-generating opportunity, especially with hopes that they would be able to attract significantly more fans to each match than what they could do at local venues in Suva, Lautoka or Ba.

FRU Board chairman John Sanday said in earlier conversations that money generated from the gatetakings would be used to help the union with its rugby stadium plan, assist in development programmes, and other needs.

At the same time, the FRU used the tour to promote Fiji as a sports tourism destination, with hopes that the home unions would consider joining Scotland, which has been the only team from up North to make tours to Fiji.

By all indications, the FRU was able to achieve its target, especially with the massive numbers that turned up at the England and Scotland games.

Sanday and the FRU expect to record a few million in profit after all the expenses are accounted for and paid out.

One thing to remember here too is the FRU had to find its own finances to pay the bills, although World Rugby made allocations for part of the costs via it tour grant to all participating teams in the competition.

But on the field, the Flying Fijians failed to spark and get the results needed. That is the worry now and one that the FRU must deal with as soon as possible.

The team lost to Wales in a game they could have won, were thrashed by England in their biggest loss to the side, and beaten by Scotland in the second half, returning home without a win.

The target was to win two.

Interim head coach Senirusi Seruvakula was given the job in April after the FRU parted ways with then head coach Mick Byrne.

Byrne has recently come out in the media to say circumstances that led to him stepping away were controversial.

Seruvakula called for time following the loss to England. His argument was the players only got together a week before meeting Wales and fans should not judge him and the team by the results of these three games.

It was a genuine excuse. For any team gathering players from around the globe, the challenge will always remain whether the players can gel for game day.

Pasifika issue

Time together is something Fiji, Samoa and Tonga will continue to battle over the coming years, unless and until all their players are able to play together regularly in a competition somewhere.

Fiji had more than 20 players based in Europe, playing in different competitions, for different teams.

Their Drua players would have been the only group playing together regularly for a long period, in this case in the Super Rugby Pacific competition.

Samoa and Tonga basically had the same setup, with their players in the now defunct Moana Pasifika being the only ones that played together regularly.

The All Blacks got together a week before they took on France too, but the difference for them was the fact that just two of the players in the current squad were playing in Japan, while the others were in the Super Rugby Pacific competition here in New Zealand.

In addition, the players were together in their different clubs throughout the competition, which made it easier for them to gel in time.

They started a bit rusty in their performance against France but then picked up against Italy and were 70 percent better against Ireland in their third and final game of the July series.

Going for them as well was the fact that all their players are professionals who have been tested through and through, and they brought that into the national team setup.

But Fiji was not able to do that, while Samoa and Tonga showed promise early but fizzled out in the end.

While there have been many negative comments against the coaches, the focus should also be on the players and what they brought into the team.

There will always be differences between coaches and how they work their way around things, but the onus is on the players to produce the results and perform.

Gone are the days when Fiji, Samoa and Tonga had players who were playing solely for family and country. Those days are gone when players were selected from around the local teams competing in the major union competition.

Players back then wore their national team jerseys with pride, they knew what the vanua (people and country) demanded, what they had to do, and they would leave everything on the pitch for the jersey.

Modern players still carry the pride of representing their country, no doubt. But money talks and dictates the modern game.

The raw passion which had fuelled the Flying Fijians, Manu Samoa and 'Ikale Tahi back in the 60s, 70s and 80s is now largely a tale of the past.

Sure, players need to be paid. It is their right, and their welfare must be looked after through proper systems and channels.

But to demand more when you get called up to represent your country can appear questionable.

The FRU is not France, Japan or World Rugby. Neither is Lakapi Samoa or the Tonga Rugby Union.

Players must understand, especially in the Pasifika context, the resources available, the challenges faced, and the financial limits.

They must also realise they need to be playing for their national teams for their own good. Contract offers are more lucrative to those who have played for their national teams than for those solely coming out of clubs.

So, perhaps, the ultimate goal for players should be to play for their national team, as it opens the door to many more opportunities.

Professionalism demands you do your part and leave the rest to those in charge to do theirs.

All Blacks captain Ardie Savea barges over for a try. Brett Phibbs / www.photosport.nz

All Blacks captain Ardie Savea is the example Pasifika players should look up to.

He's the benchmark - he has always stressed the need for players to focus on what they need to be doing. Do your part first, leave the rest for later.

For Fiji, Samoa and Tonga going forward, that is a discussion that needs to happen now.

All three unions must get players to sign on and fully commit to the course. No in-betweens.

Player contracts must be finalised ahead of getting players on tour, with that signed and sealed for good. Player welfare must be a priority.

Anything less will result in disappointment for everyone.

Marcelo Hernandez / World Rugby/World Rugby via Getty Images

On the field

Samoa and Tonga started their Nations Cup campaigns well and got wins at the start. However, they fell short in their next two matches.

Reviews of their matches showed they were in it throughout. It was finishing things off that let them down, especially when the fight for possession was tight and close.

Inconsistency is something that needs to be addressed in its totality by the respective coaches and their coaching teams.

Key areas like winning the set-pieces, making the right decisions with opportunities presented and playing the right game plan in the right part of the field must be worked on.

The Fijians were the most disappointing of the Pasifika lot, simply because they had so much promise but just could not produce the results.

Big-name players were on their match-day 23s for all three games.

Even then they could not find the right rhythm to get the wins in the end.

Poor game management, ineffective game plan implementation and ill discipline stood out in all three games.

Yes, they had the talent, but what is talent when you cannot combine that into a winning combination?

The All Blacks were different. They showed what should have been done and they ended up with three wins, keeping a clean record against international teams at Eden Park to cap their schedule off.

A 50-50 performance against France in their first Test under new head coach Dave Rennie and his coaching team was worrying for some critics.

They lifted that to 60-40 against Italy, coming back strong in the second 40 to beat the Italians in the New Zealand capital.

Against Ireland it was a 70-30 ranking as they raised the bar and won the confidence of some doubting fans with their winning performance.

That performance and the overall improvement seen put the team in good stead as they prepare for their upcoming tour of South Africa, where they will also play four Test matches against the world champions.

Moving forward, the Flying Fijians will compete at the Pacific Cup in September against Japan, Canada and the USA and then round off the year with the second leg of the Nations Championship.

Samoa and Tonga will wait until November for the second round of the Nations Cup competition.

It is critical for all three teams to get their homework done, patch up the areas that need patching up and get some clarity on player contracts and allowances, making sure player welfare issues are taken care of.

The lessons need to be taken on board now, with at least 15 months left to the Rugby World Cup.

World.title: Good Samaritan bill should look at friend group drug sharing - MPs told
World.content:
MPs have been asked to consider how friend groups may share drugs, as they look at a possible law change to protecting overdose call-ins from prosecution.

The so-called 'good Samaritan' member's bill championed by Green MP Kahurangi Carter would prevent low-level drug prosecutions in situations where people are seeking help due to the risk of overdose or an "acute" reaction to illicit or prescribed drugs.

Police could not charge people at the scene after an ambulance had been called, and officers would not have grounds to search for evidence resulting from an emergency call being made.

Drug dealers would not be protected but there would be an exemption for people engaged in "social sharing", defined as gifting or sharing between up to five people so long as doing so was not for the purpose of gaining a "material benefit" (making money) or avoiding "a material detriment" (like debt).

Emma Carroll appeared before the select committee on Wednesday in a personal capacity, but said her experience was also informed by being the operations manager for drug testing service Know Your Stuff.

She told MPs the social sharing limit should be increased to 10, saying that would better reflect the practical reality.

"Commonly, substances are purchased by the gram or by the point and shared within a social group ... could be 10 standard doses of MDMA, or a point of heroin.

"Often this could be shared for up to 10 people within a friend group. I would like to at least consider raising the threshold to 10."

Carroll said MPs should also consider that friend groups pooling resources to buy drugs - which might involve "cash, covering a meal, providing transport, trading favours", could technically be caught out by the "material benefit" clause.

"Putting them under material benefits risks unintentionally criminalising routine social behaviours," she said.

Know Your Stuff's general manager Casey Spearin appeared separately before the committee and pointed to the Ministerial Advisory Group on Organised Crime's findings that police seizures of drugs were no longer affecting levels of supply or use.

Casey Spearin Leah Hollingworth

"The availability of illicit substances is rapidly increasing overseas and here, and novel psychoactive substances are being developed more quickly than we can identify and legislate for them," Spearin said.

She said Know Your Stuff had estimated the law could save 18 to 29 lives a year based on current overdose rates.

"That's enough reason to pass it, we are already losing people."

Other countries like Canada and the United States already had laws like this, she said, and the law was needed to get ahead of the development of new drugs and the spread of opiates like fentanyl.

"Our current approach is akin to rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic. I would consider this bill to be a lifeboat. It's a small one, it's not going to change everything, but it will save lives and will buy us time in a crisis."

"This bill isn't going to stop people from using drugs. That's not the point of it. But what it does make sure is that when something goes wrong, people don't hesitate to make a phone call that could save a life."

She said it would also help with inequities, with a 2019 amendment allowing police to use discretion over drug possession and use "not evenly applied across different communities".

Peer support worker Zoe Deans underlined how valuable the law could be to make it easier for people to choose to prioritise the health and safety of their loved ones.

"Over the years I have supported dozens of people who are in acute physical or mental distress relating to their use of drugs. It may not be caused by the use of drugs, but often the fear of getting help has actually compounded that distress or made that worse for them," she said.

"In Sydney in 2017 I was with a loved one who began experiencing extreme distress while under the influence of drugs and alcohol - and their distress wasn't caused by the drugs or alcohol, but it was part of the factors that led to that situation."

Her friend had ended up "running down some train tracks" and she knew they had drugs on them.

"The New South Wales police ... don't exercise the same sort of discretion that they are able to here, and so calling for help was an incredibly painful situation for me. It meant that I was worried for my loved one's life, but I also knew that it was more more than likely that they would be searched and would face charges.

"Ultimately, I did call for help. My friend ended up getting searched, and they were charged with possession, and it's just a decision that I wouldn't wish on anybody and I've replayed it so many times wondering if there was another way I could have done things.

World.title: Spanish chief accuses FIFA boss of 'destroying the football industry'
World.content:
Gianni Infantino should resign as head of FIFA for "destroying the football industry" by expanding international competitions, according to Javier Tebas, the president of Spain's football league La Liga

It is not the first time he has lashed out at Infantino over fixture congestion and for considering a proposal to expand the 2030 men's World Cup from 48 teams to 64.

"Increasing the number of national teams makes no sense. The football industry isn't just the World Cup, which is the most important event. But not everything can revolve around the World Cup," Tebas told La Gazzetta dello Sport.

Players and fans made the World Cup a success, but the politics shouldn't be forgotten The biggest ever World Cup brought diverse communities together and galvanised its non-traditional footballing co-hosts, but the concerns raised from the start have not disappeared in the positive afterglow.

"In my opinion, yes, I think his time is up," he said of Infantino. "However, he has the support of the system and the federations, so there's not much more to add, is there? There's no opposition candidate, nobody wants to stand just to lose. This is the system and it's rotten at its core.

"He shouldn't stay, but he won't leave. I've heard many people who are against Infantino. They say it, but then they do nothing. I don't know what's worse, the silence or the complicity, because those who stay silent are perfectly aware of the damage football is suffering."

South American soccer's ruling body CONMEBOL has made an official proposal to expand the 2030 World Cup to 64 teams. The competition is already set to be the most sprawling edition, with six host nations spread across three continents.

"It's national competition that sustains this sport," Tebas added. "They are destroying the football industry, which generates tens of thousands of jobs, for an event that lasts 40 days and involves a minority of players."

The World Cup final had a 27-minute half-time interval thanks to a half-time show featuring artists such as Justin Bieber (pictured). (Reuters: Amanda Perobelli)

He also criticised world football's governing body FIFA over the new hydration breaks implemented at the World Cup, which ended on Sunday, as well as the extended 27-minute half-time interval — rather than the standard 15 — during the final, in which Spain defeated Argentina 1-0.

The hydration breaks midway through each half were introduced to help players deal with the summer heat in the United States, Canada and Mexico. But critics say they had unintended consequences, ruining the flow of the game and giving coaches a chance to tactically shift momentum in their team's favour.

"FIFA arranges things as it pleases, for what it wants, for its own interests, certainly not for football," Tebas said. "Hydration breaks are a lie. We have them in La Liga, but only when it's genuinely hot. Here, the pitches in Dallas, Los Angeles, and Atlanta had air conditioning. It was a lie and just a break for advertising."

Infantino announced in April that he would run for re-election for a fourth term as president. The vote for the 2027–2031 period is scheduled for March 18 in Morocco.

La Liga boss Javier Tebas has not been shy about attacking Infantino in the past. (Getty Images: Oscar J. Barroso/Europa Press)

The Football Supporters Europe (FSE) group also called on the wider soccer community to hold FIFA to account.

In a statement on its website headlined "A World Cup that failed supporters", the FSE demanded "structural governance reforms to hand decision-making power back to the FIFA Council and Congress and ensure full consultation with clubs, leagues, players and supporters".

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

It added: "The 2026 World Cup should have been a celebration of the game and the supporters who give it life. Instead, it has too often become a case study in what is so deeply wrong with football today.

"From the outset, supporters were asked to place their trust in FIFA and "chill", but it prioritised spectacle and commercialisation over the match-going experience with key elements of football's identity being messed with. Over the last month, we've seen football contorted to the whim of Gianni Infantino and the Trump administration."

The FSE, accepted by European soccer's governing body UEFA as the recognised group representing fans in the region, then went on to attack "historically high ticket prices" and "skyrocketing transportation costs, bending of rules and procedures, exclusion of swathes of the global population and a lack of transparent communication".

"All this created an environment of confusion and distrust that has severely damaged the reputation of FIFA, the World Cup, and the integrity of football itself," its statement said.

"The lessons from this World Cup are clear: FIFA is unfit to govern global football. The future of the game cannot rest in the hands of a man who has proven yet again that he puts financial and political interests ahead of the future of our game."

AP

World.title: Cameron McEvoy has lived a life between trips to Glasgow
World.content:
When Cameron McEvoy travelled to Glasgow in 2014, he was a 19-year-old "kid".

Twelve years later, he returns to the site of his Commonwealth Games debut as a completely different man with a completely different outlook on a sport that is almost unrecognisable.

McEvoy emerged as part of the ill-fated batch of sprint stars at the 2012 Olympics — the so-called "weapons of mass destruction" who returned from London without a gold medal from any male swimmer.

Two years later, McEvoy won six medals, including two relay golds, at the Commonwealth Games despite still trying to find his place in the squad.

"I still felt like a new person on the team back in 2014," he told reporters at Glasgow airport on Wednesday morning (AEST).

Cam McEvoy says his 50m freestyle world record is just the beginning When Cameron McEvoy broke the long-standing 50m freestyle world record in March, he was at great pains to note that he believes he can go even faster.

"I was super shy; I wasn't really outspoken. I'm in the same sport but the way I'm conducting training on a day-to-day basis, the way being on the team feels now compared to as a rookie, almost feels like it's a new sport.

"It's going to be almost nostalgic being back at the Tollcross pool, seeing the set-up and going through the same thing I did as a teenager."

As he and the Dolphins touched down in the Scottish capital once again, McEvoy is a brand new man and one of only two Australian swimmers, along with Lakeisha Patterson, back for another go.

"A lot has changed," he said.

"I was basically a kid [in 2014], and now I've got my own kid. Things are very different now.

A baby-faced McEvoy won three individual silvers as part of a six-medal haul in Glasgow 12 years ago. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"There's actually a member on the swim team who's 14 [Mia Hogan], so she was only two when I was back here competing last time.

"A lot has happened; basically, my entire international career has unfolded."

Do you know an athlete competing at the Commonwealth Games? Share with us Whether you are you a family member, a friend, a colleague or a coach, share your connection with us and how you will be supporting them.

McEvoy missed out on individual medals at his first three Olympic Games and is surprisingly still hunting his first individual Commonwealth gold.

At Glasgow 2014 he finished second in the 50m, 100m and 200m. At his home Games on the Gold Coast in 2018, the pain was amplified when he picked up bronze in the 50m but missed the medals in the 100m despite entering as the Commonwealth record holder and fastest qualifier for the final.

McEvoy struggled to bounce back from those setbacks, particularly at Rio 2016 and Gold Coast 2018, to the point that when the last Commonwealth Games were on, he was at home considering his future in the sport.

He said he was "in the wilderness", unsure if he wanted to continue swimming after so many painful disappointments, but teammate Elijah Winnington's mental resilience got him back in the pool.

"Elijah had just won the 400m freestyle world title on the back of falling short in Tokyo [2021 Olympics]. For me, I saw that as a massive inspiration," he said.

"I fell short in Rio and couldn't bounce back that following year, but seeing Elijah go from Tokyo seventh in the 400m final to world champion, that was definitely a factor in motivating me to want to take that next step and come back."

ABC Sport will be live blogging every day of the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
